Débats de la Chambre des communes

Content.ParaText: It being Wednesday, the hon. member for Elgin—St. Thomas—London South will be leading us in the singing of the national anthem.
[Members sang the national anthem]

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian dental care plan exists because New Democrats fought for it. We pushed the government to deliver this benefit to millions of Canadians, many of whom could not afford to see a dentist before, and now Danielle Smith wants to take this program away from Albertans. She wants to pull Alberta out and have the federal government hand the money directly to her. This comes mere days after Albertans voted “no” to this in the referendum. They voted for better access to federal programs, not worse.

Let us be clear. The Canadian dental care plan is a fully federally funded and administered insurance plan, so the very idea of an opt-out should be absurd. The Prime Minister must refuse to hand over federal funding in a way that would allow Smith to dismantle the programs that New Democrats fought so hard for. All Canadians deserve dental care. New Democrats will continue to fight for it.
Mr. Speaker, our community is grieving the loss of a dear friend and an extraordinary Canadian. Ruth Foster passed away September 28.

Ruth and fellow teacher Rod MacVicar brought eight students to a neglected creek in Port Moody, 50 years ago. Together, they transformed Mossom Creek into a thriving salmon habitat, world-class hatchery and education centre. For half a century, Ruth Foster inspired generations of young people to care for our environment. Many became scientists, educators and conservation leaders themselves. Her shoes will be impossible to fill, but because of her, thousands will walk in her footsteps.
To her husband John, her family, Rod and the entire Mossom Creek community, our deepest condolences. I thank Ruth. Her legacy lives on.
Mr. Speaker,

Verse.Line: Tomorrow we will hear the same old song, the same refrain.
“We have good news”, and you will say, “Here we go again”.
Strip away the malarkey, the spin and the show,
the numbers tell a story Canadians already know:
jobs on the run, investments taking flight,
groceries through the roof and debts out of sight,
more taxes, less pay, more bills on the way.
And now, another budget with more billions to blow.
Just how much deeper in the hole can this government go?
Mr. Speaker, is your robe waterproof?
Because all of us are about to get hosed again, and you know that's the truth.
Halloween has come and gone. The tricks must end.
It's time to spend responsibly, not just pretend.
Show some respect to the taxpayers who foot the bill.
They deserve accountability, not another spending thrill.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as Remembrance Day approaches, I rise to recognize the retired master corporal Matthew Logan, who served with the Seaforth Highlanders of Canada. Together with his daughters, Juliette and Alexandra, he helps organize Newton's annual Remembrance Day gathering. They share memorial cards that tell the stories of fallen service members. These cards help us remember the people behind the names.

This year, Matthew is sharing the stories of Canadians who died in the Korean War. Their efforts encourage younger generations to learn about these stories and keep their memory alive. On November 11, residents will gather at Newton Seniors Centre to honour those who served and remember those who never returned.
We thank Matthew, Juliette and Alexandra for their dedication.

Mr. Speaker, at the 11th hour on the 11th day of the 11th month, we pause to remember those who sacrificed so much for the country we call home. Each year we stand in a moment of silence, and this year, new names are carried within that silence, because on October 17, four Canadian soldiers lost their lives during training at CFB Wainwright.

Among them was Private Hayden Lykkemark from Langley, British Columbia. He was only 19 years old, a young man with dreams for his future and an entire life ahead of him. The tragic loss reminds us why we gather every November 11 to honour the great generations of Canadians who served us, those who made the ultimate sacrifice and those who returned forever changed.

As we gather in remembrance across Abbotsford—South Langley and across Canada, we stand with every veteran and every Canadian family that carries the weight of loss. We will remember them. Lest we forget.
Mr. Speaker, as Remembrance Day approaches, I rise to honour Pilot Officer Gordon James Strutt from Shawville, Quebec, who made the ultimate sacrifice during the Second World War.

Born in Shawville, Gordon enlisted in the Royal Canadian Air Force and served with the 58th Squadron. On August 6, 1942, he and five fellow airmen took off from Wick, Scotland on a patrol over the North Sea. Their aircraft never returned, and the crew members were never found.
Gordon's story reminds us all that behind every name on a cenotaph was a person, a family and a community forever changed by their sacrifice.
We will remember Gordon James Strutt and all those who served and sacrificed for our country and for freedom.
Lest we forget.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians used to make grocery lists, but now they are making grocery sacrifices. They are no longer choosing what goes in their carts, but what they have to leave out.

Half of surveyed Canadians say they are using their savings for basic necessities, and nearly one in three Canadians surveyed are skipping meals or eating less because they cannot afford groceries. Toronto food banks record over four million visits per year, which is over a 300% increase since 2019. In my home province of Manitoba, food banks recorded more than 71,000 visits in March alone, with nearly 25,000 households seeking help every single month.

Canadians are cutting back at the checkout while the government keeps running up the bill. My constituents do not need another Liberal handout. They need honest tax relief so that they do not need to go to food banks, but can, once more, afford to go to grocery stores.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Salma Zahid (Scarborough Centre—Don Valley East, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, in 2015, Canada welcomed Syrian refugees fleeing the civil war, and many settled in Scarborough Centre—Don Valley East. Some 11 years later, they have become citizens and integrated into the community. They have opened businesses, become professionals and are contributing to all aspects of life, yet their hearts still ache for their homeland of Syria and those left behind.

While the civil war has ended, the suffering has not. I recently joined a delegation of parliamentarians and aid organizations and visited Syria. We saw a country still recovering from conflict. We saw rubble and destruction. We also met resilient people determined to rebuild their lives and their country.

I thank everyone who welcomed us and shared their stories. I also thank the Union of Medical Care & Relief Organizations and all the aid organizations for the work they are doing on the ground in Syria.
Canada stepped up to welcome Syrian refugees a decade ago. Let us—
The hon. member for Edmonton Griesbach.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are working harder, paying more and getting less. The Salvation Army reports one in three Canadians is skipping meals because they cannot afford groceries. This is Canada under the Liberals.
The Prime Minister promised affordability. Instead, he is doubling deficits while Canadians struggle to put food on the table. Canadians do not need more empty Liberal promises. They need results.

Conservatives are demanding a federal budget that cuts spending and reduces the debt and deficits. We are calling for the elimination of gas taxes until Canada Day and the suspension of the GST on gas until summer.
Canadians work hard, follow the rules and deserve an affordable life. The Liberal government is out of touch, its spending is out of control and Canadians are out of money.

Mr. Speaker, on October 29, 38 firefighters from the city of Mirabel were honoured for their years of service. Although I do not have enough time to name them all, I want to pay tribute to them for their dedication to serving and protecting our community over the course of their careers.

Being a firefighter means choosing to answer the call in an emergency. It means showing courage, dedication and solidarity. It means accepting a responsibility that goes far beyond oneself and being able to act quickly under difficult circumstances, always keeping in mind that the only priority is the safety of others.

Among those honoured were firefighters, lieutenants, captains, department chiefs, a district chief and a director, with 20, 30, 40 and even 50 years of service. Every decade represents thousands of hours on call, countless hours of training and an unwavering commitment to the community of Mirabel.
On behalf of myself and my fellow citizens, I want to thank each and every one of them for their work. Most of all, I thank them for continuing to keep our communities safe.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to recognize the thousands of Islanders who exercised their democratic right on Monday in our municipal elections. Strong communities start at the local level, and I want to acknowledge the dedication shown by everyone who stepped forward to put their name on the ballot and those who volunteered over the last few weeks. Above all, I want to congratulate the new and returning councillors and mayors across eastern P.E.I.

Whether in our larger towns or our rural municipalities, local leadership handles the daily services that make Cardigan such an incredible place to live, to work and to raise a family. From maintaining vital infrastructure to supporting recreation and community life, municipal leaders play an essential role in the well-being of Islanders every day.
I look forward to working collaboratively with all our new and returning municipal leaders in P.E.I.

Mr. Speaker, when I go grocery shopping, I am always shocked at the prices. My heart breaks for those millions of Canadians who can barely make ends meet. A new Dalhousie University survey found that one in three Canadians is drawing from their savings or borrowing money just to buy food. After years of Liberal spending, inflationary budgets and economic mismanagement, Canadians are paying the price. The numbers are staggering. Canadian food banks recorded 2.5 million visits in a single month, more than double since 2019, and one-third involved children.

In B.C., food bank visits have also doubled. Seniors on a fixed income, single parents and working families are increasingly turning to food banks because they simply cannot make ends meet. Canadians deserve a government that makes life more affordable, not Liberal budgets that make putting food on the table increasingly difficult.
Mr. Speaker, single-use plastics are one of the greatest environmental challenges of our time. A team of researchers in Trois-Rivières is trying to come up with solutions to address this issue.

Today, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada will present a Synergy Award for Innovation to Julien Bley, Martin Dubé and Tarik Jabrane of Innofibre at the CEGEP de Trois-Rivières, as well as Simon Barnabé and Bruno Chabot of the Université du Québec à Trois‑Rivières, alongside their industrial partner, Kruger. Together, they are transforming our forest resources into packaging to replace single-use plastics. This includes recyclable and compostable paper, cellulose film and packaging that keeps food fresh longer. Their partnership illustrates what can be achieved when colleges, universities and industry work together.
On behalf of the people of Trois‑Rivières, I would like to thank them and offer my congratulations.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to honour Private Shaun Farrell of the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, who lost his life in the recent CFB Wainwright training accident. Today, Shaun's family, friends and comrades, and members of the community, gather to pay their respects at a military service with full honours at the Prince Albert Armoury. I stand with them in their grief.

Born in South Africa, Shaun made Canada and Prince Albert his home. As a new Canadian, Shaun answered the call to duty with courage and professionalism. Training accidents remind us of the real risks our soldiers accept every day, even when they are far from the battlefield.

Shaun leaves behind his loving parents Roland and Patricia, his brother Byran, his grandmother Lynette, his extended family and his friends. On behalf of the House, I offer my deepest condolences to Shaun's family and to those who served with him. His sacrifice will not be forgotten. We will remember him.

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessTitle: Teachers Institute on Canadian Parliamentary Democracy

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as a former educator, I know that teaching civics is about more than explaining how our institutions work. It is also about inspiring young people to participate in our democracy. That is why I rise today to recognize the Teachers Institute on Canadian Parliamentary Democracy, which brings outstanding teachers from across Canada this week to Parliament Hill to experience our democratic institutions first-hand.

These 80 educators return to their classrooms with a deeper understanding of Parliament and a renewed ability to engage students in the democratic process. At a time when misinformation and political polarization can undermine our trust in public institutions, civic education has never been more important.

I want to thank the people participating this week, as well as the House of Commons staff who make this program possible every single year. Together we are helping to build a more informed, engaged and democratic Canada.

Mr. Speaker, just days before Remembrance Day, a 59-year-old member of the Canadian Armed Forces was assaulted while supervising young cadets at a poppy drive in Hamilton. The attack left him with life-altering injuries. I am absolutely disgusted by this violent attack, especially given the significance of the Remembrance Day poppy drive.

Every year, Canadians proudly wear their poppy to honour the brave men and women who served and sacrificed for our country. For a CAF member to be violently attacked while volunteering his time to support our veterans is heartbreaking and completely unacceptable. I can confidently speak for every member of the House when I say our thoughts and prayers are with the victim, his family and the young cadets who witnessed this horrific act.
Our veterans fought to protect the freedoms and values we hold dear. There is no place for this kind of violence in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, Rick Hansen turned an extraordinary journey 40 years ago into a movement that changed Canada and the world: over 26 months, 34 countries and 40,000 kilometres, powered by his own physical strength and the strength of his belief. He challenged all of us to think bigger about disability, about opportunity and about the country we can build together.

Tonight we welcome this great Canadian to Ottawa for a screening of Man in Motion: The Rick Hansen Story right here on Parliament Hill. Four decades on, the Rick Hansen Foundation's work continues to break down barriers, champion accessibility and open doors. Rick's example calls on members of the House to build a Canada where everyone can participate, contribute and belong.
We thank Rick for helping Canada dream bigger and for shattering what we thought were the limits of disability. His journey around the world may have ended, but what he set in motion never will.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is all well and good to watch the results south of the border, but we also have to look at the real problems real people are having here, at home. People are really suffering, and things have only gotten worse after two years of this Prime Minister and his grand theatrical gestures. People cannot afford groceries, housing or gas.
Will the Prime Minister do his job here at home? Will he stand up in the House and announce that he will take action to save Canadians money by eliminating all gas taxes?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, of course, we have repeatedly taken action to support Canadians who have—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
The hon. Leader of the Government in the House of Commons may start his answer from the beginning.

Mr. Speaker, of course, this Prime Minister has repeatedly taken action to support Canadians who are suffering because of rising prices, wars in the Middle East and Europe, and factors outside our country. We will always take action. However, we are taking note of the Conservative Party's systemic opposition to any initiative designed to support Canadians in need.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the question was for the Prime Minister and concerned the rising price of gas due to Liberal taxes.

There are two economies: one for the Prime Minister's friends and another for everyone else. Under the Conflict of Interest Act, it is illegal for the Prime Minister to intervene in the awarding of contracts to companies connected to friends. Mr. Goldberg of Telesat belongs to both a book club and a running club with the Prime Minister. He has also attended two of the Prime Minister's swearing-in ceremonies.
Did the Prime Minister discuss the $2-billion contract awarded to Telesat with his staff?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, for years, Canadians have been able to take pride in the fact that we have a company capable of operating satellites in Canada. Successive governments have supported this company because we believe it is important for Canada not to rely on foreign companies, but rather to rely on companies that manufacture here at home. That is why Telesat is such an important company.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is all well and good to watch the results south of the border, but we have real problems as well here in Canada, real problems in the real lives of real people who cannot afford eat, heat, or house themselves, real problems that have gotten much worse since the Prime Minister took office.

Meanwhile, the Prime Minister distracts with grand theatrical gestures, so my question is, will he actually stand up and do his job in the House, in our country, to save Canadians money by taking all taxes off gas and diesel so Canadians can afford to eat, heat, and house themselves?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister and the government have and will continue to, and I note that the budget is tomorrow, support Canadians who are feeling pinched by foreign wars, wars in the Middle East and a number of external factors, including trade wars, that have affected their quality of life and affordability.
I have to also note the systematic opposition of the Conservative leader and party to every single possible initiative that we put forward to help Canadians in need.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, if the Prime Minister actually believed that, he would stand up and say it himself. The question was about the 20¢ a litre he adds to the price of gas, including with a tax that takes money out of the pockets of hard-working Canadians to subsidize American biodiesel and biogas firms.

In the middle of a trade dispute that the Prime Minister has been unable to solve here at home, he drives up the costs for single moms, seniors and small business people to subsidize the Americans. Enough is enough. There are real problems here at home.
Will the Prime Minister take his taxes off gas so Canadians can afford to eat?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Julie Dabrusin (Minister of the Environment, Climate Change and Nature, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we take affordability very seriously. That is why, in fact, many people in the Leader of the Opposition's community and, frankly, in communities right across the country, are going to be able to, with this heating season, take advantage of the heat pump rebates we have put in place. That is going to be a very tangible way to save Canadians, on average, over $1,000 every single year. These are true savings.
If the Leader of the Opposition wants to talk about clean fuel regulations, I am sure he might like to have a conversation with Imperial in Strathcona. It is right outside his riding.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the question was not about how much Brookfield can get in heat pump subsidies from the Prime Minister. The question was about the cost of living.

There are two economies right now: the economy for those who follow the rules and one for those who make the rules. It is illegal for the Prime Minister to discuss matters that affect the financial interests of a friend, under section 9 of the ethics act. Dan Goldberg, from Telesat, is in two clubs with the Prime Minister, travelled to see him in London and attended both of his swearing-in ceremonies.
Did the Prime Minister ever discuss with any of his staff the $2.3 billion in contracts that went from the government to that company?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, in the House, there are two philosophies that are contradicting themselves. First, the Conservatives are never talking about the American tariffs. Then there is us dealing with the impacts of a trade war, knowing that Canadian companies are key to our sovereignty and the protection of our people. That is Telesat. That is a company we need to protect. Why? It is because we need to have sovereign capability when it comes to satellites in this country.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, there we go. There we have it. Every time they get caught with their hands in the cookie jar, they raise grand theatrical distractions. It is illegal under the ethics act for the Prime Minister to be in any way involved with a company with which he has a friendship.
Dan Goldberg, the CEO of Telesat, is in a book club and a jogging club with the Prime Minister and attended two of his swearing-in ceremonies. He even flew over to London to see the Prime Minister.
Given that it is illegal to help a friend, did the Prime Minister ever discuss this contract with anyone in the government?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it has been constant industrial policy for decades now to support being able to have companies operating telecommunication and satellite services. The Harper government, the Trudeau government and this government have all supported Telesat. We believe that thousands of jobs in this country are linked to the company.
I would like to know what the Leader of the Opposition suggests. Is it more Telesat, or more of an American company?
Mr. Speaker, today is November 4 and tomorrow, a budget named “Masters of Our Destiny” is going to be tabled. The real question, however, is who is going to end up master of whose house.

The Liberals caved to Donald Trump by sacrificing our culture. They used our own money to buy a pipeline for American oil company owners. They want to sell our airports to foreign interests. We even found out this summer that they are toying with the idea of allowing more U.S. dairy products onto our shelves to make Donald Trump happy.
Why does it seem like, under the Liberals, it is the Americans who are becoming masters in Quebec's house, instead of Quebeckers?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, would anyone like to know what being masters of our destiny means? It means doubling our hydroelectric generating capacity. It means major projects like the one at Churchill Falls. The CEO of Hydro‑Québec says that project will ensure prosperity for generations of Quebeckers.
For once, will the Bloc Québécois show it is capable of supporting a project that is building Quebec?

Mr. Speaker, Quebeckers would feel a little more like masters in their own home if their money were used to meet their needs. That means Ottawa would need to reverse all its environmental rollbacks and fossil fuel subsidies and invest here instead. It would need to reverse its cultural concessions and make American tech giants contribute to our creative industries. It would need to invest in housing, in combatting homelessness, and in lowering the cost of living, instead of investing $40 billion in dirty oil pipelines.
Will the government meet Quebeckers' real needs?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, if my colleague wants to talk about addressing Quebeckers' real priorities, we can talk about the Canada child benefit, which has reduced child poverty by nearly 40% in Quebec. We can talk about Canada's national school food program, which helps 100,000 young people in Quebec. We can talk about the Canada groceries and essentials benefit. We can talk about the Canadian dental care plan, which helps millions of Quebeckers.
It would be nice if, for once, the Bloc Québécois would rally behind initiatives that truly help our community.

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow is budget day, and Quebec's finance minister, Nicolas Marceau, has outlined his expectations. He is calling on the federal government to finally pay back the debt it has owed Quebec since 2024 for costs related to taking in asylum seekers.

Quebec is also calling for an increase in health transfers, as the Liberals are about to cut the growth rate from 5% to 3% beginning in 2028. That rate needs to be locked in at 6% annually for a minimum of five years.
Will the government listen to these two reasonable demands from Quebec?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it goes without saying that all 44 members from Quebec on this side of the House will always want to work with Quebec. Take, for example, what we have done in the past 11 months: $11 billion for the Davie shipyard, 5,000 jobs, the biggest contract—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
I am not in the habit of rising to respond, but I am hearing a lot of noise at the back of the room.
The hon. minister can continue his answer.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleagues for their enthusiasm. It is true that what we have done for Quebec is impressive. I spoke about the Davie shipyard, but I could have also mentioned the $10 billion we are investing in infrastructure, including $1 billion for health care infrastructure at Quebec's request. We will continue to work with Quebec to build Canada strong.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michael Chong (Wellington—Halton Hills North, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, four times I have asked a question about the government's fiscal targets and four times there has been no answer. Here is why the question is important. Here is what economist Christopher Ragan said in today's Globe:

Quote.QuotePara: They are doing what is easy and painless in the short run, but avoiding the tougher decisions that would better prepare them for an uncertain and risk-filled future.

Content.ParaText: For the fifth time, will the Prime Minister and the government meet fiscal targets to reduce the deficit and debt in tomorrow's budget?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Wayne Long (Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I have good news for the member and all members across the House. Tomorrow, we will table budget 2026. On this side of the House, we are serious about building a strong economy and the most resilient and diversified economy in the G7. We are going to continue to attract outside investment. We are going to bring down barriers. We are going to invest coast to coast in infrastructure, major projects and housing. Also, as something that party would never do, we are going to make sure we address affordability for Canadians who are struggling.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michael Chong (Wellington—Halton Hills North, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's new national security framework states that Canada needs to “Prepare for all contingencies up to and including war and other worst-case scenarios.” It puts economic security at the heart of that plan. Canada had the fiscal capacity to deal with the 2008 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic, but the government's rising debt and interest are reducing the capacity of the federal government to deal with the future crisis that the Prime Minister says is coming in his upcoming framework.
For the sixth time, will the government hit its fiscal targets in tomorrow's budget?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Wayne Long (Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we are going to continue the work of building a strong economy, the most resilient economy in the G7, for all Canadians. We are going to invest in our country. We are going to continue to bring down impediments to investment. We are going to develop and double our non-U.S. investments.
We believe that we can build the strongest economy in the G7 while looking after those who need support. That party has voted against every affordability measure we have ever brought forward.
We stand with Canadians. Tomorrow, we will be proud to table budget 2026, another step to becoming—
The hon. member for Thornhill.

Mr. Speaker, the evidence is impossible to ignore. Yesterday, The Salvation Army reported that one-third of Canadians are skipping meals or cutting their portions, up almost 30% from just last year. Food bank visits have hit 2.35 million in a month, and that is double from 2019. This is not just some rough patch caused by something somewhere else far away. It is a slow and consistent leak in every household budget. The Liberal government has offered absolutely nothing to fix it. It has an affordability problem. Will Thursday's budget fix it?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Leslie Church (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretaries of State for Labour, for Seniors, and for Children and Youth, and to the Minister of Jobs and Families (Persons with Disabilities), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, any time a child or family in Canada is hungry, it should stop us all. It is why this government made the national school food program permanent. It is why we tied the Canada child benefit to inflation. It is why we introduced the Canada disability benefit. It is why we are not finished.

I would invite the member opposite to stay tuned tomorrow, when we introduce budget 2026. Those guys talk about spending in the budget and they talk about inflation, but they leave to the rest of our imaginations what they would cut. We know that and Canadians know that, because they vote against all of these measures time and again.
Mr. Speaker, if any of those programs worked, then food bank use in Toronto would not be up 333% since 2019.

On Monday, I asked if the government would cut taxes on gas. There was no answer. On Tuesday, I asked whether Canadian tax dollars would stay here instead of going to Europe. There was no answer. The government has an affordability problem and it looks like it does not care.
Once more, will the budget offer anything, one word, one sentence, to help save Canadians money?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Leslie Church (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretaries of State for Labour, for Seniors, and for Children and Youth, and to the Minister of Jobs and Families (Persons with Disabilities), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, if we look at the report from The Salvation Army, it notes that 83% of respondents say that support services improved their family's well-being, and 53% say that it improved their access to food. That is why our government is funding these services through things like the national food security strategy.

When we look at these reports, they talk about services like the groceries and essentials benefit, the Canada child benefit, the school food program and even the work that we are doing through Build Canada Homes to create affordable housing. These are the ways we bring about affordability for Canadians. We are focused on it and they are not.

Mr. Speaker, there has been one consistent theme over the past 10 Liberal budgets: reckless spending. Each budget has delivered record-breaking expenditures. The results have been deficit-fuelled inflation, high interest rates and a crushing cost of living crisis.
Tomorrow, will the government finally reverse course, meet its own financial targets and restrain spending so Canadians can afford to live?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, tomorrow's budget is named, for good reason, “Masters of Our Destiny”. Why? It is because in a moment when our economic security and our sovereignty are being tested at all levels, our government is standing up to protect the country we love to build industries, support families, diversify trade and move quickly to get shovels in the ground and create tens of thousands of new jobs.
If the Conservatives wrote the budget, it would be called “Servants of Surrender”. Why? It is because they waved the white flag before the battle even started.

Mr. Speaker, here is a riddle. Which former Quebec Liberal finance minister said, “Balancing the budget is not an obsession.... It is a basic requirement so that we can move forward with all of our other public policies”? Which finance minister said that? I cannot name him, because he is currently serving as a Liberal MP and as a member of the Standing Committee on Finance. He is someone I hold in high regard, and I agree with him on the importance of balancing the budget.
Does the Prime Minister agree with his MP?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for giving me the opportunity to pay tribute to my colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry.

He did a great job when he served as Quebec's finance minister, and he is also doing a great job as parliamentary secretary. We are working together every day to manage the tariff crisis. When I hear my colleagues talking about all the crises that Canada has faced in recent years, I do not understand why they do not think that we are in a crisis right now, given that we are in the midst of a trade war, dealing with job losses and trying to create economic growth, when the U.S. administration wants to—
The hon. member for Richmond—Arthabaska—des-Sources.

Mr. Speaker, let me try a second riddle. Who said during the election campaign that we must “ensure that government debt-to-GDP declines over the budget horizon”? Who said that? It was the Prime Minister, on page 55 of his election platform. The Prime Minister made a formal commitment to reduce Canada's debt-to-GDP ratio.
What measures will be taken to keep his promise, so he can keep his word, given that the government is announcing a $63‑billion deficit?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, when my friend across the way started his question, I already knew that he was not talking about Brian Mulroney or Stephen Harper, who drove the country into debt in a way that had never been done before.

I would like to remind members that we will have the documents and budget numbers here in the House tomorrow. I encourage my colleague to join us here and stay tuned for the economic plan to build a very strong Canada.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-39 is so bad that even the National Women's Liberal Commission is against it. These courageous women are speaking out against the way the current crisis is being exploited to give the Prime Minister excessive powers. They want accelerated authorities to be reported to Parliament and subject to independent review, as well as being time-limited. These women are being sorely let down by their representatives in the government caucus, because no one has had the courage to criticize the overreach in Bill C-39.
Will any minister have the courage to do that today?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Julie Dabrusin (Minister of the Environment, Climate Change and Nature, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I am going to say this again, because I think it is very important to reiterate it for everyone here. We will work to improve the effectiveness of our regulations, but we will not change the environmental standards under those regulations. We will continue to protect the environment, but we will build major projects. These major projects, such as large-scale power generation projects, will actually help us reduce our emissions.
Mr. Speaker, they are not doing a very good job.

Speaking of strong women who oppose Bill C-39, on Monday, Magali Picard, of the Fédération des travailleurs et travailleuses du Québec, criticized the restrictions on the right to strike. She announced that she would challenge Bill C-39 all the way to the Supreme Court, arguing that it is unconstitutional and would impose the most restrictive labour regime in the G7. Yesterday, AFN National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak likewise called for Bill C-39 to be withdrawn, because it is unsalvageably flawed and violates the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.
When will the government finally realize that Bill C-39 belongs in the dumpster?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Ms. Picard and I agree that the Government of Canada must invest more to prevent labour disputes, lockouts and strikes. That is why Bill C-39 proposes introducing special measures, special mediation, new techniques and new approaches. The goal is to ensure that not just 95%, but a much higher proportion of labour disputes are definitively resolved through collective agreements, rather than through strike action.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister called this the greatest crisis since the Second World War. Then he said Trump is a transformational president. He said integration is subordination and then wanted more integration to “make America great again.”
He decried a world of fortresses and then “fortress North America”. He said that we are “at war” and the U.S. wants to break us to own us.
Now he has a chat with the President about T-shirts and dress shirts. There is a new deal, the best deal, then no deal beats a bad deal, and now a bad deal beats no deal at all.
Every position changes except for one: whatever helps Liberals in December's by-elections.
What is the actual plan, or is it just putting his party ahead of the country?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Dominic LeBlanc (President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade, Intergovernmental Affairs, Internal Trade, and One Canadian Economy, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, speaking of some positions that never change, there are the attempts of the Conservative Party to connect a series of dots that do not exist.

I am surprised the Conservatives continually talk about by-elections. I am not sure it is going to be something they will like to talk about in a few weeks. Some of them, in fact, were caused by members of their own party evacuating the caucus.

I understand our friends on the other side want to connect a series of dots. They know very well our government is hard at work to defend workers and businesses in Canada, and we will continue to do that.

Mr. Speaker, “defend workers”? Last month, economist Trevor Tombe told the foreign affairs committee there is no evidence the Liberal countertariffs changed American behaviour, none. What they did was raise prices across the board and slash the income of Canadians earning under $30,000. Liberals are taxing our most vulnerable to punish Washington, and Washington could not be bothered.
Beyond the domestic Liberal politics designed to control our national debate, what is the plan beyond “elbows up” to actually level up?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Dominic LeBlanc (President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade, Intergovernmental Affairs, Internal Trade, and One Canadian Economy, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, again, we see members of the Conservative Party attempt to attribute a series of motivations in circumstances that do not exist. They know very well. Our government was very clear. When the Americans increased unjustified and illegal tariffs on Canadian businesses and workers, Canadians expected our government to take a strong position, something the opposition would never have done, because they continually find excuses as to why Canada should not have stood up to the Americans and done the right thing to defend workers.

Mr. Speaker, while businesses are shutting down, workers are losing their jobs and families are struggling to make ends meet, the Prime Minister would rather play his Trump card. He said last week that he could wait two and a half years to secure a trade agreement. Conveniently, after calling by-elections, he suddenly picked up the phone and called the U.S. President. Canadians do not want theatrics. They want results.
When will the Prime Minister finally deliver the major trade deal he promised?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Dominic LeBlanc (President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade, Intergovernmental Affairs, Internal Trade, and One Canadian Economy, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I am not sure whether my colleagues would agree, but hearing the member talk about theatrics seems a bit ironic, considering his behaviour in this place. Once again, the Conservatives are trying to connect a series of events that they know full well are completely unrelated.

Yes, we called by-elections, because those ridings deserve to be represented in the House of Commons by strong members of Parliament. Yes, we will stand up for Canadian workers and businesses. We will stand up to the Americans. These are things the Conservatives would never do.

Mr. Speaker, after 11 years of Liberals, there are two worlds: one where Canadians follow the rules and count every dollar but cannot get ahead, and another where political and business insiders get a seat at the big table and make up their own rules. Companies pay staff in the Liberal Major Projects Office, which makes decisions worth billions of private and public dollars. I questioned it six months ago and last night, but the minister will not even say which sectors the staff are from. So much for accountability and transparency for taxpayers.
How many MPO staff are paid by companies whose projects the office reviews, and will the minister name the companies?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Dominic LeBlanc (President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade, Intergovernmental Affairs, Internal Trade, and One Canadian Economy, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity to have this conversation with our colleague on the other side last evening at the building Canada committee. She just asserted that we did not talk about which sectors these interchange employees come from. Last night I said, and I am happy to repeat it again, the transportation sector, financial services sectors and agriculture sectors.

Many of these interchange positions, something that has existed in government for well over 50 years, include other orders of government, and they also allow public servants to work in the private sector and for non-profit organizations as well.
Mr. Speaker, last night the minister actually called disclosure a “gotcha moment“ when accountability is literally his job.

Companies help pay staff inside the Major Projects Office, but conflicts are reviewed internally without independent ethics oversight. The Liberals want Canadians to trust the safeguards but hide how and to whom those safeguards apply. The minister should release the rules, name the companies and say how many staff have been recused.
If the safeguards are so strong, why is the secrecy even stronger, and what does the minister have to hide?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, while the Conservatives want to think about conspiracy, what we do at the MPO is create jobs, like the 5,000 new jobs at Churchill Falls, the 8,000 new jobs at Contrecoeur, the 1,000 new jobs at Nouveau Monde Graphite, the 5,000 new jobs at LNG Canada and the 7,000 new jobs at Ksi Lisims.
Instead of talking down the MPO, why do they not help us build jobs?

Mr. Speaker, as part of the alliance for the future, the new partnership of nations that will leverage the strategic capabilities of Canada and the EU, our government is making a historic investment of up to $2.5 billion in financing for Alberta-based De Havilland to dramatically increase water bombing production capacity.
Can the Minister of Emergency Management and Community Resilience tell the House how this financing will help European partners and Canada fight wildfires and support thousands of jobs across Canada?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Eleanor Olszewski (Minister of Emergency Management and Community Resilience and Minister responsible for Prairies Economic Development Canada, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this is an investment in Canadian workers, Canadian aerospace ingenuity and community safety. It will help Alberta-based De Havilland double production of its iconic 515 water bombers, supporting thousands of great jobs in Alberta. This investment will get more of these life-saving aircraft where they are needed sooner.
The Leader of the Opposition called the EU-Canada summit “political theatre”. I doubt the workers benefiting in Alberta, the province he represents, would agree.

Mr. Speaker, after 11 years of the Liberals, one thing is clear. There are now two Canadas, one for hard-working Canadians who play by all the rules and one for the Liberal club. While Canadian families struggle to put food on the table, private corporations are paying employees who work inside the Major Projects Office, and the Prime Minister refuses to reveal who they are. Imagine an employer having their own employees working inside the very office responsible for advancing the projects the employer's company wants approved.
Can the Prime Minister tell Canadians exactly how many corporate-paid employees are working inside his MPO and which companies are paying for that?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joanne Thompson (Minister of Fisheries, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I actually have some very good news for the member opposite. Today we were proud to announce the removal of China's tariffs for two years—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
We need it to be a little quieter so the minister can answer.
The hon. Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has the floor.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take it from the top, if I could, because this is such important, good news for the province I share with the member opposite.
There is a two-year removal of the Chinese tariffs on lobster and crab, which is so significant for Atlantic Canada. On top of that, there is over $300 million over five years for AFF funding.
Instead of reading prepared notes, let us get together and do something that actually makes sense.
Mr. Speaker, I would not want to talk about the Major Projects Office either.

Last year, the Prime Minister told Canadians to prepare to make sacrifices. Well, guess what. They are already making them. Food bank visits have reached a record 2.35 million in a single month, with 776,000 of those visits being made by children.

Canadians are being made to make sacrifices, yet private corporations are paying employees working inside of the Prime Minister's Major Projects Office, and the government refuses to disclose which companies are involved. Again, Canadians deserve transparency.
How many employees working inside the Major Projects Office are being paid by—
The Honourable Minister of Energy.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, rather than come up with conspiracy theories, why does the member not talk about what the MPO did at Churchill Falls? It is the largest renewable energy—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
The member may continue.

Mr. Speaker, rather than come up with conspiracy theories about the MPO, the member might recognize that the MPO helped make Churchill Falls happen. It is the largest renewable energy project in the history of North America, with 5,000 new jobs in her province, new mines in her province. Instead of coming up with conspiracies, why does she not help the MPO get—
The hon. member for Cambridge has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised lots of things about his new Major Projects Office, but he forgot to mention that it would be done with unprecedented secrecy. It could be up to one-third corporate-sponsored employees working inside the office, and we do not know which private corporations are paying them. Canadians have a right to know who has a seat at the table. These insiders have direct access to government decisions that could benefit their employers.
Yesterday at committee, I asked a simple question. Which companies do they work for? The minister refused to answer, so I will ask again.
Will the minister be transparent and release the list of corporations, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, just as with the last member, I would invite the member, rather than focusing on conspiracy theories about the MPO, to focus on the 18,000 jobs at the Darlington nuclear reactor. It is one of the most important renewable energy projects in the world, the first SMRs in the world, and the Conservatives are talking down the office that made that happen. Maybe they should get with the program.
Mr. Speaker, there is clearly something to hide. The minister refused to identify the corporations that are paying their employees to work inside the Major Projects Office.

This is the same Liberal government that has been found guilty of ethics violations time and time again, and now Canadians are supposed to trust them. Why should they? How can Canadians be expected to believe that large corporations are paying employees to work inside the Major Projects Office simply out of generosity? Canadians do not know who these companies are, how conflicts are being screened or whether those companies stand to benefit from government decisions.
If the government has nothing to hide, why is it hiding?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we have talked about Atlantic Canada, we have talked about Quebec, and we have talked about Ontario. Now it is time to talk about British Columbia, where I was last Friday to announce, with the help of the MPO, it must be said, the listing of Roberts Bank Terminal 2. It is a megaproject for all of Canada, with $6 billion and 17,000 jobs for British Columbians and Canadians, to export our goods, our farm goods and the products of our ingeniosity over to Asia and create—
The hon. member for Montmorency—Charlevoix.

Mr. Speaker, the way the Prime Minister is managing taxpayers' money is starting to become extremely worrisome. On one side, we have ordinary citizens who are affected by those decisions on a daily basis and who are paying the price every day. On the other, we have the people who make the rules and the friends of the people who make the rules. They are the ones reaping the benefits.

We have learned that many of the employees of the Major Projects Office are there on loan from private companies and banks. These are the people who are responsible for deciding which companies will receive billions of dollars from the Liberals. They get to choose the winners, and their boss might be one of them.
How can we expect Canadians to have confidence in our institutions when transparency—
The hon. Minister of Government Transformation.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, what I do not understand about the Conservatives is the way they talk about helping ordinary people and then systematically vote against those people's interests. That member specifically voted against 19,223 children who are receiving an average of $5,000 through the Canada child benefit, in addition to the 19,000 people in his riding who are benefiting from the Canadian dental care plan.

The confusion and hypocrisy across the way do not stop there. Yesterday, the member for Bellechasse—Les Etchemins—Lévis accused us of helping businesses too much. However, when we were in her riding, visiting Prevost and helping businesses deal with the trade war, they were quite happy to be there on the sidelines and applaud the announcements we were making to support Canadian businesses.

Mr. Speaker, the most alarming thing about all this is that these employees' potential conflict of interest is not subject to any independent oversight. The Privy Council Office is staffed by employees who work directly for the Prime Minister. The Major Projects Office is the Prime Minister's creation and tool. They are the ones who decide whether or not there is a conflict. When we asked for the names of the companies involved in all that, they responded that the information is confidential and that revealing it could cause embarrassment.
Since when is transparency something to be embarrassed about?
Are the Liberals going to reveal which businesses are paying employees to pick the winners, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Major Projects Office has selected Quebec winners as well.

I implore the member to support this side of the House, because we revealed the investment and the start of construction on the Contrecoeur project, which will increase the Port of Montreal's container capacity by 50%. What is that going to accomplish? It is going to create wealth, opportunities and supply chains for Quebec manufacturers, farmers and producers to reach the entire world. It is creating jobs in Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, at a time when many Canadian families are feeling the pinch of the cost of living crisis, how can the Liberal government justify taking $1.6 billion out of the pockets of Canadians and giving it to Cohere, an AI company valued at more than $36 billion?

Is this AI company so strapped for cash that it has to take it from taxpayers who are struggling to put food on their tables and gas in their tanks, or is this just another example of the Liberals giving taxpayer-funded handouts to big corporations and their Liberal friends?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Evan Solomon (Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation and Minister responsible for the Federal Economic Development Agency for Southern Ontario, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we have a choice. We can either build this strategically important technology here in Canada, or we can buy it from someone else. We choose to build in Canada, support Canadian champions and build safe, sovereign AI.

With this company, we are taking an equity position so all Canadians can benefit. This company will create 1,000 jobs and invest $1.7 billion in computing here. This is what it means to build Canada strong and build sovereign, safe Canadian AI.

Mr. Speaker, the federal government recently announced that it purchased a $1.6-billion stake in the artificial intelligence firm Cohere. We soon found out this money was being funnelled to well-connected Liberal insiders. Dominic Barton, the chair of Invest in Canada, and Patrick Pichette, the head of digital transformation Canada, were early investors in Cohere. They also have long-standing ties to the Prime Minister. Having been promoted to these high-profile government roles, they now stand to gain from the Liberal government's so-called investment in Cohere.
Why is it that every time the Prime Minister spends millions or billions, a Liberal insider is so easy to find?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Evan Solomon (Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation and Minister responsible for the Federal Economic Development Agency for Southern Ontario, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we are not going to wait for others to build AI. We are going to build safe Canadian AI. We are going to invest in Canadian companies. We are going to keep the jobs here in Canada. We are going to keep the intellectual property here in Canada. We are going to make sure that Canada has a seat at the table with this safe, sovereign technology.
We will not do what the Conservatives would like us to do, which is nothing. We are building in Canada, because that is how we have control over the future.

Mr. Speaker, this AI scandal perfectly illustrates why the government should not be in the business of picking winners and losers. It is a masquerade that is simply about using taxpayer dollars to reward their friends in the Liberal club. It is a hallmark of virtually every Liberal government.

Let us take Dominic Barton, for example. As a former global managing director at McKinsey, he benefited from hundreds of millions of dollars in Liberal government contracts. Now, as an early investor in Cohere, he stands to gain once again.
Can the Prime Minister please explain why his Liberal friends are doing so well, while so many other Canadians are just barely hanging on?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Evan Solomon (Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation and Minister responsible for the Federal Economic Development Agency for Southern Ontario, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this is not about what the Conservatives say, picking winners or losers. This is about investing in Canadians. They should try it for a while.

Canadians are winners because they build here in Canada. We are one of the few middle powers. There are only four countries that have the capacity to build safe, sovereign companies. Cohere is a Canadian champion. It will put 1,000 jobs here in the next three years. It will invest $1.7 billion, and Canadians now can benefit from this company staying Canadian. The Conservatives should try to build Canada strong for a change.

Mr. Speaker, I have had the opportunity to speak with families, businesses and workers in my riding. They all understand the importance of rising to the challenges of this unique moment and seizing the opportunities before us. They understand that being “masters in our own home” means building a better future, that being “masters in our own home” means a stronger and more resilient Canada.
With just over 24 hours to go before budget 2026 is introduced, can the minister tell us how we will become masters in our own home?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Dominic LeBlanc (President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade, Intergovernmental Affairs, Internal Trade, and One Canadian Economy, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I thank our colleague for his excellent question. He knows very well that our government was elected to strengthen the Canadian economy, diversify our trade, rely on partners who want to invest in and trade more with Canada, and strengthen the armed forces through Canada's industrial strategy. Whether in natural resources or manufacturing, we are here to support Canadian industries. Tomorrow will already be—
The hon. member for Bowmanville—Oshawa.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians have questions about the $2.3-billion contract given out to Telesat. Its CEO, Dan Goldberg, is close personal friends with the Prime Minister. Liberals were deflecting questions about this earlier today, but the core question is this: Why is the AI minister including Dan Goldberg in his ethics screen but the Prime Minister is unwilling to do the exact same? Canadians want to know why the Prime Minister's ethics screen is incomplete, and when it is going to be fixed.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister, like all ministers, all members of the House and all senior officials throughout the government, must live under some of the most stringent ethics rules in the world. Declarations are filed regularly. Much attention is paid to making sure of the exactitude of all of these documents, and I would encourage all members of the House and all senior members of the government to continue to rigorously adhere to these very high standards.
Mr. Speaker, it is another week, another letter sent to Cleveland-Cliffs, yet workers are still facing layoffs.

Now, on October 26, the industry minister said she would provide the House with the demand letter that outlines the numerous breaches Cleveland-Cliffs made in its contract, yet she has not followed through. I have asked for that letter repeatedly in the House, yet parliamentarians still have not seen it, but I did learn that the media has a copy. Therefore, if she is willing to provide it to reporters, certainly she could provide it here for members of the House. Will she table it today, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, when it comes to Stelco, our position is clear. We want the workers to be back working, period. That is why we are waiting for Stelco and we are waiting for Cleveland-Cliffs. There are three days left. If not, we are suing.

Mr. Speaker, the minister keeps sending letters and moving deadlines, but what workers really need is a more competitive industry. Conservatives have offered some concrete solutions, like pre-approving LNG projects so we can signal demand to industry for Canadian steel and getting rid of the industrial carbon tax. We have also argued for regulatory and tax reform.
Will the Liberals today commit to advancing our proposals and work with us to make Canada the most competitive place to do business in the world, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I have a lot of respect for my colleague, and I am always willing to work with him. We know that together we need to deal with the American tariffs, we need to protect our steel sector and we need to make sure that, when it comes to Stelco, the workers are back.
At the same time, I must say that my colleague needs to look at the budget tomorrow. I am convinced that he will be convinced by our plan to build Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, in a rapidly changing world, one thing is clear. Meeting this moment gives us all the opportunity, as well as the duty, to build a stronger, more independent and resilient Canada. We have what the world wants. That means new jobs, new investments and new opportunities for all Canadians. It means we are masters of our own destiny.
With budget 2026 just over 24 hours away, can the Secretary of State for Financial Institutions give us a sneak peek of what Canadians can expect tomorrow afternoon?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Wayne Long (Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the member for Sudbury asked an amazing question. Indeed, this Thursday, we will table budget 2026.

Unlike the Conservatives, who continue to talk down the economy, our workers, our unions and our country, we will build on Canada's strengths. We will unlock investment. We will move projects forward and create good jobs at home. We will strengthen our economy and support small and medium-sized businesses. Unlike the Conservatives, we will make life more affordable for Canadians. Join us for budget 2026—
The hon. member for Selkirk—Interlake—Eastman.

Mr. Speaker, the tragedy at CFB Wainwright took four precious lives, left 39 soldiers hospitalized and countless others exposed to heavy smoke. For many, their recoveries will not be quick. Some will have health challenges for the rest of their lives. Unfortunately, the long-term benefits are different between reserve force and regular force members based on their terms of service. This could result in one survivor receiving adequate support, while another slips through the cracks.
Will the government ensure every soldier with an injury attributable to service receives the same benefits?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. David McGuinty (Minister of National Defence, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, there are 27 Canadians now still in the hospital. We are with them. We are providing all the support we can. We have brought in personnel from Ontario. We are providing surgical help. I would ask all members to stick together as we provide the support that they need.
I take due note of the member's question. We will look at it and come back with an answer.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is willing to spend $50 billion on a pipeline, a decision that guts Canada's climate strategy and tramples on indigenous rights, but we do not see the same ambition when it comes to his so-called wartime housing program.

With Canadians facing mounting bills, higher interest rates and skyrocketing housing costs, will the Prime Minister declare building community housing a national interest and increase the housing budget to build one million non-market housing units for Canadians?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Jennifer McKelvie (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Housing and Infrastructure, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for the question because it gives us the opportunity to reflect on the hard work we have done over the last year. Over the last year, we have worked with provinces to reduce red tape and fees. We have reduced GST for new homes for first-time homebuyers. We have invested in housing-enabling infrastructure so that we can build more homes.

Here are the results. Let us talk about them. RBC confirmed improved housing affordability. Rent prices are down 24 months in a row. PwC says optimism in housing is back. According to Canadian real estate, housing starts are up in Vancouver and Montreal and, listen to this, up 65% in Saskatchewan—
I wish to draw the attention of members to the presence in the gallery of the 2026 Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council award recipients.
With us is the 2026 Gerhard Hertzberg Canada Gold Medal for Science and Engineering prize winner, Dr. Linda Nazar.
Also with us are the winners of NSERC's John C. Polanyi Award and the Brockhouse Canada Prize for Interdisciplinary Research in Science and Engineering.
Also with us are the winners of the Synergy Awards for Innovation and the Arthur B. McDonald Fellowships.
Some hon. members: Hear, hear!

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed from November 2 consideration of the motion.

Content.ParaText: It being 3:15 p.m., the House will now proceed to the taking of the deferred recorded division on the motion to concur in the ninth report of the Standing Committee on Justice and Human Rights concerning the extension of time to consider Bill S‑233.
Call in the members.

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: (The House divided on the motion, which was agreed to on the following division:)

Content.ParaText: I declare the motion carried.

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed from November 2 consideration of the motion that Bill C-269, An Act to amend the Income Tax Act (heat recovery tax credit), be read the second time and referred to a committee.

Content.ParaText: The House will now proceed to the taking of the deferred recorded division on the motion at second reading stage of Bill C-269 under Private Members' Business.

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: (The House divided on the motion, which was negatived on the following division:)

Content.ParaText: I declare the motion lost.
I wish to inform the House that because of the deferred recorded divisions, the time provided for Government Orders will be extended by 24 minutes.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36(8)(a), I have the honour to table, in both official languages, the government's responses to nine petitions. These returns will be tabled in an electronic format.
To mark Veterans' Week and commemorate our war veterans, I invite the House to rise and observe a moment of silence.
[A moment of silence observed]

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Jill McKnight (Minister of Veterans Affairs and Associate Minister of National Defence, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as Veterans' Week begins and Canadians prepare to gather on Remembrance Day, we are reminded of a simple truth: Remembrance matters.
Today, we remember.

Across our country, Canadians will gather in communities large and small. They will stand at cenotaphs and memorials, wear a poppy, observe a moment of silence and remember. They will remember generations of Canadians who answered the call to serve in times of peace, war, conflict and uncertainty. They will reflect on those who never returned home and on those whose lives were forever changed by service. Their courage helped protect the freedoms we enjoy today. Their sacrifices helped safeguard the democratic institutions that define our country. The Canada we know today was shaped not only by the service they gave, but by the sacrifices they made.

However, remembrance is not only about those who served in the past. It is also about recognizing service that continues today. We see it in those who continue to serve Canada in uniform. We see it in veterans, whose commitment to our country continues long after their service has ended.

As we begin Veterans' Week, we do so carrying heavy hearts following the recent loss of four members of the Canadian Armed Forces at CFB Wainwright: Sergeant Morgan Wong, Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding and Private Hayden Lykkemark. Our hearts are with their families, friends and fellow service members. We see the profound impact of this loss on all who knew and loved them. Canadians share in their sorrow.

We will remember those we have lost, those injured and those still recovering, and we recognize the grief being felt across the Canadian Armed Forces among military families, throughout the veteran community and by Canadians from coast to coast to coast.

The deaths of those military personnel, along with other losses suffered in Wainwright, remind us that this is not just part of our history; it is also part of our present, in times of peace as well as in times of war.
Canada sees every veteran, every serving member and the families who stand beside them. Canada is grateful for their service, and Canada will always honour their contributions to our country.

No one serves alone. Behind every veteran and every serving member are families who share the realities of military life, families who endure separation, relocation, uncertainty and sacrifice in service. In a country as diverse as Canada, remembrance remains one of the moments that bring us together.

Canadians come from different backgrounds, live in different regions and hold different perspectives, yet during Veterans' Week, we are united in gratitude for those who have worn Canada's uniform. We are also privileged to serve in this House alongside colleagues who have worn Canada's uniform and continue their service to Canada in public life.
Every generation has a responsibility to remember them.

It is a responsibility shared by all Canadians. Remembrance is not passive; it is an active responsibility to learn the stories of those who served, to remember them and to ensure that their sacrifices are never forgotten. As November 11 approaches, Canadians can fulfill that responsibility through simple but meaningful actions. Wear a poppy, attend a ceremony or thank a veteran or serving member. These actions may seem small, but they are how remembrance endures: through a conversation, a handshake, a young person learning a veteran's story or a community gathering together.
These are the ways in which we ensure that memories live on. Remembering must be a choice. Each of us must choose to remember.

Veterans Week is a time of reflection, a time of gratitude and a time to recommit ourselves to remembering, so let us choose remembrance. Let us honour those who served by ensuring that their stories continue to be told. Let us honour their sacrifices, not only in words but through actions.
It is now our turn to carry the torch.
Lest we forget.
Mr. Speaker, today we pay tribute to our veterans.

As a former member of the armed forces, I know that serving our country requires courage, but it also requires sacrifices for the whole family. Canada will always be grateful to our veterans and their families. Their service and sacrifices will never be forgotten.

We will remember them: the Canadians who have served and continue to serve our country. It is a tradition of service that men and women, and in fact those who we would say are boys and girls, have engaged in selflessly for as long as we have been a country and before we became one.

We will remember them: those in the First World War and the Second World War, and those who answered the calls to Korea and Afghanistan. We honour those who served in the Persian Gulf and those who kept the peace in Cyprus and the Balkans.
We must recognize the men and women who continue to serve today, including those deployed at this moment in Latvia with our NATO partners and allies in defence of freedom and security.

We remember those who serve at home in disasters, emergencies and training. This point hits home especially hard this year as we reflect on the tragedy that recently took place at CFB Wainwright. Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding, Private Hayden Lykkemark and Sergeant Morgan Wong fell in service to our country on our own soil, while training to mitigate risk while abroad but knowing that their service here at home carried risk as well. Thirty-nine of their brothers and sisters were also injured, including more than two dozen who are still in hospital. Their families are preparing for a life of, in the case of the four who perished, grief and loss, and for the families of those injured, a life of finding ways to support them.

I would also like to note the veterans and members of the Canadian Armed Forces whom we have lost to suicide. Their deaths do not diminish their service. They do not diminish their sacrifice. We need to look on those members with dignity and compassion and to thank them for their service.

As the rolls of the fallen continue to grow, in this very building we have the Books of Remembrance. I encourage anyone who has the privilege to join us here for a tour of this great place, and all my colleagues who serve here, to take a moment to visit the Room of Remembrance to see the names of our fallen, the men and women, some of whom were just boys and girls, who signed up to serve our country selflessly.

The act of remembrance is so important. It is wonderful to look across the House and see everyone wearing a poppy, and to see that in our streets. I encourage everyone to buy a poppy and to wear it proudly, to visit a cenotaph service on Remembrance Day, to visit the grave of a veteran, to thank a serving member and to thank a former member of our Canadian Armed Forces.

Members who have served know how important a buddy check is, to check in to ask how someone is doing. They do not have to give us any details or a response beyond an acknowledgement, but checking in on them counts, as does thanking them for their service. It is not something anyone joins to receive bouquets of roses thrown to them. They do it selflessly, so please thank them.

The number of names continues to grow, of those we lose every year, those who have served, but we are blessed to live in a country where men and women continue to sign up to serve, protect and defend what we are so blessed to enjoy here.

Our gratitude cannot be measured simply by our words of remembrance but must also be measured by our deeds. We collectively need to do better every single day in delivering on our obligations to the men and women who have served Canada. They serve us with unlimited liability. We need to repay that by making sure we take care of them when their service concludes. It is something we all need to put our shoulder to the wheel to do for them, just as they did for us.
We will remember them.

Mr. Speaker, in Quebec, where I live, the sound of jackboots is just an expression for most people, and the sound of gunshots can be mistaken for fireworks, not the other way around. For most of us, war is something distant, something that happens elsewhere. However, that is not the case for veterans and their families.

Remembrance Day is a time to remember all the soldiers who bravely gave their lives in war so we could have peace. We remember the soldiers who died during the war that was supposed to be “the war to end all wars”, which clearly it was not, as we can see today from the fact that our world is in turmoil.
