We remember the soldiers who died in all the conflicts that unfortunately followed: the Second World War, the Korean War and the war in Afghanistan, as well as the peacekeeping missions, particularly in the Balkans. Time may go on, but the memory of our heroes never fades.

It is also an opportunity to thank all those who have served, have put their lives on the line and are still with us today. Their courage does them honour and will forever honour us as well. It is now our turn to honour our obligation to them. We need to send a message to the federal government: Our veterans deserve treatment that lives up to their dedication. That is not the case when struggling veterans have to wrestle with the federal government for the right to keep their own psychologist, with whom they have developed a deep relationship. That is not the case when francophone veterans face discrimination from service delays that are completely disproportionate to those experienced by their anglophone counterparts. It does not honour the memory of the Quebeckers, Acadians and French Canadians who served to erase the French language from the Canadian military, as the current government is condoning. We are currently witnessing a decline in the way veterans are treated. That needs to be said, and it needs to stop.

As Remembrance Day approaches, I also want to honour and thank the men and women who are currently deployed. They can be found on every continent, in hot spots, such as the Russian border, the Congo and the Middle East. They play all sorts of roles in all sorts of circumstances, but one thing remains constant: Their families miss them and worry about them. They deserve our full support.

Let us also take a moment to reflect on the role that the armed forces play in Quebec. They are on the ground helping during devastating spring floods and out-of-control wildfires. We owe them a debt of gratitude.

In the coming days, ceremonies will take place across Quebec to honour our fallen. I encourage people to come out in force to attend. From now until November 11, let us proudly wear a poppy over our hearts. Let us not forget that the money collected goes directly to veterans and their families.

In closing, on behalf of the Bloc Québécois, I would like tell all those who gave their lives in the line of duty, all those who served and all those who are serving today that we remember them and that we will continue to remember them.
The hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway is rising.
Is there unanimous consent to allow the member to speak?
Some hon. members: Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to rise to offer Remembrance Day remarks on behalf of the New Democratic Party of Canada and our leader, Avi Lewis. As Veterans Week begins and communities across Canada prepare to gather for Remembrance Day, we come together to honour all those who have served our country in uniform. We remember those who never came home; we remember those who returned carrying wounds, both visible and invisible; and we honour the families whose love, strength and sacrifice sustained those who served and who serve.

This year, Remembrance Day is made even more poignant by the recent loss of four Canadian Armed Forces members during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright: Sergeant Morgan Wong, Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding and Private Hayden Lykkemark. Many more were injured, some gravely. As their loved ones grapple with this unfathomable, heartbreaking loss, we stand with them today in their grief.

Behind every uniform is a human being: a son or daughter, a brother or sister, a partner, a parent, a friend. When tragedy strikes, it is not just military families that mourn, but entire communities and a grateful nation. That is why we wear a poppy, not as a symbol of military glory but as a symbol of remembrance and gratitude; a reminder of lives interrupted, of futures never realized and of the profound human cost of war.

The history of military service in Canada is not one story but many, each bound by the same willingness to sacrifice for their country. One of the most remarkable chapters in this history is the service of indigenous veterans. Even when they were denied the rights of their fellow citizens, first nations, Inuit and Métis peoples answered our nation's call. They served with courage and distinction, fighting for freedom overseas even while facing injustice at home.

As I hail from Vancouver, I must also recount to this House the many moving ceremonies I have experienced at the Chinatown Memorial Monument in historic Chinatown, along with my colleague from Vancouver East. Like their indigenous comrades, Chinese Canadian soldiers also bravely served overseas while facing discrimination and denial of their own civil rights by the society they valiantly defended. Their contributions, sacrifices and resilience must never be forgotten.

Canada stands proud of the oversized contributions that we have made in the cause of freedom. In the First World War, over 600,000 people served, out of a population of eight million. From daring exploits in the air to their unbelievable courage at places like Ypres and Vimy Ridge, Canadian soldiers helped birth the independent country we know today. More than one million Canadians took up arms to defeat fascism during the Second World War, one of humanity's darkest chapters. They stormed the beaches of Normandy, fought through Italy, sailed dangerous Atlantic convoys, liberated occupied peoples and helped defeat the Nazi regime and its machinery of genocide. As fewer veterans of those generations remain with us, the responsibility to carry forward their stories now belongs to all of us. That sacred duty extends to Canadians who served in Korea, the Balkans, Afghanistan, on peacekeeping missions and countless operations undertaken in the service of all of us.

In honouring this service, we must also recognize the brutal reality of war. Those who have witnessed it first-hand understand, like no others, that beneath the language of strategy, of victory and of national interest lies something far more profound. War's true cost is measured in shattered families, lifelong trauma and lives that can never be restored. It invariably kills and wounds the innocent as well as the enemy. It destroys property, cities and cultural monuments. Its consequences outlive the conflicts themselves. That is why remembrance is not about celebrating war. It is about understanding its tragedy and renewing our commitment to peace.

It also calls us to action. The greatest tribute we can pay our veterans lies in how we treat them when they return home. To fully honour veterans, we must ensure timely access to health care; provide robust support for mental health and operational stress injuries; and ensure that no veteran is ever left homeless, isolated or living in poverty.

We must keep the promises made when they answered our country's call. Remembrance requires more than gratitude. It demands respect and resources. Most importantly to veterans, it demands that we work for a world in which our children are never again asked to bear the brutal burdens of war.

As we all gather in our communities this week, let us reach out and do something simple but meaningful, such as wear a poppy, attend a ceremony, thank a veteran, listen to their stories and share those stories with the next generation. In the end, we remember because democracy, freedom and human rights have never come without sacrifice. We remember because the most fitting way to honour those who served is to build a country worthy of their sacrifice, and a country that cares for its veterans, rejects the forces of hatred and strives always for a more just, compassionate and peaceful world for all.
Lest we forget.

I thank the hon. Minister of Veterans Affairs, the hon. member for Leeds—Grenville—Thousand Islands—Rideau Lakes, the hon. member for Vallée-du-Haut-Saint-Laurent and the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway for their words in honour of Veterans' Week and Remembrance Day.
Lest we forget.
I wish to inform the House that because of the ministerial statement, the time provided for Government Orders will be extended by an additional 22 minutes, for a total of 46 minutes.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the following three reports of the Standing Committee on Industry and Technology: the sixth report, entitled “Driving Canada's Electric Vehicle (EV) Future: A Study of the Federal Government's EV Policies”; the seventh report, entitled “Understanding and Preventing Digital and Financial Fraud and Scams in Canada”; and the eighth report, entitled “Bill C-267, An Act to establish a national framework to promote the durability of electronic products and essential home appliances”.
Pursuant to Standing Order 109, the committee requests that the government table a comprehensive response to its sixth and seventh reports.
Mr. Speaker, I will be presenting a dissenting report to the sixth report to make a simple point. Canada's automotive future cannot be dictated by political deadlines and government mandates.

I would like to take a moment to thank the witnesses who appeared before the committee and provided valuable testimony. Many submitted briefing materials. We are also grateful for the hard-working clerks, analysts and other support staff who helped us during the deliberations.

Conservatives support cleaner vehicles, innovation and reducing emissions, but Canadians should have the freedom to choose what works for their families and their wallets. In Windsor, this is not an academic debate. It is about paycheques, manufacturing jobs, our tool and die industry, and thousands of workers whose livelihoods depend on a competitive automotive sector. The government cannot force transition faster than consumers can afford it. Infrastructure and support have to be there. We most certainly oppose the admission of Chinese-made EVs into our country. The CCP is known to weaponize EV investment across the globe and engage in unfair trade practices. Reports from international agencies suggest they use slave labour. Is that what we are looking for here?

More importantly, we need to remind our American neighbours that they run a trade surplus with us when it comes to automobiles, and we will remain each other's primary customer. We need to get back to the negotiating table and work on a good deal that works for workers and taxpayers in Canada and the U.S.A.
Competitiveness cannot be legislated. It is earned by building things, creating jobs and giving Canadians and Canadian workers a fighting chance.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the fifth report of the Standing Committee on Agriculture and Agri-Food in relation to Bill C-226, an act to establish a national framework to improve food price transparency.
The committee has studied the bill and has decided to report the bill back to the House with amendments.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the ninth report of the Standing Committee on Canadian Heritage regarding Bill S-211, an act respecting a national framework on sports betting advertising.
The committee has studied the bill and has decided to report the bill back to the House with amendments.

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessTitle: Canada Pension Plan Investment Board Act

Content.ProceduralText: Bill C-295. Introduction and first reading
Content.ParaText: moved for leave to introduce Bill C-295, An Act to amend the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board Act (investments).

She said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to reintroduce an NDP bill brought forward in the last session by my former colleague, Alistair MacGregor, that would ensure investments made on behalf of Canadians through the Canada pension plan reflect our country's commitment to human rights, workers' rights and environmental responsibility.
I want to thank my colleague, the member for Courtenay—Alberni, for seconding this bill. He is always a champion for the people and for justice.

The Canada pension plan is a cornerstone of retirement security for millions of Canadians. The Canada Pension Plan Investment Board manages hundreds of billions of dollars on behalf of contributors and beneficiaries. Canadians should be able to have confidence that their retirement savings are not being invested in entities that engage in serious violations of human, labour or environmental rights.

This legislation would require the investment policy, standards and procedures of the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board to provide that investments could not be made or held in entities where there are reasons to believe the entity has committed human, labour or environmental rights violations.

The bill would also prohibit investment in entities involved in the production of arms, ammunition or other implements of war prohibited under international law, as well as entities responsible for directing certain forms of corruption prohibited under Canadian law.

This is fundamentally about accountability and responsible investments, and with that scale comes responsibility. Our pension investments should not contribute to practices that violate fundamental human rights, undermine workers or damage the environment. I hope members of the House will support this important bill.
Content.ProceduralText: (Motions deemed adopted, bill read the first time and printed)

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I rise today to present a petition signed by Canadians opposed to the Liberal government's firearm buyback and confiscation program.

The petitioners note that the program targets law-abiding, licensed firearms owners and does nothing to address gun smuggling or gang violence, which is responsible for the sharp rise in violent crime. This program diverts resources from measures that would actually reduce violent crime, and the public safety minister has also admitted that it is costly and ineffective.
Therefore, the petitioners call on the government to end the buyback program and prioritize public safety through real reforms, including stricter bail for dangerous and repeat offenders.
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour once again to rise on behalf of the great people in Simcoe—Grey and, more specifically, those in Clearview Township.

This has been mentioned before in the House many times, but this is a new petition about the over-the-horizon radar system that is going forward. Phase one was the purchase of 711 acres. It was a simple buy because all of the land was bought from one farmer. The project has already started, with the moving of the earth, and it is moving forward.

The petitioners in the area are really upset. The township is opposed to it. The residents are opposed to it. There is also big fear about phase two, which is another roughly 3,000 acres that may face expropriation. This is prime farm agricultural land that we will not get back. They understand that there is always a balance between food security and national security, but there are other options out there.

The petitioners are calling for three things: Number one, halt construction activities associated with the proposed over-the-horizon infrastructure in Clearview Township until environmental and alternative analysis have been completed; number two, make public all documents relating to alternative locations and conduct a transparent review of existing federal Crown and defence lands; and number three, ensure the defence infrastructure is not sited on prime agricultural lands and ecologically connected lands, including those associated with the Minesing Wetlands. There are a lot of concerns here.
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition signed by members of the Cambodian community in the riding of Honoré‑Mercier in Montreal.

The 20th Francophonie Summit will be held in Phnom Penh in November. The petitioners note that this event will draw international attention to Cambodia. They believe that this is an opportunity for member states of the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie to tangibly advance human rights and democracy.

They call upon the Government of Canada to use its participation in the summit, as well as its discussions with Cambodian authorities, to pursue four objectives: secure the release of political prisoners and prisoners of conscience; encourage the protection of civil society and freedom of the press; promote the restoration of genuine political pluralism; and combat transnational crime and ensure accountability.

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessQualifier: Pacific Coast Feeding Group of Gray Whales

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and privilege to table a petition on behalf of the residents of Tofino and Ucluelet.

The Pacific coast feeding group of gray whales is an ecologically and culturally significant population of whales that feed in the coastal waters of British Columbia. The Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada assessed the Pacific coast feeding group as endangered in November 2017. The committee recognized its small population and vulnerability to threats, including oil spills. Nearly nine years has passed since that assessment without the population being listed as endangered under schedule 1 of the Species at Risk Act.

Gray whales face growing pressures from changing ocean conditions, reduced food availability, vessel strikes, entanglement, underwater noise and noise pollution. Recent reports of malnourished and gray whales along the Pacific coast have heightened concern about the survival of these animals. Increased marine traffic and industrial activity on the Pacific coast underscores the need for timely, science-based protection of these gray whales and their habitat.

Petitioners are calling on the government to immediately, under the Species at Risk Act, list the Pacific coast feeding group of gray whales under schedule 1 as endangered. This would be consistent with the 2017 COSEWIC assessment. The government should identify and protect habitats essential to the survival and recovery of this population; strengthen measures to reduce preventable threats to these gray whales, including vessel strikes, entanglement, underwater noise, pollution and oil spills; and work in partnership with indigenous nations, scientists and coastal communities to develop and implement effective measures for the long-term recovery of gray whales in Pacific waters.
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise on behalf of the people from Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola.

I rise for the sixth time to bring forward a petition to help with the funding and fast-tracking of the rebuilding of the Red Bridge by the federal government. The Red Bridge was destroyed by arson in 2024. It was a cultural landmark and a vital link between Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc territory and mainland Kamloops.
I encourage the government to stop leaving Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola out when it comes to funding announcements. Let us fund Red Bridge in tomorrow's budget.
Mr. Speaker, it is always an honour to rise on behalf of the people of Guelph. I have two petitions today.

The first petition I present is on behalf of 40 constituents who are calling for the establishment of a Canadian centre for peace and justice. They recognize that lasting security requires not only strong national defence but also meaningful investments in diplomacy, conflict prevention and peacebuilding.

They call on the government to establish and fund an independent national centre dedicated to research, policy development, peace education and training for civilians, police and military personnel. Petitioners believe that such a centre would strengthen Canada's capacity to address the root causes of conflict and contribute to lasting peace, both at home and abroad.

Mr. Speaker, the second petition I present is on behalf of 85 constituents concerning Canada's immigration system. They express concerns about immigration processing delays and recent changes to immigration policies, emphasizing the importance of fairness, dignity and inclusion.

They are calling on the government to increase resources for IRCC and CBSA, maintain or increase immigration levels, and strengthen the interim federal health program. They also call for a special pathway to permanent residency for Ukrainians who arrived under the CUAET program and urge everyone to avoid rhetoric that unfairly blames immigrants for Canada's housing challenges.

Mr. Speaker, it is always an honour to stand for the people of Yellowhead. Today I rise to present a petition, signed by more than 11,000 Canadians, calling on the government to immediately reverse Parks Canada's decision to end the search and rescue dog program in Banff National Park. This decision sparked widespread public outrage and attracted attention locally, nationally and in international media. For decades, these highly trained dogs have saved lives, located missing people and supported avalanche rescues.

One dog, Leroy, alone located 57 missing people in just seven years and has received three different commendation medals of bravery. With the avalanche season approaching, Canadians are rightly concerned about the consequences of eliminating this life-saving program.

I have also sent letters urging the Minister of Environment to reverse this decision. I hope the minister acts on the letters faster than it takes for the government to formally respond to the petition. The petitioners call on the government to immediately reverse this decision and restore canine search and rescue capabilities in Canadian national parks.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to table three petitions. The first petition is signed by 20,634 people who are calling on the Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship to increase the annual permanent residence admissions target for 2027 onward from the current 380,000 to approximately 415,000, representing 1% of Canada's population, and, with this increase, to allocate sufficient annual quota to the humanitarian pathways for Hong Kong, Sudanese and Ukrainian PR applicants and to clear the backlog of the 62,000 pending applications within three years.

The petitioners also say that Canada has a long-standing humanitarian tradition of assisting people affected by crises through special immigration pathways, yet applicants in these humanitarian pathways face processing wait times of over 10 years, with only 4,000 admissions allocated for 2027-28. These are applicants who are already living, working and studying in Canada.
Granting PR now would reduce the temporary residence population and would not create significant new demand for housing, education or health care. I urge the minister to heed the call.

Mr. Speaker, the second petition is signed by 38,455 people and was initiated by Vancouver residents who are concerned that AI data centres are being built with high secrecy and low community involvement. The petitioners agree that AI data centres are known for noise and water pollution and for straining water reservoirs and energy grids. They are concerned about AI's impact on jobs, digital sovereignty and other negative social implications.

They call on the Government of Canada to stop all incentives, subsidies and expedited permits for AI data centres, as well as revoke permits and supports for any AI data centres not sought out by the local community and not put through a rigorous vetting and transparent and democratic local approval process. They call for a public study on the unintended negative impacts associated with AI data centres in Canada and elsewhere and call for AI products to be subject to genuine taxes and enforceable regulations of safety, transparency, and power and water use.

Mr. Speaker, the third petition, signed by 1,048 people, is about the tragic attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Iran. They know that the February 28, 2026, missile attacks on the elementary school killed at least 165 school children and constituted a grave violation of international humanitarian law. They call on the Government of Canada to issue a formal and unambiguous condemnation of the attack. They call on the government to suspend military aid and related assistance to the U.S. and Israel during the current conflict pending a full and independent investigation, and to table in Parliament a full accounting of Canada's relationship with the United States and Israel regarding this conflict.

They further call on the Government of Canada to work with the UN, the ICC and relevant bodies to ensure accountability, and for the Minister of Foreign Affairs to publish a formal compliance assessment of current and pending arms transfers to the U.S. and Israel.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today on behalf of thousands of petitioners in my riding of North Island—Powell River who are calling on the Liberal government, now that there is a new Conservative provincial government in B.C., to abandon their condo billionaire bailout, a $1.5-billion plan to use taxpayer money in British Columbia to purchase unsold condos, instead of their developer friends having to lower prices and sell at a loss.

The petitioners are especially concerned that this plan would essentially use their money to artificially inflate what is already one of the least affordable housing markets in the world while lining the pockets of billionaires, many of whom have close ties to the Liberal Party and the current Minister of Housing.

They also express their frustration that these condos are already built and that this plan would therefore create zero new units of housing. A lack of transparency remains as to who lobbied for the policy, where it came from and who exactly stands to benefit the most.

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed from November 3 consideration of Bill C-31, A second Act to implement certain provisions of the budget tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025, as reported (with amendments) from the committee, and of the motions in Group No. 1.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is always an honour and a pleasure to stand in the House and speak on behalf of the people of Miramichi—Grand Lake.

The Prime Minister fancies himself as an economist. He has the degrees. He has spent years telling Canadians that he understands how money works. Since being elected, many Canadians actually think he is a travel blogger, apparently. He loves the way bubbles from champagne tickle his nose, and he has a very refined palate for caviar and fine foods, but as he is a man who apparently understands money, I have a simple question for him: Has he ever read Milton Friedman?

Friedman had a straightforward way of explaining why governments so often waste money. He said there are four ways to spend it. First, if we spend our own money on ourselves, we care equally about the price and the quality. Second, if we spend our own money on someone else, we care about the price but not so much about the quality. Third, if we spend someone else's money on ourselves, we care about the quality but not so much about the price. Fourth, if we spend someone else's money on someone else, we do not care much about the price and do not care much about the quality. That last one is the government. When it comes to defence procurement in this country, that is exactly what we have been watching with the Liberal government.

Canada is known for a lot of things, like hockey, maple syrup and politeness that sometimes goes too far. We are not known for the success of our bureaucratic defence procurement. If we asked any contractor who has ever tried to get a job done on time and on budget, we would learn pretty quickly that the more layers of people we have spending other people's money, the more things go wrong.

In this country, Liberals have spent 11 years proving that point. Fighter jets are still not settled, helicopters have become a national punchline and submarines do not exist. Even the Snowbirds were flying aircraft older than most of the people watching them, and they are now grounded until sometime in 2030.

This is not news; this is the Liberal record. Now the Liberals want to fix it by creating another agency and another minister, with broader powers to sole-source contracts and skip competitions. They want to take the most inefficient way to spend money and give it a new name and a bigger chequebook.

Division 16 of the bill would hand that unnamed minister the authority to sole-source almost anything that can be tied to national defence or national security. The list of exceptions is long. It includes urgent operational requirements; supporting a sector of the economy; sensitive technology; research and innovation; agreements with other governments, probably the countries where our Prime Minister also holds citizenship; and a catch-all that lets regulations add still more reasons. Once these powers are in place, the competition can be skipped and the supplier can be excluded on security grounds without a full explanation or a real appeal.

The bill would also remove the ordinary consequences if a competition that should have been run is not run. At the same time, it would allow the government to buy shares in corporations and replace directors and officers. This is not a minor technical change. This is power to take control of a company when it suits the government of the day. It sounds like socialism to me. There would be no serious requirement to report back to the House on how the powers are used, no clear obligation to tell Parliament when a national security exception is invoked and no meaningful check on loans, advance payments, guarantees or grants.

I am sure the Prime Minister's friends over at Brookfield Asset Management are grinning like the butcher's dog. I can just imagine the world of opportunities that the bill would open for those who are fortunate enough to be in business with the Prime Minister.

There is an old line attributed to Churchill: “Gentlemen, we have run out of money. Now we have to think.” Under the Liberal government, we ran out of taxpayers' money a long time ago, but the difference is that the government is still not thinking. It is just adding more people to spend other people's money on other people and calling it a success.

The Defence Investment Agency has already been operating for over a year. It has held signing ceremonies. It has announced preferred partners. It has not delivered a single piece of equipment to the Canadian Armed Forces. When its own CEO reportedly considered stepping down because the bureaucracy was still too slow, that should have been the end of the argument. We do not fix bureaucracy by giving it a new letterhead and a larger budget.

In my experience as a construction worker and a contractor, in my line of work, if a job keeps going over budget and past deadline, we do not solve it by hiring more project managers who have never swung a hammer. We put on our work boots, roll up our sleeves, figure out what is broken and fix it. We lead by example.

The Canadian Armed Forces do not need another layer of bureaucracy deciding what they get, when they get it and what the company affiliated with Brookfield gets in the contract. Our men and women in the military need equipment on time and at a price that makes sense, with someone who can be held accountable when it does not happen. This bill would not do that. It would build a department around a problem and make it official.

There was a famous line spoken by an American sailor at Pearl Harbor, spoken by our allies, I might add. Aboard the USS New Orleans, a man said, “Praise the Lord and pass the ammunition.” The line was celebrated throughout World War II and soldiers sang songs about it, because it rang true. In 2026, under the Liberal government, our soldiers now have neither of the two things that success in battle requires.

I asked a question in the House yesterday about the forced closure of St. Luke's Chapel at CFB Gagetown. Canadians and veterans' groups have been told that there is no room for the Lord or for prayer in our military. Now the Liberals are keeping the ammunition from them as well. If the Liberal government keeps going, we are going to have to train our military on fighting with rocks and sticks. I can only speak for myself, but let me tell the House that I am ashamed of sitting in the House while we treat the brave men and women who serve this nation and put themselves in harm's way with such disrespect.

Conservatives have been clear about what we support: one point of accountability for defence procurement and a special secretariat in the Privy Council Office so that military contracts are treated as the priority they are, not another agency, not another minister with a new title and not a CEO paid more than the Prime Minister with no background in national defence who is secretly shuffling contracts to Liberal insiders. Conservatives will fight to get the sailors, soldiers and aviators of the Canadian Armed Forces the equipment they need, with efficiency and accountability and consistent with the interests of Canadian security, not Liberal insider advantage.

This bill fails the test. It would expand control. It would reduce transparency. It would treat the Canadian Armed Forces as a problem to be managed by another bureaucracy rather than a force to be properly equipped and deserving of the respect and thanks of a grateful nation.

The first duty of any government is defence of the realm. That duty is not fulfilled by creating more agencies; it is fulfilled by equipping the people who stand on the wall. That duty would not be fulfilled by this bill, so Conservatives will not support it. We will stand with the men and women who have to use this equipment, not the system that keeps failing to deliver it to them.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, that speech failed to meet reality, quite frankly. It was off on so many points, and I wish I had the time to legitimately critique the member's comments.

The member started off by talking about credentials. I will compare the credentials of our Prime Minister to the credentials of the leader of the Conservative Party any day, as Canadians did in the last federal election. Then he went on to talk about our men and women in the forces. Is he serious? The Prime Minister, in his first six months, achieved the 2% target. We have seen more people putting in applications to be members of the forces this last year than in the last 30 years.
In many ways, we are moving forward. The Crown corporation he was referring to would ensure more accountability, more efficiency and more transparency.
The member needs to get outside of the Conservative—
The hon. member for Miramichi—Grand Lake.

Mr. Speaker, the member opposite asked about accountability. Let us talk about accountability and what this bill would do. It would hand an unnamed minister the power to sole-source almost anything tied to defence and national security, 13 different reasons to skip a competition and the ability to exclude a bidder on security grounds without a full explanation, with no serious requirements to come back to the House and report how those powers are used. At the same time, it would allow the government to buy shares in corporations and replace directors and officers. That is not a minor technical change. That is the power to take control of a company when it suits the government of the day. It sounds like socialism to me.

In my line of work, if someone wants to spend other people's money with almost no questions asked, we do not call that efficiency; we call that a problem. The Canadian Armed Forces do not need more unaccountable power in the hands of one minister. They need equipment that arrives on time, with someone to hold—
Questions and comments, the hon. member for Gaspésie—Les Îles-de-la-Madeleine—Listuguj.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my colleague. We can agree that Bill C‑31 covers a great many things. There is one part that particularly bothers me. It is that public servants will be allowed to make mistakes. One of the divisions of Bill C‑31 introduces a new form of immunity. What does that immunity mean? It means that if a citizen has been wronged, they cannot sue a public servant, an official or an employee if the mistake was made in good faith. That means it allows incompetence, it allows mediocrity, and citizens are being stripped of their rights.
What does my colleague think about that?
Mr. Speaker, the member wants to know why we oppose this agency. He should look at the Liberal record. Fighter jets took decades and are still not settled. The Snowbirds are grounded until the 2030s.

Canada is known for a lot of things. We are not known for success in Liberal defence procurement. The Defence Investment Agency has been operating for over a year, with signing ceremonies and preferred partner announcements, but not a single new piece of equipment has been delivered to the Canadian Armed Forces.

Mr. Speaker, we have one more sleep until the November budget. It is coming up tomorrow, and I believe Canadians will see a continuation of what the Prime Minister and every member of the Liberal caucus have been pushing forward: dealing first-hand with affordability, supporting the Canadian Forces and building a stronger and healthier Canadian economy, one that works for all Canadians. Bill C-31 is a good example of the types of things the government can do.
Does the member believe there is anything the government can do to support the Canadian economy outside of stepping aside and doing nothing?

Mr. Speaker, this bill would not improve value for money. Let us go back to the basics. The Liberals do not care much about price. They do not care much about quality. That is the Liberal mentality. That is exactly what this bill would expand, with more powers to sole-source, more ability to skip competitions, more people in the middle spending other people's money on other people, and almost no reporting back to Parliament. They are just adding more people to spend more of other people's money and calling it reform. That is not a plan. That is a problem.
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak today.

There are many reasons why MPs decide to run for office and are here today. We have different pathways and different motivations, things that have happened to us in our life that have led us here to the House of Commons. I have said this many times: I believe that every single member of the House has the intention to build a better country, a better Canada. I have never moved away from that. Some of our decisions come from so many different things. Our pathway in life and our trajectory can change based on just one simple incident. It could be anything that happens to us that brings us here.

I remember when I was about 19 years old, standing in front of the House of Commons and saying to myself that one day I would like to be in the House of Commons as a member of Parliament to speak on behalf of my community. I was from a neighbourhood called Flemingdon Park, a small neighbourhood in Toronto. It is one of the suburbs. It was a neighbourhood that was very challenging. There was poverty, youth incarceration, youth violence, and youth gun violence that caused murder. It was a really challenging place to grow up for many people. A lot of people felt disconnected from the element of change.

However, at 15 years old, something happened to me that was remarkable. There was a pool outside my apartment building. The pool had several buildings around it. It was full, and it was the end of winter. There was a hole in the fence, and kids were playing on the ice. I was afraid that some kid was going to fall through, so I told the superintendent that someone was going to get hurt. No one listened to me. Then I spoke to the manager a week later. No one listened to me. Then I picked up the phone and called the member of the provincial parliament, who was a Conservative, I have to say. Within one hour, the MPP fixed the hole in the fence.

I was shocked. How could a 15-year-old just pick up the phone after a week of trying, and have that fence fixed? It changed my whole perspective on how we get things done. I was just amazed. I was very interested in politics because of that experience I went through. That simple experience sparked an interest in me. Over time, it became a passion. In my neighbourhood, often people felt like they were discounted, pushed aside and not listened to. That phone call gave me a completely different understanding of how we could actually help people.

In my neighbourhood, there were so many young, talented people. I saw intelligence, creativity, ambition and potential. I went to elementary school with many of these young people. By the time we ended up in high school, or even junior high school, we started to see people go off on different pathways. There were a lot of young people I knew in my neighbourhood who were incarcerated. I was once interviewed when I was a school board trustee, and I said that I knew more young people from my neighbourhood, my community, who had been murdered than had gone off to university. People did not believe that, but it was the absolute truth.

These were not statistics to me. They were people I grew up with. It always created a sense of sadness in me. I decided when I was a kid, after I saw that change with respect to the swimming pool and after I made these observations, that one day I would grow up to make changes to balance the playing field, open up opportunities and make things a bit more fair.

I thought about going off to university. The next-door neighbour told me that I should really try. He had been a teacher in the Caribbean. He gave me the $50 to apply to go to university. I got in and got involved in politics. I did not know a single person involved in politics. I went to the public library. I decided that I was a Liberal, based on all the different information I read about multiculturalism, the creation of these great national programs, and the change in immigration policies that allowed my family to come to this country. I read about Louis St. Laurent's bringing forward old age security in 1952, and about the Canada pension plan by a Liberal government in 1966 and the guaranteed income supplement in 1967.

The philosophy of the Liberal Party really aligned with the observations that I experienced in my life. I went to the Liberal headquarters and I asked if I could volunteer. They opened the door, and I got involved.

This brings me to this budget debate. When I look at a federal budget, it is not just the numbers I see. It is the opportunity that presents itself for Canadians. The decisions that families in Scarborough and the rest of the country have to make based on finances are tough decisions, and people are looking for ways to remove barriers in order to provide more opportunities. We have been able to create new national programs over the last decade, such as $10-a-day child care, the Canada child benefit, the dental plan, the pharmacare plan and the disability benefit.

These are pieces that really resonated with me, to add to those national plans I talked about. It made me feel as though the principles behind what we were doing as a government, these good Canadian values, were aligned with the whole point of what equity and inclusion are.

When I see parents struggling to afford child care, someone with a disability struggling, a child arriving at school hungry or a person who cannot get a certain prescription, I see that building these types of programs is about equity. It is about removing barriers so people have the opportunity to reach their full potential without encountering those types of barriers that are so challenging. Inclusion means ensuring that everyone has the opportunity to participate fully in our communities, workplaces and our country. It means that a parent has a better chance of accepting a job offer, because they can get to work because there are affordable opportunities for child care.

My entire life in politics has been about taking items such as a budget and looking for ways to make sure opportunities are there for Canadians. I often think about being 19 years old, standing in front of the House of Commons, looking at this institution and imagining that one day I could serve as a member of Parliament. I think about being 15 years old and figuring out that someone could pick up the phone, engage with their representative and get some change done. I think about the young people I grew up with and their missed opportunities. Those experiences shaped my entire perspective on what public service meant. They taught me that a person's circumstance should never define their potential. It taught me that the government can actually make a meaningful difference in the lives of people. Governments can create opportunity for people who might otherwise be left behind.

The experiences reinforce my beliefs that a person's income, disability or postal code should never determine or limit their future, and that is what equity and inclusion mean to me. This is where the opportunities come through a budget. I believe that a budget should be about seeing more than just a financial commitment or trajectory. I see an opportunity to build a country where more people have a chance to succeed, where families have the support they need, where children can realize their potential and where no one is left behind because of the circumstances they were born into.

This is the Canada I believe in, and this is what has brought me here today. I believe that this budget would provide an opportunity to remove barriers, set people up for success and allow people to reach their full potential. That is why I am a Liberal, that is why I support this budget, and that is why I support the government.
Mr. Speaker, I salute my colleague.

He raised a rather important point. A budget contains more than just budgetary promises. That is true. Under Bill C-31, the government wants to suspend the re-evaluation of pesticides, which was normally required every 15 years. However, members know that Quebeckers are strongly opposed to the use of pesticides in Quebec. A recent poll shows that over 70% of Quebeckers oppose the government reintroducing pesticides that were banned because they were dangerous to humans and harmful to our environment.

I would like our colleague to comment on this today. Does he believe that it is in the interest of science, in the interest of protecting public health and protecting the environment for his government to stop evaluating pesticides and to reintroduce some that were previously banned?
Mr. Speaker, any question that is about the environment and protecting the spaces around us is a very valid question with a very valid point.

If we look at the history of the Liberal Party and the Liberal government with respect to their commitment to the environment, we will not find another political party or government in the history of this country that has done more to protect and embrace the Canadian environment.
A budget is really about finding a balance. This budget is about many things, and that is why I support it.

Mr. Speaker, I really enjoyed my colleague's speech. As I have talked about many times in the House, I spent well over a decade in the public education system, so his reference to young people was one I appreciated.

I am wondering if the member can offer some commentary further to what he gave in his remarks a moment ago about how the budget process and this exercise we undertake here in Parliament can be used as an educational tool for those he represents in his riding.
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his commitment to young people, to families and to education.
There is no question that education is the best tool we can use for success and to build a strong Canadian individual and family. That is the best investment, I believe, we can make.

I try every single Friday to go to at least one elementary school. Last week I was at a school, and we talked about Bill C-34 and the impact the bill would have on the school. In fact, a high school has invited me to come talk about the bill.

That type of engagement, that type of consultation, is important. I always leave the classroom telling students not to let people make decisions on their behalf without their paying attention, because throughout their lifetime, there will be people in rooms such as this, at city halls and in provincial governments, who will be making decisions on their behalf, and their political literacy has to be at such a level where they can figure these things out and challenge the people who are making decisions if they are bad decisions.

Mr. Speaker, the member for Wellington—Halton Hills North has tried for the last several days to get an indication from the government as to its commitment to its stated goals of relying on fiscal anchors. A number of good things the member spoke to are covered in budget 2025, but it has to be done in the overall context of fiscal responsibility.

Due to the lack of responses the House received during question period, I wonder if the member would opine on his view of whether the government should be held to fiscal anchors that it states, and whether they should be carried forward, let us say, even into the budget tomorrow.
Mr. Speaker, as the member knows, Canada is in a good position when it comes to its financial rating. We have budgets, so we project what is to come, and we look for ways to balance that.

Ultimately, the voters will decide who leads this country. It is our responsibility, as MPs, to hold ourselves accountable by communicating with our community and having people agree or disagree with the approach we have taken.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak to Bill C‑31. The bill contains a number of new measures, and it would also amend several existing laws. Changes will be made to the income tax regulations, the Excise Tax Act, the Air Travellers Security Charge Act, the Income Tax Act and the Global Minimum Tax Act, among others.

Today, I want to focus more on the part that will help us build Canada strong and build it faster. As I have often said in my speeches in the House, over the past few years, we have been building less and less and, in some cases, we have been building little or nothing at all. How can we build faster?
I often wonder why it is so difficult for a nation as developed, innovative and educated as Canada to build housing, energy infrastructure and other essential assets.

We did it before. Just consider the St. Lawrence Seaway. Major construction work was carried out between 1954 and 1959. In barely five years, a 300-kilometre stretch of water became a navigable waterway, which developed into a navigable system connecting the St. Lawrence River to the heart of the Great Lakes, covering more than 2,000 kilometres. I will let that sink in.

There is hope. Canada's new government is building one Canadian economy through major nation-building projects that will connect our regions and create hundreds of thousands of high-paying career jobs in fields ranging from skilled trades to advanced technology.

We are moving forward, protecting our sovereignty and diversifying our markets. In my region alone, the greater Quebec City area, important commitments have been made. These include the construction of six icebreakers valued at $11 billion, built by Davie. This project represents 5,000 jobs but, most of all, it represents predictability for the workers and for businesses and suppliers in the greater Quebec City area.
My remarks will focus on six aspects of the bill, and I will give a few examples to help everyone grasp the scope of each measure.

First, as I mentioned earlier, the bill seeks to fast-track nation-building projects in close partnership with the provinces, territories, indigenous peoples and private investors. For example, consider the creation of the Major Projects Office, which serves as a one-stop shop to speed up the approval and construction of major projects of national interest. Another example is Bill C-5, the one Canadian economy act, which serves as a legislative framework to fast-track projects of national interest, particularly in the energy, transportation and critical minerals sectors. I could also talk about the trade and energy corridors we are developing. Priority is being given to port infrastructure, including in my riding of Beauport—Limoilou, as well as to rail and energy links, to make it easier for Canadian businesses to access international markets.

Second, we need to launch the first buy Canadian policy, ensuring that public funds are used to strengthen our supply chains and support local innovation. Let us look at the buy Canadian policy. This is a commitment to leverage federal procurement as a tool to support Canadian businesses, workers and suppliers. I am also thinking about how public funds are invested in infrastructure. This approach is about prioritizing Canadian steel, aluminum and other materials in federally funded projects.

Third, we are currently witnessing Canada's largest defence investment in decades. I am thinking of the launch of the defence industrial strategy to build out our defence sector and increase the competitiveness of our local suppliers. Here are some more examples. Defence spending officially reached 2% of gross domestic product on March 26. We made a concrete commitment to significantly increase investments in the Canadian Armed Forces in order to modernize its equipment and operational capacities. Our approach to defence procurement reflects our desire to strengthen Canadian businesses' participation in military contracts and supply chains.

I spoke here in the House last week about the strategic importance of Bill C-40, which will allow an investment corporation to support companies that want to contribute to the defence sector in any number of ways, whether through loans, guarantees or insurance. We are investing in and supporting the modernization of our Canadian Armed Forces while developing a stronger Canadian defence industry and creating good jobs, all with a view to strengthening our sovereignty.

Fourth, we must seize new opportunities in a changing world by launching a trade diversification strategy that will double our overseas exports within a decade. For instance, take our target of doubling exports to Europe and markets other than our neighbour to the south over the next 10 years. This represents about $300 billion in new trade opportunities. Over 20 new trade agreements have been signed in the past year, opening up markets for Canadian producers and manufacturers. We are also creating the strategic exports office, which was announced this year, to support Canadian businesses in the aerospace, defence, energy and infrastructure sectors.

Fifth, we must stimulate growth and innovation by lowering investment costs for Canadian businesses through a new productivity superdeduction. The benefits are estimated at more than $9 billion per year. Canada has the most favourable tax system in the G7 for new business investment. Here is a concrete example. Imagine a business that wants to invest in modernizing its production line. It wants to invest in robots to automate its assembly line. For these major purchases and equipment, the business will need cash and will need to take out loans. From now on, that business will be able to deduct its capital cost in the first year. The same goes for Brûlerie Vieux-Limoilou, where I like to get my morning coffee in my riding of Beauport—Limoilou. If this coffee roaster needs to replace a coffee machine, it will be able to write off its purchase. The important thing to understand is that this applies to both large and small businesses.

As the October 2026 Monetary Policy Report states, “Rising business investment—bolstered by federal tax incentives such as the Productivity Mega Deduction—and increased adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) support production and labour productivity.”

Sixth, we must support a clean economy through Canada's new climate competitiveness strategy, which involves strengthening industrial carbon pricing, streamlining regulations and introducing tax incentives to attract investments in clean technology. Clean economy investment tax credits provide tax support for eligible investments in clean electricity, clean technology and other decarbonization activities. Fast-tracking clean energy and critical mineral projects will help to develop strategic sectors for the energy transition and improve Canada's industrial competitiveness.

Thanks to Canada's position as a world leader in clean technology and clean energy, we will be able to create jobs while reducing industrial emissions. Through our climate competitiveness strategy, we want to make Canada a world leader in clean energy and clean technology, while attracting investments, creating jobs and reducing our emissions. The time has come to build our economy bigger and faster than ever, so that Canada can become less dependent on others, more independent and better prepared for the future.
Mr. Speaker, how does Bill C-31 fit in with our objective of building a stronger Canadian economy while supporting workers and households?

Mr. Speaker, we are indeed at a pivotal moment, a crucial juncture. The cost of living is a major concern for our constituents, and we must be there to help them. That is why we brought in measures such as the tax cut for more than 22 million Canadians, the Canada groceries and essentials benefit, tax incentives for young people buying their first home, and the Canadian dental care plan, which has been an incredible success. It is brought up every time I talk to people in my riding. We are here for our constituents in these difficult times.

Mr. Speaker, I would like my colleague to clarify these economic sovereignty concepts for us. The government wants to propose major projects. I just mentioned LNG Canada as an example. This project is owned by foreign interests, including Shell, in the United Kingdom, Petronas, in Malaysia, PetroChina, in China, Mitsubishi, in Japan and Kogas, in South Korea. It is wholly financed by foreign capital.

I would therefore like my colleague to clarify how we can be masters in our own home, as he proposes, and strengthen our economic sovereignty, when the major projects of national interest that we are building are owned by foreign interests. The decisions that these companies make will be based not on our interests, but on theirs, which are not the interests of people here, in Quebec or in Canada.
Considering my colleague's expertise in investment and his professional experience in the financial field, can he shed some light on this issue, in the public interest?

Mr. Speaker, my colleague is right: Canada's economic sovereignty is important. Everyone knows what is happening with our neighbours to the south when it comes to the tariffs we are facing. We are supporting our businesses.

As for Quebec, my colleague knows full well how we support the Churchill Falls project, which will double electricity production. These are concrete actions. I also spoke earlier about Davie in Lévis, not far from his riding. That is an $11‑billion investment in our region. I remember that when I visited the Davie shipyard, there was talk of creating predictability for more than 600 suppliers within the region alone.
When we talk about economic sovereignty, helping SMEs and making decisions about the direction we want to take our economy, that is how we do it: by supporting our local SMEs.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question about the minister who would be responsible for the Defence Investment Agency. The minister would be able, for no reason, to disqualify a company for procurement purposes without explanation or justification and with no avenue for appeal. The minister would also have the ability to sole-source contracts without any accountability.
Does the member have a good understanding of why the Liberals have abandoned basic fairness in tendering? Why have they chosen to not be transparent in the process?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question about the investment agency and defence. I gave a speech on this issue because it is so important. I worked in banking for 20 years helping businesses secure funding.

Often, when there are new investments or new calls for tenders like these, businesses are unable to adapt. Banks also have a hard time adapting. By setting up this investment agency, which will be able to grant loans, offer insurance and provide guarantees to banks, we will help this sector grow. We are talking about companies that would like to contribute but that are unable to because they lack the liquidity, agility or time to do all that.
This agency will enable SMEs to grow and contribute to the defence sector. This is where we need to step in to help the defence sector.

Mr. Speaker, it is really fitting that we should be here today discussing budgetary matters the day before the Liberal government tables its 2026 budget. This is a budget implementation act, so it is an opportunity to talk about the state of federal finances, to have a look at where we are, how we got here and what the road ahead looks like. We should all buckle up because it looks like it is going to be a bumpy ride.

Let us start with where we are now. Well, for starters, we are in the red. There is a lot of debt. Even the Prime Minister's own economists confirm it. The Parliamentary Budget Officer, a non-partisan finance and accounting expert appointed by the government itself, just came out with a scathing report card saying exactly that. She said that our deficit now is more than double the size of the one left behind by Justin Trudeau just 18 months ago. Canadians already watched Justin Trudeau spend unprecedented amounts of money. Can members imagine just how much someone would have to spend to double that? Somehow, the Prime Minister and his finance minister found a way.

The Parliamentary Budget Officer warned that borrowing is backloaded and will get even worse before the end of this decade. What happens when someone spends more money than they earn? Anyone who has ever taken out a mortgage or carried a balance on a credit card knows the answer. Eventually, they have to pay for that borrowing. That is exactly what is happening here in Ottawa. The bankers and bondholders are not donating this money out of kindness. Every dollar of deficit the government borrows must be repaid, complete with interest. The Liberal government may run up the tab, but the bill always arrives in the mailbox of Canadian taxpayers, and that bill is becoming increasingly expensive. The federal government could take every single dollar it collects in GST from everything bought and sold across Canada for an entire year and it still would not be enough to cover 12 months of interest payments on our national debt.

The Parliamentary Budget Officer's calculations show that interest on the debt now costs Canadians more than the Canada health transfer. Ottawa is spending approximately $59 billion a year on debt charges, compared with about $57 billion for health transfers to provinces. Let us think about what that means. We have reached a point where the interest of past borrowing exceeds the federal government's largest transfer for health care. That should concern every Canadian, regardless of political stripe. Every single year, tens of billions of taxpayer dollars leave the federal treasury before a single hospital bed is added, before a single doctor is hired and before a single Canadian receives faster access to care.

We can imagine what $59 billion could do if it remained available for Canadian priorities. It could help reduce wait times in our health care system. It could provide meaningful tax relief to families struggling with the cost of living. It could strengthen the Canadian Armed Forces and support our brave men and women in uniform. Instead, that money is being consumed by debt charges while Canadians see no improvement in services, no shorter wait times and no direct benefit in their daily lives.

We all know the Prime Minister used to be the governor of the Bank of Canada. Given that background, Canadians could reasonably expect fiscal discipline from the government. In fact, David Dodge, another former governor of the Bank of Canada, offered a simple rule of thumb. The federal government should keep debt servicing costs below 10% of its total revenues. Beyond that point, borrowing becomes increasingly expensive as lenders demand compensation for the greater risk. When too much of the government's income is being consumed by interest payments, it becomes a warning sign that the country's finances are heading in the wrong direction.

The Liberal government crossed that threshold, and the problem has only gotten worse since. With more people and an aging population, there is a greater demand for services, so people might expect the fastest-growing federal expense to be health care, old age security or the Canada child benefit, but it is not. In fact, it is not even a service provided to Canadians. The fastest-growing line item is the interest on our debt. Just a few years ago, every Canadian owed about $600 in interest on the government debt. Right now, that stands at nearly $1,500. In five years, it will be nearly $2,000, or more than three times what Canadians were paying only a few years ago.

I want to speak directly to the people at home in Cambridge and North Dumfries who are watching today. They can think about what $2,000 could do for them right now. That is a month or two of groceries to help feed their family. It could cover a month's rent or help make a mortgage payment to keep a roof over their head. It could help pay down student loans, cover rising utility bills, replace a broken appliance or put a little money aside toward a down payment on a first home.

For most Canadians, $2,000 is not a small amount of money. It is the difference between getting ahead and falling further behind. That is the real cost of the Liberal government's reckless spending. Money that could be helping Canadian families build a better future for themselves is instead being used to pay interest on the government's debt.

That brings us to the next bump in the road. How did we get here? Deficits and debt do not appear overnight. They are the result of choices. The Liberal government repeatedly assured Canadians that there was a plan to keep the country's finances on track. It told Canadians that it could be trusted with a national credit card. The Prime Minister pointed to a series of so-called fiscal anchors that were meant to guide spending decisions and limit borrowing. The problem is that what he says and what he does are two very different things.

This week, the Parliamentary Budget Officer was clear. She said those anchors provide very little fiscal discipline when it comes to spending. Specifically, the Liberal government set out two fiscal anchors: a declining debt-to-GDP ratio and a declining deficit-to-GDP ratio. However, instead of going down, both of those ratios are going up. The government's problem is not that it missed its targets. The government's problem is that its targets are moving in the wrong direction. By its own metrics and standards, the government is failing.

It is perfectly clear that the government cannot be trusted to self-regulate when it can simply sit back and spend someone else's money, and that is why Conservatives are here: to hold the government accountable when it goes too far, to ask the tough questions Canadians deserve to have answered and to be the voice of reason and responsibility in this place.
The question is not whether there is a problem. The numbers make that perfectly clear. The real question is whether the government is prepared to change course before the situation gets worse.

More importantly, where do we go from here? The government is set to table another budget tomorrow, and Conservatives have some suggestions. To start, the government needs to rein in reckless spending and start living within its means. Fiscal responsibility does not mean abandoning priorities. We are not talking about cutting important social programs. We want to always be able to afford these programs, but in order to do so, we need to cut back on wasteful spending.

Conservatives have identified $150 billion in wasteful spending on foreign aid, consultants, bureaucracy and pointless projects that could be cancelled tomorrow to save Canadians money. If the Prime Minister does not want to do that, then we at least want him to keep his word and stick to the so-called fiscal anchors that he himself laid out. They are insufficient, but they are a start. More importantly, they are something the Prime Minister promised Canadians. Promises are easy to make. Fiscal discipline means keeping them when it counts.

Finally, we want the Prime Minister to save Canadians money on gas, groceries and everything else. He can do so by eliminating punitive taxes like the GST on fuel, the industrial carbon tax and the fuel standard. At the end of the day, this really is not all that complicated. Every person understands that one cannot spend money one does not have. They know that when the credit card bill comes due, somebody has to pay it.

Every dollar the Liberal government spends ultimately comes out of a hard-working Canadian's pocket. That is why we expect the government to exercise a little common sense, to prioritize the things that matter, to make responsible decisions and to recognize there is a limit to what taxpayers can afford. However, that is not what we are seeing from the government. Instead, we are seeing a government that wants to spend more, borrow more and tax more, while asking Canadians to simply have faith that everything will work out in the end. Canadians have heard that story before, and they are paying the price for it today.

Tomorrow, the Prime Minister will have another opportunity to demonstrate that he understands the seriousness of the situation. He can present a budget that gets spending under control, restores fiscal discipline and gives Canadians some much-needed relief, or he can double down on the same approach that got us here in the first place. Conservatives will be watching very closely, because our job is not to give the government a blank cheque. It is to make sure that every dollar of taxpayer money is spent responsibly, that families get a break wherever possible and that the next generation is not left holding the bill for today's decisions. If the Prime Minister cannot do that tomorrow, then Canadians should know exactly why.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my colleague on the opposite side a question. The bill also aims to strengthen Canada's defence and national security capabilities. Do the Conservatives support the development of a Canadian defence industry capable of supporting our armed forces and our workers?

Mr. Speaker, I agree that our defence program should be supported. Our men and women in uniform are definitely in need, but that shows the failures of what the government has been doing. These are things that should have been done years ago.

Currently, I am looking at businesses shutting down and investors leaving Canada. Manufacturers are telling me they can no longer wait for the supplies they need to fulfill their contracts. Jobs are being lost, and that is not building a stronger Canada. It is making a weaker economy and making life more unaffordable for Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague's speech addressed this government's debt load. For 10 years, we denounced the policies of Justin Trudeau's government, which relied on massive borrowing.

In light of last year's budget and what will be announced tomorrow, the current Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance, after incurring twice the debt and spending twice as much as their predecessors, make the Trudeau government look positively frugal. Are these spending choices really worth the level of debt they are producing?

The government takes pride in saying that we are in the best or in one of the best positions in the G7 or in the western world, yet it fritters away this advantage from one budget to the next. What does my hon. colleague think about that?

Mr. Speaker, I agree. The Parliamentary Budget Officer gave a scathing report. Spending is unprecedented. The government is spending more money than Justin Trudeau ever did, double the amount, and debt charges are now the fastest-growing piece of federal spending. This is leaving our children and future generations with generational debt, and that is not a sign of success. It is a complete signal of failure by the government.
Mr. Speaker, why is it that Liberal government overspending makes life unaffordable for Canadians? It makes life more expensive for everybody.

Mr. Speaker, right now over four million visits to the food bank in Toronto are happening. There is a senior in my community who is 71 years old. The amount of money she makes does not cover her rent, food and bills. She is on a wait-list for affordable housing, but the wait-list is 10 years long, and she is looking for a part-time job. At 71 years old, she is trying to get back to work. She cannot find a job and cannot pay her expenses. She reached out to ask me what I can do for her, what we can do for her or what government can do for her.
This amount of spending is not making life affordable. Seeing our seniors struggle after a lifetime of hard work is shameful.

Mr. Speaker, it was interesting this summer that I saw the member opposite post about announcements of regional tariff relief in her riding, and yet the members opposite voted against the budget, which had large liquidity supports to help businesses affected by the tariff war, the strategic response fund and the regional tariff relief that is keeping people employed.
Is the member opposite also opposed to infrastructure spending, housing and helping these industries pivot to defence? Those are jobs that are important in her riding and mine.

Mr. Speaker, being the tallest in a short room is not much of a plan. The measure that the Liberals like to quote is net debt, which counts the assets in our pension plan against what Ottawa owes. Those pension plans belong to Canadian workers and retirees and not to the government. This budget needs to focus on the concerns we are hearing from Canadians, and those are about making life affordable.

Mr. Speaker, if you will indulge me, I will note that just a short while ago, the member for Prince George—Peace River—Northern Rockies and I were notified that there was a mass casualty event impacting our ridings. As a matter of fact, a code orange has been declared by the hospital in Prince George as well as in Mackenzie due to a large bus accident. We are sending our thoughts and prayers to all those who are injured. Our thoughts and prayers are with all those involved, including the first responders who have attended this incident and the doctors, nurses and health care workers who are treating the injured. The extent of the injuries and casualties is not known at this point. It is not public knowledge, but I want to let everyone back home know that we are praying for them. I know that my colleague from Prince George—Peace River—Northern Rockies echoes my sentiments.

Canadians were promised a government focused on economic growth, investment and affordability. We were told that the Prime Minister was the man with the plan and the adult in the room, and that he had all this experience that was going to lead Canadians and our country to the promised land. Canadians made a choice, and they took it hook, line and sinker.

What we have seen over the last year is that food bank visits have more than doubled under the Liberal government. We have seen our debt more than double as well, and more than what the previous prime minister did in 10 years. In one year, the Prime Minister has more than doubled the debt. We now spend more money servicing the debt than we do on health care transfers to our provinces, which is absolutely shameful given the mental health and addictions crisis we have in this country.

We have more Canadians and working poor having to use a food bank just to put food on their table, yet day after day, the Prime Minister, the Liberal front bench and others stand up and say that Canadians have never had it so good. When we raise the issue, they say we are talking down projects and Canadians, but I disagree. We are fighting for Canadians. On this side, the Conservatives, the official opposition, are fighting for Canadians.

When a Canadian wakes up in the morning, the first thing on their mind is not the war overseas. It is the fact that they cannot put food on their table. They are worried if they are going to be able to make rent, make their mortgage payments or pay their bills. At the end of the month, there is far less of their paycheque left. In my riding of Cariboo—Prince George—Omineca, we have been hit so hard with job losses due to the forestry crisis. The government, like the previous Liberal government, has been unable to secure a softwood lumber agreement or put the hard-working families and communities that depend on forestry dollars first. It should care about them and make them a priority.

We have veterans who are struggling to make ends meet. I know there are some in the audience today. They are phoning Veterans Affairs to get help, and when pleading for help, they are being offered MAID.
An hon. member: Oh, oh!

Todd Doherty: Mr. Speaker, to my colleague heckling me across the way, I will say it is true. If she would like the information and the proof of it, she can come see me or any of my colleagues who have sat on the veterans affairs committee previously or sat on the MAID committee through the summer and heard the testimony. It is absolutely true, and it is shameful. The colleague across the way, who has been here for a minute, is doubting what I am saying. She should check my record of standing up for veterans and standing up for those who fight for our communities and fight for our country yet have been forgotten by the Liberal government. It is shameful.

Tomorrow is another day, and tomorrow the government has an opportunity to provide more hope and provide real action that will make life more affordable for Canadians. What are we going to see? I hope it is not more band-aids. I know the people in my riding are not looking for handouts. They are looking for an opportunity to work. They are looking for the government to stand up for them when they are at the negotiating table, but it is absent. The government likes to talk a big game, but it is not there.

Debt interest is projected to reach $83 billion a year. Food bank visits, as I mentioned, have doubled. Grocery prices are 33% higher now than they were in 2020. Canadians are working harder and paying more, yet too many are struggling to afford the basics. Conservatives believe the government should respect taxpayers, control spending and put affordability first. How about putting Canadians first? The Prime Minister spends more time in the air collecting air miles than he does in this House.
