In fact, the Supreme Court has told us that it is enshrined in the charter under Canadians' section 7 rights of liberty and security of the person.

Madam Speaker, I did appreciate the opportunity to work with my colleague opposite on the special joint committee. She is very passionate about this issue. She actually has co-hosted an event with Dying With Dignity Canada. The CEO of Dying With Dignity said the following: “Dying With Dignity Canada envisions a world where everyone who wishes to consider a MAID death can do so.” There is no acknowledgement in that line of any medical condition or any suffering whatsoever. Does my colleague agree or disagree with that vision?

Madam Speaker, in the House and around the committee table, we had the great benefit of hearing from so many people from a variety of backgrounds and with differing perspectives. In fact, it was a journey for me, too, to listen, because I came to the table with my own perspectives as well. Opening up one's mind, as we are doing here today in debating this bill, is so crucially important.

What I am envisioning for Canadians is what I have been talking about all along: the right to determine their own decisions with respect to their bodily autonomy and how they want to, if they choose to, leave this life in the way they choose is best for them.

Madam Speaker, the member pointed out that this legislation says that if a person were to resist, then the act of ending their life should stop, but what she does not acknowledge and should, I think, is that the legislation would not require that the person be informed before their life is taken. Very likely what would happen, based on an advance directive, is that someone would have something put in them without—
I have to allow the hon. member to provide a very brief answer.

Madam Speaker, I am without the benefit of hearing the entire question. However, no medical practitioner is going to want to put themselves in a position where they have administered MAID without informing the person ahead of time.
Madam Speaker, I will be splitting my time with the Leader of the Opposition.

The Liberals have learned absolutely nothing over the past five years from their disastrous planned expansion of MAID for mental illness. They decided to move ahead with this planned expansion before studying the issue. They did so by accepting an eleventh-hour Senate amendment to Bill C-7, legislation that had nothing to do with MAID and mental illness, until of course they accepted the amendment. They then proceeded to shut down debate and ram through the bill without any meaningful debate, consultation or study, thus setting the train in motion for MAID for mental illness.

Had they studied the issue first, rather than recklessly moving ahead with it, they would have heard what has been now made loud and clear by leading experts, including psychiatrists, namely that MAID for mental illness cannot be implemented appropriately and safely. The Liberals, because they did not do their homework, had to bring in two emergency bills to delay implementation. Here we are, five years and four bills later, and they have finally admitted they got it wrong all along and are now bringing forward legislation to put an indefinite pause on MAID for mental illness.

At the same time, here we are again, with the Liberals' recklessly seeking to ram through a new expansion of MAID, this time advance requests, by shoehorning advance requests into a bill to put an indefinite pause on MAID for mental illness, an expansion that will take place unless a bill is passed by March of next year. What the Liberals are doing is shutting down parliamentary debate and parliamentary scrutiny of the complex issue of advance requests. If there ever was an issue that deserves careful scrutiny, it is advance requests, because there are profound legal, ethical and practical issues at play, and there are significant risks.

The most significant risk identified in its 2018 report by the expert panel the Council of Canadian Academies, which is appointed by the government, by the way, is that in the case of advance requests, MAID could be administered against a patient's wishes. That is not an isolated or remote risk. It is a very real risk underscored by Health Canada's data in its annual reports on MAID, which show that each year, anywhere between 10% and 20% of patients who withdraw their consent withdraw it immediately before the administration of MAID.

The possibility that MAID could be administered against a patient's request really gets to the heart of the central issue around advance requests, and that is the issue of consent. On the question of consent, the Supreme Court of Canada, in the Carter decision, said that in order to qualify for MAID, a patient must clearly consent. The court used those words multiple times in that decision, “clearly consents”, which arguably implies that such consent must be contemporaneous. Hence, advance requests raise serious legal questions about whether they fall outside the parameters for MAID set by the Supreme Court, and whether explicit contemporaneous consent is constitutionally required.

Not only are there issues that are legal in nature, but there are also profound ethical concerns involving consent, because when consent is made in advance, it can never be fully informed consent. That is because it is made based upon future assumptions about one's circumstances, capacities or preference, not upon one's lived experience.

There is abundant research into effective forecasting that demonstrates that when a person is diagnosed with an illness or a condition, they are often poor predictors of what the future will look like. As Dr. Romayne Gallagher, a clinical professor in palliative medicine, told the Special Joint Committee on MAID:

Quote.QuotePara: ...medical and social science literature reminds us that people are poor at anticipating what life would be like with a life-changing illness or disability. People adapt to illness and disability and adjust their needs for a decent quality of life. Many medical conditions have long and unpredictable courses.

Content.ParaText: If consent cannot be contemporaneous and therefore cannot be fully informed, it raises the question, can there be true consent? If there cannot be true patient consent, then how can we ethically proceed with an advance request regime?

Now, proponents of advance requests often cite individual autonomy, but I would submit that individual autonomy in the context of advance requests is illusory. That is because advance requests necessarily result in not patient consent but third party consent, based upon observations that are often highly subjective in nature. After all, how does a MAID assessor confidently and accurately determine if a patient is suffering intolerably, which is a prerequisite for MAID to be administered, if the patient cannot communicate the degree to which they are suffering? That is what we invite with advance requests, namely, the administration of death based upon third party, often highly subjective observations of patients who cannot communicate and often have no ability to withdraw their consent.

Then there are other issues that need to be considered, including legitimate concerns that advance requests will lead to abuse and coercion resulting in vulnerable persons having their lives ended. There are concerns from a human rights perspective that advance requests undermine human dignity and will lead to discrimination against persons with cognitive disabilities, that a message is being sent that their lives are not worth living and that they are lesser human beings, completely undermining a fundamental principle of human rights: the universal and equal value of all human beings.

All of this underscores the need for careful study and meaningful consultation, none of which has happened, by the way. The Liberals have not done any meaningful consultation since the 2018 expert review, which recommended against moving ahead with advance requests, but instead the Liberals have learned nothing. Here we are again with the Liberals recklessly trying to ram through a complicated expansion of MAID. Canadians deserve better.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, I am going to go back to a question I have asked some of the member's colleagues. I think it is an important question. What I am hearing from the Conservatives, I believe, is not necessarily a fair reflection of the overall opinions of Canadians as a whole.

Does the member have any sense, in terms of the positioning by the Conservative members who have spoken so far, of whether it is truly reflective of what he believes a majority of Canadians might feel about the issue?

Madam Speaker, on a question of life and death involving an advance request regime, we need to proceed with caution. If the last five years is an illustration of the need for caution and the need to consult, it is precisely that. Yes, public opinion is one thing, but we need to look at how the regime could be rolled out, the risks involved, whether it is appropriate and, if it is appropriate, what safeguards need to be put in place.

Instead of doing that work, the Liberals are trying, yet again, to shut down debate and just ram it through under the deadline with respect to the expansion of MAID for mental illness, with the need to pass that bill to put an indefinite pause on that completely ill-advised and reckless planned expansion.

Madam Speaker, I would like to point out to my colleague that advance requests were the flagship recommendation of the first joint special committee. No one opposed them except, of course, my colleague and the Conservatives.

I would like to point out to him that the very principle of an advance request is to be able to work with a health care team to establish the threshold of what is tolerable, in other words, the criteria beyond which a person does not wish to continue their end-of-life in a state of deterioration that can ultimately lead to a level of stiffness akin to rigor mortis. Often, people do not die from Alzheimer's. They die from a host of concomitant illnesses. The bill states that all of this must be assessed in accordance with best practices.
Does my colleague fully understand that, in a sense, his reasoning is not ethical and his objections are not ethical, but rather purely legalistic, based on a theological foundation?

Madam Speaker, contemporaneous consent and issues around the ability to withdraw, or the inability to withdraw in the case of advance requests, which are fundamental to fully informed consent, are not legalistic issues. Yes, there is a legal element to it, but these are profound ethical questions around whether advance requests can be implemented safely.

The member spoke of the Special Joint Committee on MAID. All I can say is that there was a very limited, cursory review of the issue of advance requests at that committee, which studied multiple issues.
Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for his work on the Special Joint Committee on Medical Assistance in Dying.

I note that several of the members of the Liberal government who have spoken in favour of stopping the expansion of MAID to people with mental illness were, a few years ago, speaking in favour of expanding MAID to mental illness. The difference of a couple of years was enough for people to realize that this expansion should not be allowed to proceed.

In that context, I wonder if my colleague could offer his thoughts on why we should accept the government's artificial timeline to ram through advance requests when it is more than likely that in a few years, we will reach the same conclusion that we are reaching now on mental health, which is that the safeguards are failing and that can never be adequately woven into our MAID system.

Madam Speaker, I completely concur with the member for Elgin—St. Thomas—London South. There is absolutely no reason the provision for an advance request regime needs to be shoehorned into this bill. For years, the Liberals did nothing around advance directives. They did no studies, they had no consultation, and now, all of a sudden, they drop it into a bill in the face of a deadline to pass a bill by March.

It is completely unacceptable, it is cynical, and it is really just an attempt to ram this through, just as they did with mental illness, without any of the scrutiny that comes with careful study and review.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, imagine someone's phone rings and the voice on the other end of the line, a stranger, gives them the surprise request that they need to pick up their 26-year-old son at the morgue because of medical assistance in dying. He had no life-threatening illness. He had type 1 diabetes and some vision problems, but other than that, it was just depression. He had been denied medical assistance in dying because he was not eligible.

That was the story recounted to me by Margaret Marsilla, who came to visit me in this building. Kiano was only 26 years old, and although he struggled with diabetes and depression, he was not facing any end-of-life medical emergency. In fact, in Ontario, medical professionals had said he was not eligible. He shopped around for a different opinion and got one from a British Columbia doctor. I met his heartbroken mother in March, and her story is all too common.

In the last few years, we have seen the predictable consequences of a medical assistance in dying regime that fails to protect the vulnerable and even preys on them. Canada has become famous around the world as a cautionary tale for abuses in a system that too often sees death not as a last resort for patients suffering but as a first option for an overburdened health care system.

The statistics are stark. More than one in 20 Canadian deaths are by MAID. If we dig in, the numbers get even worse. One in 10 Canadians knows somebody who was offered medical assistance in dying even though they had no life-threatening condition and all of their conditions were treatable. Almost half of those who died by MAID in 2024 had reported feeling like a burden on family, friends and caregivers, raising the risk of induced death by guilt. Then there are individual horror stories, such as the Canadian Armed Forces veteran who contacted veterans affairs agents asking for government support for his ailments and was instantly offered MAID, or Father Larry Holland, a Catholic priest who went into the hospital for a fractured hip and was offered MAID not once but twice.

These are not isolated cases. Even the BC Civil Liberties Association, which was one of the interveners that sued the government to legalize euthanasia in the first place, now believes the procedure has gone too far. Last year, it was “aware of 'concerning reports' of people being offered MAID in circumstances that may not legally qualify” as well as people accessing MAID as a result of intolerable social conditions, not medical conditions but people living in misery, poverty or loneliness and being told that the best option for them is to die.

The organization called for safeguards to protect the more vulnerable patients so that they do not feel pressured to end their lives. Under these circumstances, the government had no choice but to pause its planned expansion of MAID for mental illness. I am pleased that the Liberals have once again reversed themselves on yet another radical experiment they had planned to impose on the Canadian people. Just as with net zero, mass immigration, catch-and-release criminal justice, legalized drugs and the carbon tax, they have been forced to reverse themselves yet again.

The committee that studied the question heard from doctors who were worried about allowing patients to make a decision in a moment of personal crisis and despair that can and often does get reversed later on. The close link between mental illness and suicide also raises a practical problem. One psychiatrist actually testified that there is a problem, an incoherence, in that “Psychiatry claims it can both prevent suicide in one patient and help finalize suicide in another with [both of them having] the same suffering.”

While I am glad the Liberals reversed themselves on one bad idea, I am disgusted that they have gone forward in the very same bill with another bad idea. In the same bill we are debating, which bans MAID for mental illness, the government would also legalize it for advance directives. These would allow persons to request MAID, at a time when they would not be eligible for it, for a future moment when they become eligible.

Doctors have sounded the alarm at the impossible situation in which this may put them and the family members of the suffering person. Imagine the case of a patient suffering with dementia. They have signed an advance directive, but now they are smiling. They are happy. They enjoy sitting outside with the sun shining on their face. Their grandkids are sitting on their lap, enjoying an ice cream after dinner. However, they have signed an advance directive. Everyone knows that this person, though they have lost their faculties, is happy going on living. What does a doctor do at that point? Do they administer MAID to a patient who looks happy and who everyone knows wants to live on, or do they refuse the directive the government says they have to follow and consider the family?
Most members would be aware of the story of Lisa Raitt, a former member of the House. She recently wrote online about her husband, who has been suffering with dementia for the last 11 years:
“If Bruce had signed an advanced directive, would I have been left to make the decision on when to apply MAiD?
“Even after 11 years, yesterday I saw him smile, laugh, interact and enjoy his meals while being non-mobile, incontinent and non verbal.

“I can promise you, I would ignore any advanced directive. Yes, he is a different man with a different life now but subjectively and objectively he is comfortable and content. I would not believe this Bruce would want to stop living.
“In this case, would the ‘state’ step in to provide MAiD over my objections and experience? We are rushing to a set of really complex entanglements. So much room for harm.”
Instead of looking for more ways to end life, we should be looking for ways to allow people to live the fullest life, with better care, more support, pain treatment, love and compassion.

We also know there is the fundamental problem that advance directives may not be accurate measures of what a patient would actually want in future circumstances. We have all said to ourselves that if such and such were to happen, we would want X or Y. Then when that eventuality comes about, we change our mind because the experience was different than what we thought. The attitude of a young person to death, for example, may be very different from an older person's and may be different from that of the person they become. It would be easy to say that someone would not want to live that or live under those circumstances, but when they find themselves in those conditions, it can turn out to be that life is better than they thought and they no longer desire death.

Many Canadians who are suffering serious health conditions can tell us from personal experience that there is hope they find and comfort they reach in the loved ones who surround them. Assuming that the conditions they live with would be reasons for someone else not to live ignores the experience and risks here, devaluing the lives of people in those circumstances.

I am not prepared to take away from doctors or from family members like Lisa Raitt the ability to act for their loved ones when no one else really knows what the loved one wants and no one else has a greater interest in the well-being of that loved one. These are painful decisions for doctors and families at the best of times. We should not make harder by rushing through dangerous legislation.

Unfortunately, the government has forced me and many others in this room into an impossible dilemma, those of us who want to ban MAID for mental illness and give people hope that they can have a brighter future and can come out of the bottom of the valley and get back to the mountain top. We want to vote to save their lives, but we do not want to vote to introduce new dangers that could end other lives that people would believe are worth living.

That is why we are calling for the government to split this bill. There is no reason to rely on the arbitrary deadline that is necessary to repeal MAID for a mental illness in order to avoid it coming into effect in March, to also then apply it to the swift passage of an extremely complex and highly dangerous new practice that is done almost nowhere in the world and that is fraught with serious risks.

This is literally a matter of life and death. I ask the government to split this bill to allow Canadians and their parliamentarians to express their conscience by voting on each section separately so that we can stand in this place and offer hope, compassion and love to the people who need it most.

Madam Speaker, I respect a number of the things the Leader of the Opposition raised. I know it is a very difficult topic for many Canadians. I can remember my father, in the final stages of his cancer battle, struggling with what he wanted to do in terms of his directions.

As we know, the bill would decriminalize advance directives. It would not set the framework. It would put forward the conversation, of course, that would take place between the provinces, but really, in this chamber it is about decriminalization. Does the Leader of the Opposition see a path in which, if he were satisfied with a framework that alleviated the concerns he raised in his speech, he would accept the decriminalized element of the process that this bill tries to achieve?
Madam Speaker, no I do not, because I do not believe that someone can grant pre-emptive consent for a subsequent death. There is a very serious risk no matter what we do.

Let us assume that I had answered the question with “yes”. That framework would take time. Serious and deadly risks would come with creating a system of rules for people to grant permission to die much later on once their ability to consent is gone, and that would require immense study and surgical precision, which cannot be done with a bill that would be rammed through before Christmas. This bill needs to be split so that we can ban MAID for mental illness and give hope to these people, but at the same time not make the deadly mistake of expanding into the unknown without doing our research.

Madam Speaker, the first thing I want to say is that there is no rush. We have been talking about this for five years, and Quebec has spent years working on it. Let us look at the models in place. They should not be dismissed just because they come from Quebec.

I want to make an analogy. I know someone who has been in politics his entire life. Image matters. Let us imagine that he unfortunately develops Alzheimer's. He makes a request to his loved ones in case there comes a day when he starts to behave completely differently, when they no longer recognize him, when he stops being able to feed himself and when he no longer behaves the way he did when he was in politics. I am not making a link here. When he arrives arrive at a long-term care facility, he keeps wanting to take his clothes off and starts flirting with all the women.
An advance request gives a person a way to say that, if they get dementia or any other disease, they never want their loved ones to let them go through this.
Is that not legitimate in terms of human dignity?

Madam Speaker, first of all, just because a person has finished one phase of their life and is beginning another does not mean that their life is over. A person may get sick, but their life still has value. Perhaps they want to continue living, but they are unable to communicate their will to live. I would not want such a person to lose their life.
I think that, in situations like this, we need to provide the best care, the best support and the most love for that person, whether they are a former politician or anyone else.
Madam Speaker, I thank the Leader of the Opposition for his tremendous intervention and for his leadership on this.

He alluded in his speech to a very important point, which is that Conservatives won the argument on stopping MAID for mental illness. Everything that my colleagues who were in the previous Parliaments warned against has happened. I note that on the Liberal side, just eight members supported a bill from our former colleague Ed Fast to stop the mental health expansion, and now they are putting it in government legislation.

Does the Leader of the Opposition agree that this is exactly why none of this, certainly not advance requests, should be rushed into on an artificial timeline? Even the Liberal government's own record acknowledges that the Liberals' minds were changed on this.

Madam Speaker, let us remember that it was the Liberal government that first legalized MAID for mental illness, which was set to come into effect in March of next year. The Liberals have all changed their minds, apparently, which proves that people change their minds.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, there are mixed emotions when approaching this particular debate because it is very much an emotional type of debate. I have had the opportunity to witness it first-hand for many years. In fact, when I look at its origins, I go back to just prior to the 2015 election, when a Supreme Court of Canada decision was made that ultimately put it on the agenda after Justin Trudeau was elected as Prime Minister. Under a new government, we had to deal with the issue. There was time for the Conservatives, even back in 2015, to attempt to bring forward legislation, but they did not do that.

If I reflect on the number of comments I have heard thus far, a lot of those comments are related to members wanting more debate. They want to have more discussion. It is not that often that I agree with a member from the Bloc, but I can tell members that I believe there has been a great deal of discussion and debate for decades now. One only needs to turn to the province of Quebec, where we see strong leadership on this debate.

It is a highly personal debate. What could be more intimate than discussions with family? I know this from my limited first-hand experience with the passing of my grandmother, when I was sitting at the St. Boniface Hospital, talking with my uncle and my father at her deathbed and listening to what the professionals had to say. Then a number of years later, and unfortunately the gap was not that great, came the passing of my father at the Riverview Health Centre. It is a bit better environment than St. Boniface Hospital, but the same questions were being asked, in particular with my father, who was scared of dying. Who blames an individual when that bridge comes?

There is a point in time in most lives where for an extended period of time, they reflect on that. When that time comes, I believe it is critically important for family, friends and health care professionals, who play a critical role, along with spiritual leadership quite often, to get engaged in a very real and tangible way. I think we often underestimate the important role that our health care providers and those who support them play when it comes to end-of-life care.

I think of my father's passing. When we got him into the Riverview Health Centre, it did not look very promising. There were some medications that ultimately made him feel a whole lot better. I remember him saying to me, “I'm feeling better today than I was three weeks ago.” I talked to the doctor about it, who said that a lot depended on the medications and that while they had been very successful, we should not build our hopes up because it would be very short term. The doctor was right. It did take place relatively quickly.

My father, in the discussions he was having with me, was talking about the cemetery and where he wanted to be buried. He wanted us to understand that he did not want something prolonged like what he had witnessed, to a certain degree, with his mother, my grandmother, at the St. Boniface Hospital.

We really never know until we are put into that position, but I do believe, at my core, that it is the person who should have the ability to make that decision. When we take a look at what has taken place over the last few decades, I go to Sue Rodriguez who, during the early 1990s, had Lou Gehrig’s disease. She raised the discussion, not only on a national level, but back then it was taken into consideration around the world.

When it came to MAID back in 1993, our Supreme Court of Canada made the decision, 5-4, not to move ahead, no doubt for all sorts of reasons. However, the debate has evolved significantly since then. I would like to read what Sue, apparently sometime in December 1992, stated. She said, “I want to be in charge of my life and my death.”

I was a parliamentarian back then and I followed the news quite closely. I can tell members that it ignited a fierce discussion, and it was not just in Manitoba. I believe that discussion has never ended. When we take a look at the Carter decision, which was made prior to the 2015 election, maybe it was at the end of 2014 or 2015, but if we take a look at the arguments, I suspect that the world had changed, because even when the decision was made about Carter by the Supreme Court, there were actually a number of countries that had already put MAID into place, or some form of MAID.

Public opinion has changed on the issue of MAID, even in the last decade since we passed the original legislation, which is why I was posing the question to members opposite. I was not trying to be mischievous. I believe that opinions have changed. If we canvassed Canadians as a whole, we would find that a majority of Canadians want us to move in this direction.

When I think of the individuals who show up at my discussions at McDonald's or in other environments, it seems to reinforce the public opinion that we need to look at moving in the direction that this legislation is bringing us. It is why I highlighted that it is important when we look at legislation, in good part, that we reflect on what a majority of Canadians would want us to be saying.

We can still have our strong personal beliefs, and that is why I asked one member what they felt their constituents would have to say. Is there not a responsibility at least to have more of a balanced approach in debating the legislation? I have not seen that balance coming from the Conservative members thus far in the debate. That even includes the leader of the Conservative Party.

I do believe we need to have a perspective that deals outside our personal opinions. This is why I think it was important for me to talk about a bit of the history and how it has been evolving. As I said, with the Carter decision, there were countries that had MAID. Since that decision, we have seen many other countries explore MAID and I suspect some of those countries are even looking at what Canada has been doing with MAID, because Canada does matter, not only on economic issues, but on social issues also.

We talk about establishing a framework that would allow provinces to put into place a process that protects the integrity of the system. I can appreciate that there are examples that are going to be brought forward during this debate and even previously where there might have been very strong allegations, some of them no doubt proven to be true, which cause a great deal of concern to every member of the House, no matter what side of the debate they are on. For example, when I hear about a veteran who has been instructed, that concerns me greatly, as it would for any Canadian who has been hoodwinked or made to believe they do not have any other options. That does disgust me, but it does not mean we get rid of the opportunity for the thousands of people who have accessed MAID because they believed it was important for them. This is why I say that this has been evolving.

When we talk about establishing the framework with strong guardrails, the debate does not end here. The debate will continue on in provincial and territorial regimes in Canada. Members across the way will say they want one standard practice across the nation. It does not work that way. We have provincial jurisdiction. They are constitutionally given jurisdictions that we have to be sensitive to and respect. This means we have to work with provincial and territorial governments in hopes that the provinces that want to continue to provide MAID are in a position to do so.

I would expect those provinces and territories to add to the very basic guardrails we would be putting into place, and I believe they will. I believe that just as I believe that every member in the House of Commons is genuinely concerned about the subject matter. After all, we are talking about life. I believe the provinces and territories will also take the issue as seriously as members of Parliament do. As we, the Supreme Court and other courts have recognized, it is time that we see the charter, understand what a right is and bring forward laws that would enable MAID not only to exist, but to be supported and, at the same time, protect the individual.

That is something that is within this legislation. There is no need to divide the legislation, as the Conservatives are arguing for. In my opinion, we cannot justify it. If someone says that they want more debate time, what they are really saying is that they do not want it to pass, because we have had decades of commentary and debate, inside the House and outside the House. The public has weighed in. Our courts have weighed in. Parliament has weighed in.

I was here through the many debates that we have had inside the chamber over the last decade since we actually decriminalized it in 2016. I witnessed members of all political entities cry, share their stories and talk about what had taken place in the committees, which was gut-wrenching, no doubt, at times. We have had the opportunity, and we are going to have still more debate and more committee meetings on the issue. However, let us say, for the sake of argument, that we were able to pass the legislation with the its principles still intact. I do not want to preclude what could happen at the committee stage.

We should be able to pass this, hopefully before Christmas. I believe that is a reasonable request, but one of the ways we can ensure that, and have time at the committee stage, would be for the House leadership teams to work on a way that we could actually pass this legislation to committee stage.

Why oppose its going to the committee stage? At committee stage, there would be ample opportunities for stakeholders and parliamentarians to continue adding comments, issues, concerns and so much more. The opportunity is there, but I believe that we need to move forward with the principles of the legislation, as I would ask of those individuals who want to continue debate.

I unfortunately do not have enough time. I would have loved to talk about the issue of hospice care. I would have loved to talk about the issue of palliative care. It is not just money. It is an important aspect, but the greatest threat to health care is not just financial resources, but it is how we manage the changes that are necessary so that we can have the type of quality health care that Canadians want and expect. There needs to be more financial accountability in that area. We need to look at personal care facilities, hospice care facilities and how our hospital institutions administer and provide palliative care, as an example.

I look forward to seeing provinces and territories enter into the debate and discussions, and to taking a look at what the province of Quebec already has on the table. There are already things in place that other jurisdictions can look at. I suspect, over the coming weeks and months as the bill leaves Parliament, that we are going to see more debates on it at the provincial and territorial level, where they will no doubt be expanding on the issue of safeguards and protecting the rights of the individual.
I see my time has expired. I appreciate the opportunity to share a few words.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Tako Van Popta (Langley Township—Fraser Heights, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, my colleague from Winnipeg North is suggesting that Conservatives should look at polls more, and I am suggesting that we should be debating these very deep, ethical, complex issues a whole lot more. Would he agree that we cannot just escape our duty as parliamentarians by looking at the polls, but that we need to do a deep dive and study this, like we did with MAID for mental illness?

I would remind the member that, after six years, all the people on that side of the House changed their mind on that issue because of the deep debate that we had on that. Would my colleague agree with me that we need to have a similar debate on this very complex issue of advance medical directives?

Madam Speaker, I would not suggest that Parliament has to follow polls. I would suggest that it is imperative, when we talk about an issue like this, that we ensure that we represent the different sides. It should not be all one-sided. For example, I posed a question to one of his colleagues and the remark was that the majority of all the people who contacted that member do not like it, or something of that nature. That is the essence of it.

I think we have seen an evolution. I say “evolution” because it really has not been all that fast. We are going back to the nineties. The legislation that the government has put forward is, ultimately, a reflection of today's times. We do need to move forward, and there is still the opportunity for the provinces and territories to administer it.

Madam Speaker, my colleague from Winnipeg North spoke about Quebec's approach to advance requests. It was a long and rigorous process, but we came up with legislation. He says that process should be respected, but when it comes to administering medical assistance in dying, rather than introducing the notion of reasonable means to relieve intolerable suffering, as his bill does, why not use the wording in the Quebec legislation, which refers to determining whether an individual is experiencing suffering that cannot be relieved under conditions the patient considers tolerable?

A person's conditions could be completely intolerable and yet, through what might be considered reasonable means, such as chemical restraint, it could become impossible to respect that individual's criteria. That is my first point.
Second, how can an experienced legislator vote in favour of the principle of a bill that is unconstitutional and discriminates against people with mental illness?

Madam Speaker, I know the member has been a very strong leader on the whole debate around MAID for a number of years, and I have appreciated his contributions, as the minister expressed to me his appreciation of the member's comments. I know he gives a lot of thought to it.

I would encourage the member to take advantage of what he brings to this Parliament on the issue. The depth of his knowledge of what is happening in Quebec could be of great benefit to Parliament. I trust and hope he will be one of the committee members, but he might want to consider bringing some of his thoughts and ideas, even before bringing them to committee, to the minister.

Madam Speaker, I am glad to see my colleague from Winnipeg North supporting, in principle, anyway, a halt to the forthcoming expansion of MAID for people with mental illness. However, the member has voted three times against stopping that expansion. He voted for adding mental illness to the MAID regime in Bill C-7. He voted against Bill C-314 in the previous Parliament, and a couple of weeks ago, he voted against Bill C-218.
To what do we attribute the change of heart?

Madam Speaker, for one of the private members' bills that the member referenced, there was already discussions of the government bringing in legislation. The member knows that. After all, there is a court order, and if we do not respect that court order, it will cause a great deal of problems. We need to be able to make changes.

At the end of the day, I would suggest to the member, as I tried to do in my comments, that as we have seen the debate evolve, we have seen significant changes. Some of those changes are brought upon us through courts and others were through lived experiences. We have had more people provide their thoughts on it since we have now had it over a decade.

One thing I made reference to earlier, which the member would no doubt be aware of, is there are many more countries today that have MAID legislation. I think it is becoming better understood, not only here in Canada, but abroad as well.
Madam Speaker, how does the government plan to work with the medical community and the provinces to make sure that advance requests are implemented smoothly and surely?

Madam Speaker, I really appreciate the member's question because it amplifies the importance of recognizing that the provinces and territories play an absolutely critical role. The province of Quebec is the one in the best position.

The minister and the Government of Canada are very open to working with provinces and territories if there are ways we can be supportive in those guardrails. We are obviously very concerned in that regard. I have faith and confidence in our provinces and territories to bring in the legislation and the regulations necessary to provide that high sense of comfort for all.

Madam Speaker, the nature of autonomy is that people change their minds. They might think that some future circumstance is intolerable to them. Then, under those circumstances, they have a different experience or an adaptation to those circumstances that they were not expecting. This is why, generally speaking, we do not allow our present selves to bind our future selves.

As it relates to MAID specifically, the latest numbers show 692 people in 2024 made requests for MAID and then changed their minds. Obviously, there are going to be a lot of people who are thinking about this, so they make the request and then decide not to do it. However, with the advance directives framework in this bill, a person would be killed based on a previous expression of their desires without even being asked in the moment. This is clear in the legislation. There is no requirement that the person be told what is about to happen to them before it happens.
What does the member think this would mean for the 692 people who thought they wanted MAID and decided they did not? Would those people be alive today under this framework?
Madam Speaker, the short answer to that is yes, they would be able to say no up until the very end. I will look a bit more into the issue.

At the end of the day, as the member himself pointed out, there are 600 and some people who said yes at one point, but changed their minds. To me, that says the system worked for those individuals because they changed their minds, unless I am missing—
Resuming debate, the hon. member for Langley Township—Fraser Heights.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Tako Van Popta (Langley Township—Fraser Heights, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, at the outset, I would like to note that I will be sharing my time with my colleague, the member for Elgin—St. Thomas—London South.

Tonight, we are debating Bill C-41, the medical assistance in dying safeguard act. This bill would do two substantially different things. First, it would permanently cancel the expansion of MAID for those who are suffering from mental illness. Second, it would introduce a framework for advance medical directives allowing individuals to make decisions in advance about receiving MAID if they later lose the capacity to consent. I support the first measure. I cannot support the second.

The permanent exclusion of mental illness as the sole underlying condition for MAID is a necessary and long overdue correction. It reflects what many medical experts have been saying, including mental health professionals and disability advocates, which is that our health care system cannot reliably distinguish between a treatable mental illness and an irremediable one. The risks are simply too great. I am happy that the Liberals have finally come to that conclusion as well.

Advance medical directives, on the other hand, raise a very different and a far more complex set of ethical and legal questions. They touch on issues of consent, autonomy and the value of human life at the moment when a person may no longer be capable of expressing their wishes. These two issues should never have been bundled together in one single bill. One requires urgent legislative action before a deadline that is only six months away. The other demands careful study and thoughtful consideration.

To understand why the government is finally reversing course on the first issue, medical assistance in dying for those who are suffering from mental illness, it is useful to explore how we arrived at this point. It all started with the Sue Rodriguez case in 1993, where the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the Criminal Code provision that prohibited assisting somebody to die, to commit suicide. Twenty years later, the Carter case came along, and the Supreme Court of Canada changed its mind. It came to quite a different conclusion.

Faced with the circumstances of Ms. Kay Carter, who suffered from ALS, a progressive and incurable neurodegenerative disease, the court found that an absolute prohibition of physician-assisted dying was a breach of section 7 of the charter. The court stated that MAID could be available for people in Ms. Carter's condition as long as that adult was one who clearly consented to the termination of life and it was a grievous and irremediable condition causing enduring and intolerable suffering. It was those two things: clear consent and an irremediable condition. Importantly, the court also emphasized that it really was limited to those specific facts, which is exactly what courts usually do. It was making no pronouncement over any other situation where physician assistance might be sought, for example, for mental illness.

Parliament responded to that Carter decision with Bill C-14, establishing a MAID framework that included a further requirement, that natural death had to be reasonably foreseeable. We thought that was going to be our MAID regime going forward into the future. Unfortunately, that proved to not be the end of the story.

For the next chapter in how the Liberals have mismanaged this whole MAID file, we turn to the Truchon decision in Quebec, where two individuals successfully challenged the “reasonable foreseeability of natural death” provision. What happened next was remarkable. Rather than appealing a lower court decision that struck down an act of Parliament, the Liberal government, the attorney general, chose not to defend the legislation that had been adopted in the House after one of the most significant ethical debates in modern Canadian history. The result was Bill C-7. The legislation created two tracks, one for those whose death was reasonably foreseeable and the other for those who were not in a situation of dying. Significantly, Bill C-7 expressly stated that mental illness alone would not qualify a person for MAID.

After Bill C-7 passed in the House of Commons, the Senate, shockingly in my opinion, proposed amending the bill. It proposed removing the mental illness exclusion after a sunset period of two years. Instead of rejecting the amendment, which the Liberals should have done, the Attorney General, who also should have done it as it is his job to defend the laws of Parliament, accepted it. They caved to the MAID activists. That decision launched Canada down a path that many experts have said is dangerous.

For example, in November 2023, the chairs and heads of numerous psychiatric departments across Canada said that there is “no...accepted definition of irremediability” in mental illness and “no reliable way to distinguish a MAID request from suicidal ideation.” That is what the experts were saying. I am happy that the Liberals finally listened to that and are convinced. They cautioned against expanding MAID in these circumstances, saying that it would risk facilitating preventable deaths and undermine suicide prevention efforts.

The Liberal government did the right thing, sort of. It postponed the implementation date, at first by one year and then later by three more years. Here we are, after six years of uncertainty. The government has finally arrived at where many experts and Canadians believed it should have been all along: MAID for mental illness alone is not sound public policy. The government made the right decision in the bill that is before us, and we agree with that part of it.

However, while retreating from one problematic expansion of MAID, the government would now advance another that is even more problematic. Advance medical directives would allow individuals to specify in advance the circumstances under which they would wish to receive MAID if they later lose the capacity to consent. Now, at first glance, many Canadians might think, well, that makes sense. We write wills. We write powers of attorney. We write health directives. Why should we not write advance medical directives for MAID?

MAID is substantially and fundamentally a different matter. Advance directives concerning MAID authorize an irreversible act that results in death, with someone else, a third party, being tasked with making the ultimate decision. The Liberals talk a lot about the importance of the autonomy of the person. Well, someone has lost autonomy when somebody else is making the decision. That is why many experts urge caution.

For example, Dr. Pageau of Université Laval told the Special Joint Committee on MAID that it is simply not ethical to permit MAID for persons with dementia through advance requests. He posed this question: As the disease progresses, are we honouring the wishes of the person who exists today, or the wishes of someone who existed years earlier? People change their mind. That question deserves much deeper examination before Parliament accedes. We should not be rushing through this very complex ethical question.

The strongest concern with advance medical directives is the issue of consent. The Supreme Court's decision in Carter began with the simple and essential principle that an individual “clearly consents to the termination of life”. Advance directives risk undermining that basic principle.

Dr. Alice Chung appeared before the special joint committee and posed an important question. She asked this: What right does the 60-year-old version of ourselves have to determine the quality of life experienced by the 80- or 90-year-old version of ourselves? She went on to note that medical evidence demonstrates that many individuals adapt to their severe illness, to their disability or to their cognitive decline in ways that they had not anticipated when they might have signed advance directives. What once to them seemed intolerable looking into the future, being uncertain of the future, may later become meaningful and a worthwhile life.

These are not abstract scenarios. They are real-world examples that we received from experts, which raised difficult questions about autonomy, dignity and the risk of ending the life of someone who may no longer share the wishes they had expressed years earlier.
In conclusion, we applaud the government for proposing to stop the expansion of MAID, but we say that it must not—
Questions and comments, the hon. parliamentary secretary to the government House leader.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, if we take the other side, what about individuals who feel very passionate about the fact that they want to be able to make that decision? Does the member feel any sense of obligation to those individuals? After all, they know they can always reverse the decision. Why does the member feel that person should not have the right to make the decision?

Mr. Speaker, I will go back to the Carter decision, which said that consent is at the centre of MAID, and the autonomy of the human being to make that decision. A person cannot change their mind anymore after they become incapable. Somebody else has to make that decision for them, and that undermines the autonomy of that person and undermines the very central principle of consent to receiving MAID. That is why I object to it.
Mr. Speaker, there has been some confusion in the debate tonight around the issue of whether a person could withdraw consent if they make an advance directive. Let us clear it up.

If I sign an advance directive today but three weeks later, still having capacity, think I actually do not want to do this anymore, could I withdraw my advance directive? Yes, I could. However, if a person signs an advance directive and then loses capacity, they are not in a position to withdraw it. In addition, if a person does not want MAID at the time they are about to receive it, they could still be given MAID, because there would be no requirement to tell them what is about to happen to them. Yes, if the person resists physically in the moment, the legislation would require that the process of MAID stop, but if a person is simply told—
An hon. member: Oh, oh!

Garnett Genuis: Mr. Speaker, I hear the member saying, “needle in the skin”. There does not have to be a needle in the skin to administer MAID. Someone could already be on an IV, and the content of the IV could be changed. There would be no requirement to tell someone what is about to happen, which is clearly concerning in terms of the right to withdraw consent, is it not?

Mr. Speaker, my colleague's question is central to the issue of medical assistance in dying, MAID. The Carter case said that MAID can be applied only when the person clearly consents. Being able to change their mind is part of that autonomy. If a patient cannot withdraw their consent, there is no longer autonomy. I think it goes against the Carter case. It certainly goes against ethics and moral law.

Mr. Speaker, this evening, I cannot help but feel that there is a great deal of hypocrisy in this House. On the one hand, we know exactly where the Conservatives stand. On the other, the Liberals' position is far less clear.

In Quebec, however, things are clear. In fact, this morning I heard on the news that Quebec reached an objective decision through a non-partisan commission that examined the issue of the right to die with dignity.

Do my colleagues understand what it means, from a clinical perspective, to administer MAID? This morning, I saw a video produced by Santé Québec Montérégie-Est, which explained that, at every stage, the doctor asks the patient whether this is still what they want.

My point is simple. In Quebec, it has been clearly established that MAID is not available to just anyone and that there is a specific procedure to follow. Are my colleagues familiar with the clinical procedures that govern MAID?

Mr. Speaker, I realize there are differences of opinion on this very important ethical and legal question, and I respect that. We are not all going to be of the same mind on these issues, but what I am saying is that the evidence we have so far from the MAID committee suggests very clearly that this requires a much deeper dive. We need to have a study. The bill should be split so we can advance with one issue and put the other to committee for a deep-dive study.
Mr. Speaker, it is always a great honour to rise in the House, and, I will say, especially so to speak to this legislation.

One of the reasons I got into politics, one of the planks of my campaign for the nomination for my party, was to put an end to MAID for mental illness. That is a position that up until a few months ago, the Liberal government was dead set opposed to. For years, the Liberals have argued that MAID must expand to include people with mental illness. Even when concerns were being raised about the lack of readiness and the lack of willingness by provinces and physicians, they would not abandon this. They instead kept kicking the can down the road.

It was a great privilege to serve on the Special Joint Committee on Medical Assistance in Dying, a committee that was assembled by Parliament and was tasked very specifically and narrowly to explore the issue of whether MAID could ever be safely or reasonably expanded to people with mental illness. The committee turned back a single recommendation, which Liberal and Conservative members on the committee were united on: that the expansion of MAID to people with only a mental illness not proceed.

To have Liberals and Conservatives in alignment on a matter of conscience, on a matter such as that, is so important, especially on something that just a couple of years ago, just in the previous Parliament, the majority of the Liberal caucus voted against doing.

When Bill C-314 was put forward, a bill to stop the expansion of MAID to mental illness, only eight Liberal members supported it. That is a huge problem. I am grateful they have now come around to the conclusion that Conservatives were warning about for years: that we must protect the vulnerable. People struggling with mental illness need our support.

Yes, we need services and treatment. More importantly, we need to be instilling hope, not sending a message that someone is better off dead than alive. I have said in the House many times, and I will reiterate it so everyone knows, this is an issue that is very personal to me. I nearly lost my life to suicide just under 16 years ago, and I very likely would not be here today if MAID for mental illness had been available in 2010, when I was in my darkest days. I can say that with a level of confidence, seeing how existing safeguards have not worked, how existing safeguards in the MAID regime have not prevented people who do not meet the legal criteria from accessing MAID.

Earlier today, the leader of the official opposition mentioned in his speech the case of Kiano Vafaeian, a 26-year-old who dealt with diabetes and partial blindness, and, more importantly, had a range of mental health issues. He was denied MAID in Ontario, but he went doctor shopping. He went to another province, found one of the most prolific purveyors of MAID in Canada and received it. His family got the call that he had died at the hands of a doctor.

There have been other cases that we heard about at the special joint committee, and others that we have heard in the media. People have also reached out to me with their stories. There are stories of people who have been offered MAID who do not want it and stories of people who do not meet anything resembling the legal criteria right now but who have nonetheless been found eligible or told they would be.

There is a very fundamental question facing parliamentarians right now: If existing safeguards on the current MAID regime right now are not working, how would it be anything other than reckless and irresponsible to expand the system in any way?

This brings us to Bill C-41. Despite the singular recommendation that Liberals and Conservatives agreed on to stop the expansion of MAID to people with mental illness, Bill C-41 is not a bill about that. In fact, the 12 pages of Bill C-41 contain three sentences dealing with MAID for mental illness. Two and a half clauses, but three sentences, of the 12-page bill would stop the expansion of MAID that would allow people with depression, schizophrenia or an eating disorder access to this regime, to a medically guided, medically directed death.

The rest of the bill, the rest of the 12 pages of Bill C-41, proposes an expansion of MAID called advance requests, MAID for people who would not be able to consent because they will have lost the capacity, but who wish to consent ahead of time. This would be people with very real, very serious degenerative neurological conditions such as Alzheimer's and other dementias.

This is something we find deeply concerning, if we have been following the lack of safeguards already. When I look at this bill, I see a range of issues, some of which we have heard mentioned in debate tonight, such as the fact that one does not need to be told that MAID is about to be administered before it is; that a doctor or nurse practitioner has tremendous latitude to make, in their own opinion, a determination as to whether someone's suffering is sufficiently intolerable for the request to be actioned, a request that might have been made a decade earlier; and that if the person says no but the practitioner believes there is sufficient doubt as to whether they were really saying no, the practitioner can simply try again in 30 days. That is what the bill says: They can try again in 30 days if there is doubt as to whether the person was refusing it.

Some of the MAID practitioners in Canada who have become quite well known talked about this issue before Bill C-41 was tabled. Some of these physicians have said that if someone who has an advance request is screaming “no” and flailing their arms around, doctors would disregard that, as they do not believe that is legitimate because they have made a determination that this person does not know what they are saying or doing. Doctors have already said they intend to ignore what I think are already quite lax guidelines and stipulations set out in Bill C-41. If existing safeguards are not working, how can we ever expect an expansion to not lead to many more problems?

At every step of the journey, as we have discussed MAID in Canada, there have been those warning of the slippery slope. If we expand it to this, then there is going to be something else next. At times, many on the Liberal benches have said they are fearmongering. We are barrelling down the slippery slope right now. Every single prediction that has been made about where this is going has come to pass.

I would note that the Liberals have done something very cynical. By marrying the provisions stopping the mental health expansion with advance requests, they are holding a gun to the heads of members of Parliament, forcing us to put a complicated and divisive bill forward on a timeline that is not necessary, because we are all committed on the Conservative benches to ensuring that the mental health expansion does not kick in in March of next year.

If we do nothing, if no legislation is passed, people with a mental illness as a sole underlying condition will be eligible for MAID. That is why Liberals could have done the right thing two weeks ago and voted for Bill C-218, legislation that I was proud to cosponsor and that was put forward by my colleague from Cloverdale—Langley City, legislation supported by the Green Party leader, New Democrats, a couple on the Liberal benches and huge numbers of Canadians, including disability rights advocates and mental health organizations. If the Liberals had supported that bill, we would have been off to the races. We could have had the time necessary to debate and discuss advance requests, hear witness testimony and ensure that all sides and many Canadians had the opportunity to have a say. Instead, we have comments like those from the member for Etobicoke—Lakeshore, who said that the first part of the bill is not only important but urgent, because if we do not pass this bill immediately, this law will take effect on March 17, 2027. He asked every member of this House to vote in favour of Bill C-41 for that reason.

The Liberals are already saying that we are the ones who have to force this bill through to meet a timeline that they are setting by their refusal to separate these two fundamentally distinct provisions. They refuse to allow separate bills or even separate votes on whether to expand MAID to people with mental illness and whether to expand MAID to people who wish to make an advance request. That is a tremendously reasonable response from us to the Liberals, if the Liberals are serious about, as they keep saying, getting this complicated issue right. They should split the bill and dispense with these cynical, divisive politics that are gambling with people's lives.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I am going to start off by giving a quote directly from the legislation. Under clause 5, it states:

Quote.QuotePara: A medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must not administer a substance to a person to cause their death on the basis of an advance request if the person demonstrates, by words, sounds or gestures, refusal or resistance to have the substance administered to them. Once the person demonstrates such refusal or resistance, medical assistance in dying can no longer be provided to them on the basis of that request.

Content.ParaText: We need to think about what the legislation says. A number of members of the Conservative Party have stood in their place and said something completely opposite to that. I suggest that that is what we have to guard against: misinformation on such a serious debate.
Mr. Speaker, I would ask the member to read the next paragraph:

Quote.QuotePara: If the medical practitioner or nurse practitioner is in doubt as to whether the person's words, sounds or gestures constitute a demonstration of refusal or resistance to having the substance administered to them, they must not, at that time or at any time within the following 30 clear days, administer the substance to the person.

Content.ParaText: If the government cannot even get its own legislation right, why is it forcing us to pass it through on an expedited timeline?

Mr. Speaker, my colleague knows full well that the role of the state is not to presume it knows better than the person who is suffering what is best for that individual in a matter as intimate as their own death. The role of the state is to ensure the conditions necessary for a free and informed choice.

This is what I would ask my colleague: On what basis should the state infringe upon or restrict the right to self-determination of a person whose mental illness is resistant to treatment, as long as their decision-making capacity remains intact? On what grounds should chronic suffering that has become intolerable be considered reasonable? On what grounds would discrimination be reasonable?
Mr. Speaker, I am never going to argue with someone who is advocating for smaller government, but I know there is a very inconsistent way in which the member is pushing for that.

The role of the state, at its core, is to protect those who cannot protect themselves, to protect the vulnerable. What we have seen in the current MAID regime, as evidenced by the litany of cases I could and have referenced about the lack of safeguards, is that the system is in many ways preying on people who do not have the capacity or independence to resist it. That is exactly why it is important to get legislation like this right. It is why I believe advance requests can never properly account for all of the issues that have been raised in the course of the debate this evening, which I do not believe can be rectified.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. My colleague need not show any contempt for my position here in the House. I was democratically elected.

We pay taxes to the Canadian government, and as long as we pay taxes to the Canadian government, we will be represented in this Parliament. I would therefore ask the member to apologize for his contempt for me.
I did not hear the rules being broken. Could the member for Montcalm briefly clarify that?
Mr. Speaker, he would not answer my question because my presence here is not legitimate, since I am not a federalist.

That is a matter of debate, and I will not intervene in the debate. I will leave it to the members to discuss it outside the House. I did not hear anything during the exchange, although I did listen carefully to the remarks that were made. I do not have the ability to listen to the interpretation provided to us by the interpreters. As such, I did not hear anything that violated the Standing Orders of the House or caused a breach of a member's privilege.
The member can check the blues or Hansard once what was said has been transcribed. If he then deems it necessary, he may raise another point of order.
Questions and comments, the hon. member for Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan.
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my friend and colleague for his excellent work on this important issue.

He has spoken a lot in the context of this issue about hope, about people finding hope, about people recovering and about people being able to continue their lives under new circumstances. I think that relates to the point about advance requests. In the last report on MAID in Canada, 692 people made a request for MAID and then changed their mind. That can happen in the absence of advance directives, but under an advance directives framework, if someone signs an advance directive and then loses capacity or is simply not told before a health care practitioner takes their life, then there is no opportunity for them to change their mind.

It is clear in the legislation that if a person actively resists, the process is supposed to stop, but a health care practitioner is not required to inform them of what they are about to do. There is no such requirement. How does that take into consideration the almost 700 people who changed their mind?

Mr. Speaker, that is exactly the problem here. Because so much is being left to how this system would be implemented, we do not actually know what safeguards in practice, if any, would exist. I will note as well that the lack of an expiration for advance requests is a key problem. Conceivably, someone could live with a diagnosis for 10 to 15 years, which means an advance request could collect dust on a shelf for that long as well. I know there have been cases where people had signed up at one point to be organ donors and later regretted it.
There is a litany of problems with this that need to be dealt with.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to Bill C-41, the medical assistance in dying safeguards act. This is one of the most profound questions Parliament can consider. It touches on life, death, dignity, autonomy, compassion, equality and our responsibilities to one another. It is deeply personal, affecting individuals confronting serious illness, their families, caregivers and medical professionals. There are deeply held differences of opinion on this issue shaped by personal experience, ethical traditions, religious beliefs and understandings of human dignity. For that reason, this is a matter of conscience and a free vote for the New Democratic caucus.

At the heart of this debate is a fundamental human rights question: How do we respect individual dignity, autonomy and rights while protecting those who may be vulnerable? Every person deserves to live and die with dignity. That means respecting the right to make deeply personal decisions about one's body, health and end-of-life care. It also means ensuring that people are not abandoned by the systems and institutions meant to support them.

Canada's debate about assisted dying has been shaped by decades of advocacy, legal challenges and difficult ethical questions. We all remember the case of Sue Rodriguez in 1993. Former NDP MP Svend Robinson stood by her. It was a difficult moral issue then, and it remains difficult today. Living with ALS, Rodriguez challenged Canada's prohibition on assisted dying. She argued that she should have the right to seek assistance in ending her life before her illness took away her ability to do so. The Supreme Court rejected her challenge in a narrow 5-4 decision, but her struggle brought questions about autonomy, equality, security of the person and dignity into the national conversation.

More than two decades later, the Supreme Court revisited those questions in Carter v. Canada. In February 2015, the court unanimously found that the Criminal Code prohibitions on physician-assisted dying violated the charter rights of certain competent adults experiencing grievous and irremediable medical conditions causing enduring and intolerable suffering. That decision was a landmark moment in Canadian human rights law.

Parliament responded with Bill C-14 in 2016, establishing Canada's first federal framework for medical assistance in dying. In 2021, Bill C-7 expanded eligibility for certain individuals whose natural death was not reasonably foreseeable, while introducing different safeguards. Subsequent legislation, including Bill C-39 and Bill C-62, delayed the proposed expansion to people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness. Now Bill C-41 is before us to respond to the courts, and Parliament is addressing two critical questions: one, the issue of advance requests and, two, those whose sole underlying medical condition is mental illness.

On the first question, what Bill C-41 would do is establish a framework for advance requests for MAID, and it would only be permitted in provinces and territories that have the required legislative regime in force. Because Bill C-41 stipulates that an advance request is permitted only in provinces or territories that have the required legislative regime in force, it raises serious concerns about unequal access. Canadians should not have different rights depending on where they live, yet this is where we are at with Bill C-41. I will have more to say about that.

On the second point, the bill would maintain the exclusion of people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness. There are different human rights perspectives on that question. Excluding people solely because of a mental illness raises serious charter equality concerns. There is an argument that people should not be denied access to a legal medical procedure simply because of their diagnosis and that eligibility should be considered through appropriate individualized assessments and safeguards.

At the same time, mental health experts and disability rights organizations have raised concerns about the ability to determine when a mental illness is irremediable, the availability of appropriate treatment, and profound disparities in access to care. There is no question that these concerns deserve serious consideration. For example, end-of-life advocacy groups view the exclusion of mental illness as discriminatory and unconstitutional, emphasizing bodily autonomy and equity under the law.

Dying With Dignity Canada expressed deep disappointment over legislative barriers, stating that preventing a group of people from having access to a legal medical procedure simply because of their diagnosis violates charter rights. The organization maintains that individuals should have equal rights to apply based on rigorous individualized assessments.

On the flip side, Inclusion Canada, a leading disability rights group, argued that expanded eligibility perpetuates dangerous ableist assumptions that life with a disability is not worth living. Meanwhile, the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health notes that there is a lack of established criteria and consensus among psychiatrists for if and when a mental illness should be considered irremediable, alongside stark disparities in access to care.

To that end, there is another dimension to this debate that we cannot ignore. The right to make a choice is meaningful only when people have real choices available to them. Experts, disability advocates and health care organizations have raised concerns about whether people experiencing profound suffering always have access to the care and support they need. Some warn that assisted dying risks becoming an answer to suffering that could be alleviated through better access to health care, affordable housing, disability supports and community services. The government's own report has identified inadequate funding for mental health services.

A person living with a disability should not have to fight for basic services, appropriate housing or the resources required to live independently. A person experiencing mental health challenges should not face inaccessible treatment, long wait-lists or a shortage of community-based supports. Someone approaching the end of life should not be denied quality palliative care because of where they live or their financial circumstances. Telling someone that a service exists is not the same as ensuring they can access it.

Palliative care, counselling, disability services and mental health treatment must be timely, affordable and appropriate. This is not an argument against individual autonomy. It is an argument that autonomy must be supported by the social and economic conditions that allow people to exercise it meaningfully. The federal government has a responsibility to work with the provinces and territories to address these gaps. Dignity cannot be separated from the material conditions in which people live.

In June, the Special Joint Committee on Medical Assistance in Dying recommended that the federal government indefinitely exclude people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness. The committee also identified a pressing need for increased and more equitable access to adequate mental health services. People deserve timely access to treatment, counselling, psychiatrists, psychologists and community-based services. The committee's call for more equitable mental health services must not be lost in this debate. Maintaining an exclusion in the Criminal Code cannot substitute for the government's responsibility to invest in mental health care.

We must also consider how this legislation would affect people differently. People living in poverty, experiencing homelessness, living with disabilities or living in remote communities can face significant barriers to accessing health care. First nations, Inuit and Métis communities have experienced generations of inequities in health care, including inadequate access to culturally safe services and palliative care.

The government must engage indigenous governments and organizations meaningfully in implementation, respecting indigenous self-determination and the diversity of perspectives within indigenous communities. We must ask whether every person can make an informed and voluntary decision without pressure, discrimination or the absence of meaningful alternatives. This is a fundamental human rights question.

I began by noting that Canada's debate about assisted dying has been shaped by decades of advocacy, legal challenges and difficult ethical questions. I suspect that this is not the end to legal challenges on this question.
