There are people who believe that the right to die with dignity is inseparable from the right to make decisions about one's own body and the circumstances of their death. There are others who approach this question through concerns for the sanctity of life, the protection of the vulnerable, disability rights and the responsibilities of society. We must make room for these differences and chart a path forward.

Regardless of which party one belongs to in the House, we can all agree that every person deserves dignity, compassion and access to appropriate health care and support. No one should be made to feel that their life is less valuable because they live with a disability, an illness, poverty or circumstances that make life more difficult. The right to make decisions about one's own life and death cannot become an excuse for the government's own withdrawal from its responsibility to provide care.

There is the important work of the parliamentary committee. People with lived experiences, families, disability advocates, indigenous organizations, medical professionals and other experts must have the opportunity to contribute and be heard. We must not rush the bill through committee. We owe Canadians a process that is thoughtful, transparent and grounded in human rights, and we must respect the dignity of people at the end of life, protect those who may be vulnerable to coercion or who have inadequate support, and build a health care system that gives everyone the opportunity to live and die with dignity.

Mr. Speaker, as my colleague said, tonight's debate deals with fundamental issues of dignity and autonomy regarding the options available to people suffering from incurable illnesses. We have heard various accounts from people suffering from diseases such as Alzheimer's, a condition that robs them of the choice to die with dignity.

I would like to ask my colleague why it is important to listen to the experiences of these individuals and to establish a framework that will allow them to make a free and informed choice while they are still able to do so.

Mr. Speaker, the member raises the issue of advance requests, and that is an important issue we are debating today as part of this piece of legislation. With advance requests, there is a set of eligibility rules and safeguards prescribed in the bill, and people would have to meet all of those requirements in order for the advance request to be valid. With that being said, of course, people experience illness and later on, in different stages of the illness, it is possible that they might have a different viewpoint. They might express that in a different way, or maybe sometimes they do not. That is the essence of the question that needs to be resolved.

Through the committee process, it would be absolutely critical for the government not to rush through but to invite different witnesses with different perspectives, for them to be heard and for the committee members to ask important questions in order to arrive at the correct decision in moving forward.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague is right to point out that Svend Robinson and Sue Rodriguez advanced the discussion on MAID in 1993 in British Columbia.

I would like to say something about the constitutional nature of equitable access to advance requests throughout the country whether or not a parliament passes legislation. I would say that this could be a reasonable infringement, according to the Supreme Court, given that the provinces are responsible for providing end-of-life care. A debate could take place in provincial legislatures that do not have a law. It could even become an election issue, in which case there would surely be an appeal to the Supreme Court if a government ever opted for a total prohibition.

As for structural vulnerabilities, I agree that it is absolutely essential to improve people's living conditions, whatever those living conditions may be. If we are talking about structural vulnerabilities in relation to mental illness, a scientific study conducted by Downar and Quinn says that structural marginalization is not a key factor in requests for MAID.
Here is a quote:

Quote.QuotePara: ...according to all available indicators....they clearly refute the notion that medical assistance in dying is driven by marginalization or inadequate service delivery on a significant scale in Canada. While there may be exceptions, the anecdotal cases cited to support this claim rarely stand up to scrutiny.

Content.ParaText: We are therefore in favour of better living conditions, but in the case of someone who has been suffering from mental illness for decades and who does not respond to treatment, I have a problem with someone like that being told to simply carry on suffering.

Mr. Speaker, two important issues were raised in that question. One is a constitutional question. I note that in the special committee's report, there were dissenting opinions that called for the government, in fact, to raise a reference question to the courts on the constitutionality of denying people with mental illness access to MAID. The government decided not to exercise that right, and I think that is an important question that should be raised at committee and explored.

On the other issue, with respect to the lack of support and services for people, there is one study that the member referenced. There are also a lot of other lived experiences, most certainly, of advocates, people who are advocates for disability, for mental health, for people living in palliative care, etc., who say it is absolutely critical that services be made available. Otherwise, it is possible that some people might opt for MAID. That is the thing we do not want to allow to happen.

Hence, I hope that in the upcoming budget to be tabled tomorrow, the government steps it up and matches its words with action, particularly in support of mental health, and provides the needed support across the country for people who need to access treatment.

Mr. Speaker, it has become evident to me, spending some time in other parts of the world talking to legislators elsewhere, how much Canada has become an international pariah. A source of its international shame relates to the protection of the rights of people with disabilities. There has been high-level criticism of Canada, and in particular, the MAID regime, in terms of how it treats people living with disabilities.

I have spoken to disability rights organizations that are deeply concerned about how, on a regular basis, people with disabilities live with unprompted proposals for MAID from people who are supposed to be supporting them, essentially sending them the message that people in authority think they would be better off dead. This is a source of shame for our country and something we need to take seriously and change. Meanwhile, the government wants to further push MAID in spite of all of these concerns.
Why do we not take this criticism seriously and listen to people with disabilities who are raising these concerns?

Mr. Speaker, I think the important issue here is this. At the nub of the issue, what I want to see is for the government to step up in providing the necessary supports for people who face difficulties and people who have mental health challenges, all the way from early diagnosis to prevention to treatment. That is not happening right now across the country, and most certainly is not happening in British Columbia and in Vancouver East. That was the case when the Conservatives were in government, and it is the case now with the Liberals in government, so I would say to everybody, step it up for the community so that people are not faced with impossible choices and decisions.

Mr. Speaker, medical assistance in dying and health care are matters of shared jurisdiction. Criminal law is defined at the federal level, while the provinces are responsible for delivering health care.
I would like to hear my colleague's thoughts on how the provinces are prepared to manage the transition to advance requests.
Are they adequately equipped to supervise health care professionals to ensure that it is carried out safely?
Mr. Speaker, that is exactly the issue. The fact is, this would now be subject to the provinces, and I think there would be different approaches, different infrastructure, with respect to that.

It does raise the question, again, around the federal health care transfers and the dollars that are necessary to support provinces and territories in order to put the framework together and support the medical practitioners in getting the job done. I would urge the member to say to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance that in this upcoming budget, they must properly resource provinces and territories in health care funding and in the transfer, and live up to what the Liberals promised when they were in opposition and when they were in government in terms of the necessary increases in funding to support provinces and territories to do the job right for all Canadians.
We have time for a quick question.
The hon. member for Shefford.

Mr. Speaker, I am hearing some interesting things this evening. There is a problem here. I wonder whether my colleague fully appreciates the clinical approach that underpins all of this. Right up until the very end, physicians support patients and ask whether this is still what they want. Quebec is prepared when it comes to advance requests.
I have two—
I must interrupt the member. I had specifically asked for a quick question.
The hon. member for Vancouver East has 30 seconds to reply.

Mr. Speaker, Quebec is always further ahead than the rest of the country. On this issue and on child care, it has always led, and so the rest of the country is always following. There is no question about it.

However, this is a really important debate to raise some of the issues that have surfaced about whether it is right or wrong. It is an individual choice in terms of exercising MAID. It is fundamental that the government ensure that those who are suffering are supported in every way, and if they exercise their autonomy to have MAID, we need to support them in that process as well.

Before I go to debate, I would remind members that we have reached five hours of debate. According to Standing Order 74(1), members no longer need to indicate to the Chair that they are splitting their time. They will all be 10-minute and five-minute questions and comments.
The hon. member for Bow River.

Mr. Speaker, it is always an honour to stand in this House and speak for the constituents of Bow River. This is a deeply held and personal issue for so many people across the country. I am often skeptical of government intervention in the economy, on the farm and in the private lives of Canadians. I believe the government should respect the freedom of people in their own decisions.

I also believe Parliament has the duty to protect life, especially when the law puts vulnerable people at risk of irreversible harm. That duty brings us to Bill C-41 with respect to medical assistance in dying, and to a straightforward request to split the bill, pass the permanent exclusion where mental illness is the sole underlying medical condition and give the issue of advance requests the separate scrutiny that it deserves.

On October 7, the Liberals voted against Bill C-218. Introduced by my colleague, the member for Cloverdale—Langley City, that bill would have permanently prevented MAID eligibility where a person's sole underlying medical condition was a mental illness. Twenty days later, the government has now introduced Bill C-41 with provisions to maintain that exclusion, but attached them to a separate proposal on advance requests. They have deliberately turned this into a moral paradox. The Liberals rejected the Conservative solution, then returned with the protection we had sought tied to a much broader change in the law, a change that would expand the availability of MAID. The first part of this bill is necessary because we cannot ensure that someone suffering from a mental illness is competent to make a final and binding decision to engage in MAID. This bill then goes on in the second part to do just that and enable MAID when a person is unable to give competent consent or competent refusal by design. The Liberals owe Canadians an explanation. If we agree that people whose sole underlying condition is mental illness must be protected, why make that protection dependent on settling a separate debate?

Conservatives are united on the way forward. Let us split the legislation. We are prepared to work with the government to pass the mental illness provisions through all stages of this House without delay and send them to the upper house. The current exclusion expires on March 17, 2027. Unless Parliament acts, the scheduled expansion will take effect. The Liberals have already delayed the expansion of MAID for mental illness more than once, which is exactly why they should not rush a separate and complex change through Parliament at the same time. They are going to make the same mistakes. There is no corresponding federal deadline requiring Parliament to authorize advance requests. The government should not use the deadline on the issue of mental illness to rush a different and complex change through this House.

The Special Joint Committee on Medical Assistance in Dying recommended that people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness be excluded indefinitely. Our proposal would have provided a lasting protection without another expiry date. The committee heard warnings about two fundamental problems that remain unresolved. First, doctors and nurse practitioners warned that they cannot reliably determine when there is no possible recovery from a mental illness. Put plainly, they cannot reliably predict that a person will never improve. Severe, prolonged suffering does not itself settle that question. Second, witnesses warned that clinicians cannot reliably distinguish a request for MAID from a desire for suicide in this context. There are different clinical views on these questions. When the consequence of an error is death, Parliament must take those warnings seriously. A person whose condition could have improved with treatment must never lose that chance because the law moved ahead of the evidence.

The committee also heard serious concerns about whether existing safeguards and oversight are working in practice. Before Parliament extends the law further, Canadians deserve answers about how those protections are enforced and what happens when they fail. Bill C-41 acknowledges significant unresolved concerns about the safe provision of MAID on the basis of mental illness. Ministers should act on that acknowledgement and work with us to put this protection into law, now. People living with mental illness deserve to have their suffering taken seriously. They deserve care that is available when they need it and a country that remains committed to their recovery.

I recognize that this debate raises questions about autonomy and equality. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association has raised those concerns about the exclusion. Those arguments deserve a serious response. Section 7 of the charter protects life, liberty and security of the person. Section 15 guarantees legal equality, including protection against discrimination. Parliament must consider all of those rights. Protecting people from the irreversible consequences of a mistaken assessment is a legitimate and necessary responsibility of government. We can respect the dignity of people living with mental illness while insisting that the law protect their chance to recover.

The second part of Bill C-41 raises a very different question. Herein is the paradox. It would permit an adult to make an advance request after a diagnosis of a serious incurable illness expected to permanently take away their capacity to consent. This is important on the “expected” part, which I will get to in a moment. By the time MAID was administered, that person would no longer be able to give informed consent to the procedure. Families facing dementia and other devastating conditions deserve a careful hearing, and so do people who fear that a past request could be acted on in circumstances that they never understood or anticipated.

The bill contains safeguards, including two independent assessments and rules about refusal and resistance. Parliament must examine whether those rules can reliably protect someone who is no longer lucid. A clear refusal would prevent MAID under that request. Where a practitioner is unsure whether a reaction means refusal or resistance, the bill would require a pause of at least 30 clear days.

The legislation proposed already anticipates uncertainty in the practitioner. How would that uncertainty be resolved after the waiting period? Who would review the decision? How would the conditions distinguish an involuntary reaction from a person trying to resist? More importantly, the real question here is can the practitioner understand what a person is trying to communicate at the last moment? I submit this is the crux of the problem. It is not so much whether the patient is able to communicate. Is the practitioner equipped to understand what they are communicating?

We have all heard examples of locked-in syndrome, where there is complete consciousness and lucidity, but the inability to move or communicate. How would suffering be assessed when a person cannot really describe it? What would happen when a request is many years old and the treatment circumstances or preferences have changed?

These questions concern the moment when someone is least able to speak for themselves. They require evidence, clear legal rules and enforceable accountability. When ambiguity exists, we must err on the side of caution and prevent advance requests.

The advance request provisions would also depend on provincial legislation. Alberta and other provinces must be heard on their responsibilities, on the safeguards they would administer and on how the federal framework would operate in practice.

Doctors, legal experts, families, veterans and people living with disabilities must have a meaningful opportunity to testify. Members of Parliament should be able to assess the proposal to allow MAID by advance request on its own merits, separately from the urgent mental illness protection.

As Remembrance Day approaches, we should reflect on our particular responsibility to veterans. Veterans Affairs' own investigation confirmed four incidents in which a single employee inappropriately raised MAID with veterans. That was shameful. It was a shameful failure toward people who served our country. The government must ensure it never happens again.

Veterans living with trauma, chronic pain or physical injuries deserve timely treatment and comprehensive support. When a veteran needs help, Canada's response must demonstrate that their life and service matter.

That responsibility extends to every vulnerable Canadian. People must have meaningful access to health care, mental health support services, disability supports and palliative care. If someone feels MAID is their only realistic option because adequate care is unavailable, Parliament has a duty to confront that failure. A list of services on paper means little to a person who cannot actually get them.

We have common ground before us. The government now proposes to prevent the expansion of MAID for mental illness. Conservatives are ready to pass that protection immediately. Members of the House may reach different conclusions about advance requests after hearing the evidence. The government should give them the opportunity to consider that question separately with the care it demands.

The Liberals keep asking for co-operation. The Minister of Justice can put aside petty politics and work with us today. Separate the two measures. Let us pass the protection on which we agree. Parliament can examine the rest. Canadians living with mental illness should not have to watch their protection evaporate.

Conservatives will continue to fight to ensure vulnerable Canadians are met with help to live, not a pathway to state-facilitated death. Split the bill, pass the exclusion and give advance requests to the study they need.

Mr. Speaker, through Bill C-41, we are establishing a framework that would allow people living with conditions such as Alzheimer's to make a free and informed decision about their end-of-life care while they are still capable of doing so. This decision was not taken lightly. We heard deeply moving testimony from many individuals living with these conditions, and they expressed a desire to be able to make that choice while they still have capacity.
I would like to ask my colleague this: What does he say to those individuals who came forward to give testimony and who are asking for the right to make that choice?

Mr. Speaker, it is quite simple. I would like to thank the member across the way for the question, because it is important. This issue is a matter of conscience, and we all have different perspectives on it, which is quite evident, but it comes down to the point that I made earlier that this is a final decision. If we get it wrong and we cannot communicate properly and evidence the refusal at the last moment, we cannot risk making a mistake in this case.

Mr. Speaker, I am outraged this evening. We have the right to have different opinions. We have the right to hold certain beliefs and to disregard general statements or science. However, what we do not have the right to do is to disregard human dignity. I am hearing so much oversimplification right now. I am not saying that what I went through with my father, who had ALS, is right for everyone.
That is not the case. We are asking if we can let people make their own end-of-life choices with dignity.

Mr. Speaker, it is important. This is extraordinarily contentious. It is absolutely a matter of conscience. We have different perspectives, but this transcends that. The role of the House of Commons transcends the individual opinion, in that we have to err on the side of caution until we collectively understand the impact.

We cannot take the risk of making a mistake. We cannot take the risk of not understanding the context. Science and the perception and reality of all of the things we study change over time. They are always a moving target. In this instance with this legislation, the consequences are literally fatal, and we cannot take the risk of making a mistake.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Homewood Research Institute, which is based in Guelph and is a global leader in mental health research, for the really incredible webinar it did outlining why it was important not to proceed with permitting medical assistance in dying for folks who have a chronic mental illness. Part of that is to continue to give them hope and to make sure that nationally we provide access to care.

What I am concerned about when listening to the debate tonight is that I feel like there is some level of disparagement toward the palliative care practitioners in this country and the people who administer MAID, who absolutely seek the consent of people and accompany them with dignity in their final moments. I just want to make sure that we are not straying into that space.
I would also point out that if we sign a “do not resuscitate” order, that order is respected should it come to that in a hospital. An advance directive is essentially the same thing.
Mr. Speaker, I am thankful for the genuine question from the member opposite.

I have been through the palliative care process with my father and other members of my family, and I understand completely the compassion of health care providers and their desire to provide the standard of care that we have come to expect. However, that does not take away from the circumstance that we find ourselves contemplating, where long periods of time can transpire between the order and the action, with a changing in circumstances and a changing in the understanding of the patient and how well the practitioner can understand what the patient wants. We cannot make a mistake.

Mr. Speaker, tonight, we have gathered to discuss a particularly sensitive issue that raises legal, ethical and social questions affecting patients suffering from an incurable disease, their families and health care professionals. I believe this is a topic we all take very seriously.

Let us take a step back. The law on medical assistance in dying came into effect in Canada in 2016. That marked a significant change in Canadian society's approach to end-of-life care. MAID provides eligible individuals with an additional choice regarding their care by allowing them to end their suffering with dignity. There are certainly strict guidelines in place. Medical assistance in dying is reserved for adults who meet strict eligibility criteria. We are talking, for example, about people living with an incurable illness who are approaching the end of life, such as cancer patients, or individuals with an incurable condition that causes irreversible physical decline and significant suffering, such as certain neurodegenerative disorders.

There are guidelines that must be followed. The consent must be informed. The person has the right to withdraw consent at any point in the process. The passage of the bill in 2016 was not the end of the debate. I would say that it was the beginning and the continuation of an ongoing societal discussion on the subject of MAID. Over the past decade alone, we have pondered substantive questions about MAID, such as whether a person has a right to set the conditions for their end of life. This led to questions about dignity and suffering. As we know, the law was expanded in 2021. Initially, it was for naturally foreseeable death. The law was amended in 2021 to include people suffering from an irreversible illness that causes significant suffering. At the time, as a citizen, I heard very touching testimony from people who asked that their situation be taken into consideration so that they could have the right to make this choice for themselves.

This also raises questions about the protection of vulnerable individuals, consent, and the ability to make a free and informed decision, as well as what to do when an illness deprives a person of that ability. With Bill C-41, we aim to update Canada's legislative framework on medical assistance in dying, particularly with regard to people with mental illness and advance requests. We are therefore clarifying matters with respect to these two elements. I would say that this is another step in a collective reflection that began more than a decade ago.

One key component of Bill C-41 seeks to allow for advance MAID requests. Under the current legislation, a person must be able to give informed consent to receive this care. They must understand their medical condition, their options, and the consequences of their decision. As a general rule, they must also confirm their consent immediately before MAID is administered. Very strict guidelines are in place. However, some diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, can lead to a gradual loss of decision-making capacity. As the disease progresses, a person may lose the ability to make an informed choice at the time they wish to receive MAID. Under the current rules, they cannot access this option, even if they had clearly expressed their wishes earlier in life when they were still capable of making that decision.

Our government believes that Canadians with terminal illnesses should be able to make informed decisions about their future care while they still have the capacity to do so. That is why, with this bill, we intend to allow eligible adults who receive an early diagnosis of a terminal illness that is likely to cause them to lose their decision-making capacity to make an advance request for MAID. For example, an adult diagnosed with early-stage Alzheimer's disease could specify in advance the conditions and circumstances under which they would want to receive MAID at a more advanced stage of their illness, when they would no longer be able to make that decision for themselves.

The underlying objective is to respect the person's wishes and their individual end-of-life choices, which I believe are based on deep and careful reflection. We heard some very moving testimony. Loved ones of people with Alzheimer's said that MAID should be expanded to allow people in these situations to make informed choices while they still can.

An advance request does not necessarily mean that MAID will automatically be administered at a later time. The eligibility criteria must be met and the strict guidelines must be followed. For example, two independent assessments will always be required for advance requests to ensure that the conditions described in the request are met. There must be confirmation that the person is in an advanced and irreversible state of decline and experiencing profound suffering, so the independent assessments still need to be carried out.

The person may also signify, through sounds or gestures, that they withdraw their consent when MAID is about to be administered. If the person does not appear to consent to MAID, the procedure will be stopped. Obviously, a family member cannot submit an advance request on behalf of someone else. The aim is really to respect the choice of the person who made the request while they still had the capacity to do so.

In our discussions tonight, it is important to understand the key role that the provinces and territories will play in this matter. At the federal level, we can amend the criminal framework, including the Criminal Code, since this falls under our jurisdiction. However, the delivery of health care services is a provincial responsibility. The federal government alone cannot oversee the implementation of advance requests for MAID. Even if Parliament were to amend the Criminal Code for this, the provinces would also have to take steps to ensure that advance requests would be available in their health care systems. As I mentioned, the provinces are responsible for the organization and delivery of health care in their jurisdictions, and it will be up to them to decide whether they want to implement this option and how it will be carried out. What I mean is that, even if the federal law changes, it does not become automatic across Canada. The provinces will have to decide whether to implement the framework within their borders. Co‑operation with the provinces and territories will therefore be critical so that everyone who is eligible can have access. As the federal government, we will continue to work with the provinces as we make progress on this matter.

I will now discuss the second part. Through Bill C-41, we will maintain the exclusion for cases when mental illness is the sole underlying health condition. After careful consideration, following committee deliberations, and after hearing from numerous experts, we came to an agreement that MAID should not be expanded to cover individuals for whom mental illness is the sole underlying health condition. That said, we recognize that mental illness can cause profound suffering, even when it is not necessarily as visible as in the case of other physical health conditions. Canadians living with mental health issues deserve to have their suffering taken seriously.

In the context of MAID, however, serious concerns remain regarding the ability to assess these situations safely and consistently. For these reasons, we decided not to expand MAID eligibility to individuals whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness. As I mentioned, this decision was not taken lightly. A parliamentary committee made up of senators and MPs from the various political parties examined the issue. Health experts and stakeholders also gave evidence. Finally, following all these consultations, the Special Joint Committee on Medical Assistance in Dying recommended against expanding medical assistance in dying. At the same time, other consultations took place. The conclusion was that uncertainty remains as to whether these situations can be assessed reliably and consistently. In light of that, our government believes that the current exclusion is the most appropriate approach.

In closing, we are debating substantive issues tonight, issues that affect the choices people make when they are considering their end of life. I think it is important that legislators put a framework in place, particularly for people suffering from conditions such as dementia or Alzheimer's. It is important to give these individuals the opportunity to make a free and informed choice about their end-of-life care.

Mr. Speaker, the member believes, as I do, that the role of the state is to ensure that the conditions are in place for a person to make a free and informed choice, not to impose what it thinks is best on a person who is suffering. However, when it comes to mental illness, on what grounds should the state restrict or undermine the right to self-determination of a person with a mental disorder who has been resistant to treatment for decades, as long as their decision-making capacity is not affected?

Decision-making capacity can be assessed. Psychiatrists are already able to assess it when a mental illness exists alongside another condition, such as cancer. Why is it more complicated when the person just has a mental disorder? On what grounds should suffering that has become intolerable be considered reasonable under section 1 of the charter? On what basis, then, can discrimination be considered reasonable, when all of the experts told us that a blanket prohibition is discriminatory?

Mr. Speaker, I want to mention that this decision was not taken lightly. Various experts were heard. Consultations were held. Work was done in committee. Of course, my colleague is well aware of that. The conclusion was that, in the case of individuals living with mental illness, there remained concerns about whether these situations could be assessed in a safe and consistent manner in the context of medical assistance in dying. Therefore, the most responsible course of action is not to proceed with the expansion at this time.

I want to mention that Bill C‑41 is consistent with Quebec legislation. In Quebec, advance requests are already in use. With the bill, Quebec medical staff who administer MAID are protected. In terms of the mental health issue, Bill C‑41 is consistent with Quebec's current legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask my colleague just a simple question about the process around an advance directive. Does he think that a person who has signed an advance directive and then would be about to be killed on the basis of that advance directive should have it explained to them before they are killed what is about to happen? In the moment when their life would be ended, should the person be told what is about to happen to them?

Mr. Speaker, I sincerely believe that people suffering from diseases such as Alzheimer's must be able to make free and informed decisions about their end-of-life care. People suffering from illnesses such as cancer or neurodegenerative disorders are able to make that decision immediately before MAID is provided.

For people with Alzheimer's, that choice is taken away from them by the disease. An advance request would allow a person diagnosed at an early stage to specify the conditions under which they would wish to receive MAID once they reach a later stage of the disease and are no longer capable of making that decision on their own. Two independent health care professionals would assess whether the conditions set out in this request are met. If at the time that MAID is to be provided, the person appears, through sounds or gestures, to be resisting or refusing the procedure, it would be stopped.
Rigorous safeguards remain in place while also allowing people with illnesses such as Alzheimer's to make a free and informed choice.
Mr. Speaker, this evening, we are discussing an issue that is really very emotional and far-reaching. In a debate such as this, I believe the words we choose matter.

Following his very thoughtful speech, I would ask my colleague to speak to the importance of personal autonomy, individual choice and the fact that medical assistance in dying must always remain an option, never an obligation.

Mr. Speaker, choosing our words carefully in a debate like this is a matter of respect. There were moving accounts from people who courageously testified about their health conditions and how they envisioned their end-of-life care. I think the least we can do is show some respect for these people and be mindful of the words we use in the debate.
The idea behind this is not to create an obligation, but to give people another choice.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin my comments today by reiterating a request that has been made by many of my colleagues here in the House of Commons, which is to split the bill.

Bill C-41 is a real moral dilemma. The way it has been politically manipulated is of great concern. It is only by splitting the bill into two separate decisions, two separate votes by members of the House, that I think it could be fairly presented to the public as an appropriate examination of the very serious medical and moral issues that are embedded within it.

I was trying to explain to one of my constituents earlier what the moral dilemma is exactly. What I found to be helpful was a reference to the movie The Dark Knight. There is a scene in which the Joker calls Batman and tells him that his girlfriend, Rachel Dawes, has been left in one room. On the other side of Gotham, the DA, Harvey Dent, has been left in the other room. The Joker tells Batman that he has to make a choice and that it is going to suck regardless. It is going to be a really hard, horrible decision. He only gets to make one decision on who he gets to save.

That is what has been presented to us with Bill C-41. Every member of the House, from all parties, is being put in this situation by the Prime Minister and whomever in the government is making the decision to combine these two elements of a very complicated and dense issue into one bill. Whoever is making that decision is putting every single one of us in the exact same situation that the Joker put Batman in.

We are not going to feel good about the decision we make at the end of the day. Either we are going to vote against the bill, which has a very important and needed element in it, to further protect people with mental illness from euthanasia, or we are going to vote against the bill, because it also expands euthanasia to include people with dementia and other illnesses. These are really two things that should not be combined.

I feel obligated to point out the cynical, cold and callous nature in which these two things have been combined into one bill. Every member of the House had an opportunity to vote on a Conservative private member's bill that would have only addressed the expansion of MAID to those facing mental illness. All members of the Conservative Party voted for that bill. All members of the NDP voted for that bill. In fact, we even had one bold, brave soul on the other side of the aisle, in the Liberal ranks, vote for that bill. The remainder of that party voted against it. Why? What would possibly be the reason, other than the cold and cynical ploy to wedge those of us, with a heavy heart and a heavy conscience on this issue, into combining our very well-intentioned opposition to the expansion of euthanasia to those with mental illness and forcing us to also reconcile that with the expansion to more Canadians?

That is not the way this place should work. I will be honest. I appreciate that politics is an ugly and dirty game. I can appreciate that a lot of this is about wedging people constantly. On something so heavy, on something that is such a matter of conscience, I really do hope that the government will reconsider and split the bill when it comes time to vote.

How I would like to use the remainder of my time is to address why this is such a concern for people. I think a good place to start is to capture the fact that since 2016, MAID, or as I call it, euthanasia, has become a very common form of death for people in this country. In 2016, it was slightly over 1,000 people that were killed by euthanasia. In 2024, it was 16,499, which is the most recent statistic, in one year. In total, over an eight-year period, over 76,000 Canadians have had their lives ended through the practice of euthanasia.

I raise this because I think that there are two ways that people look at that information. Some people might look at that and think that this is a sign of progress. I shudder at that thought, as do many Canadians. I look at that number and my heart breaks. I know many people who have been in very serious situations, facing very serious illnesses.

I am a stage 4 cancer survivor. There was a time in my life when my mother and I sat in a room and a doctor said to me that I might not live. I know what that is like. I know what it is like to sit in a cancer ward and see people who are on their third, fourth or fifth year of chemotherapy. I know what it is like to sit in a hospital waiting room and see people lined up waiting to go through radiation, hoping that maybe this time it is going to work. I have seen people face death. I have faced death, so when I see numbers like this, my heart breaks, because I wonder how many of those people made the decision to end their life based on fear and because they were scared. I have been there, and I have seen people there.

When we talk about advance directives and a medical professional approaching a sick person saying that they should make a decision now about how their life is going to end, it is very concerning. The emotional roller coaster of a serious illness is very real. There are times when a person may be depressed. There are times when their spirit may be broken, and they might consider it a good decision to end their life at some point on their own terms. However, we never know what life is going to throw at us, and we never know how our life is going to change. We do not know how it is going to feel in the moment. Opposing advance directives is about saying that at minimum, people deserve the dignity to make such a choice of great finality in the moment, and that we should not have a system designed such that potential coercion or the exploitation of a very emotional and difficult situation leads to a decision that a person may pay the ultimate price for.

We have heard from families on the other side of this debate. We have heard from people with loved ones in very extreme situations on the other side of this debate. I do not want to pretend that this is simple. I am not trying to diminish another point of view. I get that this is complicated. I am not trying to point a finger at anyone and say there is a bad guy in this story. What I am trying to do is point out that these are very serious things we are debating in the House of Commons, both from a moral perspective and from a health care perspective. I am trying to point out that people come to their conclusions on these issues for very good reasons, whether that is their personal life, family life or religious or philosophical convictions, whatever they may be.

Wherever we wind up on this debate, I believe, humbly, that it is a cheapening of the issue to combine both of these very complicated questions into one bill. If I could leave anyone listening to my words with one message, it would be to please consider the weight of this. If we are taking this as seriously as we should, then it should not be something that gets lumped into some kind of omnibus euthanasia discussion. Every single way we decide which Canadians become vulnerable to the practice of euthanasia and which ones do not should be treated with the weight of significant individual policies and legislative decisions in mind, as it should be.
I would also like to elaborate on why I think it is very important that we consider the difficulty of asking an ill person to make this decision in an advance request context.

I remember when I was first told that I might pass away from stage 4 cancer. The hardest part of the entire ordeal for the year and a half that I was a hospital patient, in the hospital every day, was seeing my mom go through it. I can absolutely understand why a sick person might say, “I do not want to put the responsibility on my family to have to make a difficult decision about my life one day.” I can absolutely understand why someone would say, “The moral thing to do is to take that responsibility onto myself.” To anyone who feels that way, my word of encouragement would be that if they talk to the relatives of people who have been in those situations, they will find that many of them were very happy to have taken care of their ill loved ones and were very happy to have been by their side even when it was difficult.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague may have lost it. Since when do members impose their personal beliefs on someone who wants to end their suffering? I am shocked.
Can my colleague explain to the House the difference between therapeutic obstinacy and dying with dignity?

Mr. Speaker, with all due respect, the member opposite has asked a very silly question. We have been very clear in saying people should make the choice in the moment that death is being presented to them as an option by their government through the health care system. We are not taking the choice away. We are saying do not hold them to a decision they may have made years prior under different circumstances. Make sure that they can make the decision in an informed capacity in the moment.

Mr. Speaker, I understand that my colleague would prefer to see this bill split and for there to be two votes. If the bill is not split, would he at least agree to a split vote at second reading stage?

Mr. Speaker, I do think, ideally, the legislation would be split. If not, a vote split would be a great idea. Anything that we can do to highlight the weight of every part of this legislation, the moral and medical significance of it, would be welcomed.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is important for us to, as my colleague has, drill into the practical aspects of advance directives, not just the theoretical questions around it. Some people who think, in theory, that advance consent makes sense, I think would maybe be chastened by some of these practical realities.

A person can get a diagnosis for something that is very frightening and also something that they have not yet experienced. They do not have any lived experience with having that illness, but they know it is coming or they know it is on the way. They are potentially presented with a worst-case scenario. There are many cases of this where people kind of catastrophize what has been presented to them in the process of encouraging them to sign something or accept facilitated death.

Hypothetically, based not on someone's lived experience but fear of the future, they sign a document and their real experience of living with that condition may be very different from that expectation. However, it is others in their life, like doctors or family members, who have to decide whether what a person signed a year ago fits with their present expressed experience.
Do these practical realities not raise serious problems for the implementation of something like advance directives?

Mr. Speaker, there are a lot of concerns, as he accurately raised. We hear from the government terms like “safeguards” to give the impression that there are appropriate safeguards already in place in the euthanasia regime in this country.

I would never cite the United Nations in almost any other circumstance but since we have a government that likes to appeal to international organizations like it, the United Nations has said these safeguards are not appropriate. Track 2 euthanasia is already wreaking havoc on people in very different circumstances than the government initially intended it to target. The safeguards do not work and believing that an expansion of euthanasia is going to be controlled by pre-existing failed safeguards makes absolutely no sense.

Mr. Speaker, in such a sensitive debate, I would like to ask my colleague why it is important to ensure that we use precise language. In Canada, the term used is medical assistance in dying. We have precise terms that we have been using for nearly a decade now. Why is it important to ensure we use the correct language when debating such a sensitive issue? In what way does this also constitute a matter of respect for the people concerned?

Mr. Speaker, I agree that using language is important, which is why I call it euthanasia. MAID is an acronym and a term made to sanitize something that is morally very consequential. I think it was used by the government to take something that is very disturbing to many Canadians and make it sound innocuous. It is not innocuous. It is euthanasia. It is about people's lives being ended. This is serious. We do not need government acronyms in order to talk about this.

Mr. Speaker, there are few debates in Parliament that are more consequential and more deeply impactful than when we are called to debate life-and-death legislation. Issues of this importance require us to look beyond being partisan, and this is not the first time the chamber has had to grapple with such profound moral weight. We just have to look at our history.

I am thinking of capital punishment. A private member's bill was introduced to abolish it in 1914. For decades, in the 1950s, 1960s, 1970s, 1980s and 1990s, parliamentarians in this chamber grappled with that issue. They debated whether deterrence prevented murders, the morality of a state taking a human life, whether life imprisonment was a sufficient punishment and the irreversible possibility of making a mistake. We fast-forward to today. Medical assistance in dying is, without question, one of the most consequential public policy decisions this Parliament has ever made. It is a matter of life and death, literally, and that is precisely why we cannot afford to get this wrong.

When Canada first introduced medical assistance in dying in 2016, Canadians were assured by the government that it would be a carefully controlled, exceptional measure built on very clear limitations and uncompromising safeguards. We were told it was strictly an end-of-life compassionate option for those facing a reasonably foreseeable natural death. That is what we were told, but look at where we are today.

The data tells us a staggering story. In 2024 alone, 16,499 Canadians received MAID. Since its introduction, more than 76,000 Canadians have died through this program. It is approaching 100,000 now, in 2026. In 2024, MAID accounted for approximately 5.1% of all deaths across Canada. This is an extraordinary number. To put this in perspective, let us look across the border at California. It is a jurisdiction with about the same population size as Canada. Medical assistance in dying was legalized in both Canada and California at exactly the same time, yet we can look at the comparison of numbers: in Canada, 76,475 deaths, versus just 5,423 in California. In 2024, as I mentioned, there were 16,499 in this country versus 1,032 in California.

I think about how dramatically our legislation has evolved. In 2021, through Bill C-7, the government expanded eligibility far beyond those whose natural deaths were reasonably foreseeable. We created two distinct tracks, including a track for individuals who are not approaching the end of life. In so doing, Canada became one of the most permissive jurisdictions in the entire world when it came to assisted dying. By removing the requirement of natural death to be reasonably foreseeable, the government extended MAID to people with disabilities and chronic illnesses who were not otherwise dying. This approach is far outside the traditional, globally recognized end-of-life care model.

Mental illness was initially excluded from this expansion, but only temporarily. Ever since, Parliament has repeatedly had to step in to extend that exclusion as a matter of crisis management. Bill C-39 kicked the deadline down the road. Bill C-62 extended it again, to March 17, 2027, a date that we are now quickly approaching.

We must ask ourselves why MAID for mental illness was delayed in the first place. It was delayed because committees heard testimony after testimony from the front lines stating that this was an incredibly dangerous direction to go in. There was substantial, overwhelming agreement among mental health advocates, disability advocates, psychiatric professionals and academic experts. The special joint committee's recommendation was clear, to permanently exclude mental illness as a sole underlying condition for MAID, and Conservatives agree entirely with this.

We believe that someone suffering from depression, PTSD or another severe mental illness should be met with access to treatment, support and hope, not a path to assisted death. Mental illness can be utterly devastating. It distorts how a person sees themselves, how they view their current circumstances and how they perceive the future. However, we know that circumstances can change. Treatment can work. People can recover. People who once saw absolutely no hope can go on to live incredibly meaningful, beautiful lives.

I have shared this before, but it bears repeating. In my early twenties, I went through a clinical depression. It was a very dark period of time in my life. I had suicidal thoughts. Thankfully, I never made any attempts, but in that darkness I received vital support from health care professionals and those closest to me. I came out of it. Today, that dark period is a very distant memory. I feel no pain from it, but at the time I felt utterly incapacitated. With time and support, I recovered. I went on to go to university, become a teacher, an MLA in British Columbia, a member of Parliament, a father and a grandfather. I have lived a full and rich life and I am thankful. If MAID for mental illness had been legal and readily marketed for people like me at that time, how many would have gone that route?

The government itself has recognized these serious concerns, which is why it repeatedly extended the exclusion. However, with the current exclusion set to expire on March 17, 2027, there is an urgent need to act, and Conservatives have acted. The member for Cloverdale—Langley City introduced a private member's bill, Bill C-218, which would have permanently and cleanly excluded mental illness as a sole underlying condition for MAID. What happened? The Liberals voted against it. On October 7, this House had a clear opportunity to advance that protective legislation and the government voted it down. Now, just weeks later, the government has introduced its own legislation, Bill C-41, which we are debating right now as we approach midnight. What has it done? It has taken the exact permanent exclusion for mental illness and attached it to a completely separate, massive and entirely undebated element, the advance request for MAID. Let us call it what it is. The Liberals do not want to subject their new expansion of MAID to the raw public scrutiny that the mental illness expansion faced. The more the expert witnesses, physicians, psychiatrists and professional organizations spoke out about mental illness, the more the general public became concerned. They do not want to go in that direction. By chaining these two issues together in Bill C-41, it is trying to sneak a massive new policy under the radar. I say, shame.

The political dynamic in this House has shifted. Following the by-elections and floor crossings earlier this year, the Liberal government now holds a majority. It no longer needs collaboration with the opposition. It no longer needs to seek multipartisan consensus on matters of life and death. Because of this, it has the raw numbers to pass legislation independently, and it is using that power to ram this through. It is rushing this bill through the House, cutting off the thorough, isolated scrutiny that each one of these profound issues desperately deserves.

Conservatives are deeply concerned with the safeguards in this bill, particularly with the sudden expansion to advance directives. The cold, hard fact is that there is already widespread abuse and inappropriate promotion with our current MAID regime. Time and again, I talk with residents in my community who tell me horror stories about family members having MAID actively promoted and suggested to their loved ones. One of my own staff members was offered MAID three separate times because of the migraines he suffered from a fall a decade ago. Another man told me how his father was offered MAID because of a hip injury. The son had to step in and tell providers that his father needed exercises and stretching, not MAID. He helped his father get the proper rehabilitation and guess what. He is out of the hospital. He is not dead.

Mr. Speaker, in 2016, the adoption of Canada's MAID legislation marked a significant change in Canadian society. It gave people living with an incurable illness and experiencing intolerable suffering an additional option in their end-of-life care: medical assistance in dying.

My colleague cited a number of statistics and shared several anecdotes in his speech, but I would like a clear answer. Is he for or against allowing individuals to make a free and informed choice about MAID based on their own circumstances?

Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to the abuse we are currently seeing in the system, with people being encouraged to pursue medical assistance in dying. Now there is an effort to introduce yet another element. There are a great many concerns that still need to be discussed.

Mr. Speaker, in his speech, my colleague said that he thought it was immoral for a person who is not terminally ill to have access to MAID. However, Bill C-14 was inconsistent with the Carter decision. Ms. Carter and Ms. Taylor were not terminally ill. They were approaching the terminal phase of their illness. Being terminally ill does not mean that death is imminent or that a person is not already experiencing intolerable and irremediable suffering.

The Supreme Court is of the opinion that creating a blanket exclusion for people who are not terminally ill but who are suffering infringes on the right to life because it forces them to cut their life short rather than allowing them to determine when their suffering has become intolerable. What people want is to live as long as possible, up to the limit of what they can tolerate. That is what MAID allows for in cases that are not related to a reasonably foreseeable natural death.
As a legislator, how can my colleague promote a bill that is unconstitutional?

Mr. Speaker, the member is talking about what is already the law. What we are discussing now is whether MAID should be available to people whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness, and there is broad agreement in this House that it should not be. However, the debate primarily focuses on end-of-life decisions for persons with Alzheimer's disease, for example, or other similar health problems.

Mr. Speaker, I am not challenging my colleague's right to his personal convictions. I am challenging his possible intention to put his rights above the rights and autonomy of others. Can my colleague explain to the House the difference between therapeutic obstinacy and the right to die with dignity?
Mr. Speaker, what we are saying is that there needs to be a debate about this. This is not something we should be rushing through. We are talking about life and death.

The Liberals made a lot of mistakes. As a matter of fact, that is the reason they delayed it once, twice and I believe three times. Now they realize that they got it wrong. They got it wrong before, and they are going to get it wrong again.

This is serious. It is very complex. There are a lot of different pieces that we need to look at, not have rushed debates in the middle of the night that have to be done by a certain period. This is not good for Canada. No matter what the member may think, we need to make sure it works.
Mr. Speaker, it is late, but it is never too late to talk about what life is all about.

In fact, death is a fact of life. That is what we are discussing tonight. Let me begin with my conclusion. We have heard our colleagues repeatedly point out that Quebec was ahead of the curve, that it conducted multiparty consultations and that it even took the time to examine each step of the process. Today, we are saying that Quebec is not only ready, but that it also needs the latitude, insofar as the Criminal Code is concerned, to fully implement its legislation.

Here, we began studying medical assistance in dying five years ago, looking in particular at what took place in Quebec. That work yielded a wealth of findings that now allow us to clearly distinguish between two situations: advance requests and individuals who have been suffering from unbearable mental illnesses for decades.

What I am beginning to realize is that we are not going to make it happen. Some people want to divide the bill, others want to have two votes. Basically, I cannot even keep up. There is one thing I do understand, though. Can we take action together and agree that if certain provinces and territories are not ready, that is their business? If we in Quebec are ready, because we have been talking about it for years, then please let us implement what we believe is right for us. This would illustrate that such a sensitive bill was drafted through a collaborative process. I do not think we will achieve that here in the House. We have perfectly legitimate differences of opinion, but when it comes to end-of-life care, human dignity is being set aside when the individual should come first regarding decisions about their own life.

When someone is making a decision for themselves, I would feel very uncomfortable doing or saying anything that might influence that person. It is not up to me to tell them, no, they cannot die, or yes, they can die. It is up to the individual.

I am saying this because I have been through it myself. I am talking about it, but I am certainly not trying to oversimplify things and suggest that the law should be based on my experience. I want that to be clear. I have lived experience. In 2017, my father was diagnosed with ALS. People who were here more than a decade ago knew the MP Mauril Bélanger. ALS is a devastating disease. It causes tremendous suffering. It can reach a point where a person is no longer able to endure that suffering, which in this case is both physical and psychological because the person is trapped in their own body.

In 2017, my father participated in several research studies. At the time, even I, as his young daughter, would tell him that he could not possibly be thinking about death. He told me that death is just part of life. However, after discussing his case with researchers and scientists, he chose to die with his illness rather than from it. In the final stages of ALS, swallowing and breathing become increasingly difficult. The heart does not stop, but people generally end up suffocating. Because my father was eligible for MAID, he chose to die without having to endure that suffering. No one wants their parents to leave them, but he made me understand something.

It was only afterwards that I realized how understandable it is not to want to lose a loved one. It is out of love. What I am hearing in these discussions is, above all, a fear that the person might miss out on something, that there could still be moments of happiness. I could have a colleague tell me that a person with dementia has experienced 24 hours of complete lucidity over the course of three months. Ultimately, it is up to the person who is caring for their loved one. We are unable to come to an agreement about the role of loved ones this evening.

I am thinking back to when my father told me he was going to die from his illness. Of course, there was the possibility of intervention, but no one was ever able to intervene. I experienced it myself. How many times did we have to reaffirm the legitimacy of my father's right to refuse treatment, to ask that he not be allowed to suffer, and to have his end-of-life wishes respected?

He had been trapped in his body for 20 years. He told me one day that he had been using a ventilator, a BiPAP, for eight years, that he never took it off and wore it 24 hours a day, seven days a week. He could not take it anymore. The ventilator had replaced his lungs. I told him it was a natural reaction.

That is what this is all about. Let nature take its course and let us not try to save lives. If we are sick, let us die. That is what I hear, and it troubles me. In my father's case, he lived for eight years with a device that prolonged his life, but on the day he could no longer bear having that machine on his face all the time, we respected his wishes. It may have been that way from the start, eight years earlier, but he would have missed my wedding, he would not have seen my children grow up. Is it not selfish to want more time with our loved one?

Essentially, today we are debating and talking about other people. When we are talking about others, perhaps we should ask the person who is making the choice what they want, particularly in the case of advance requests. That is also what worries me. Some say that people can live a whole other life.

Earlier, I shared an analogy, or rather a story, about a colleague. I asked him what an advance request was. Simply put, sometimes we know somebody for 50, 60 or 90 years, and then they are diagnosed with Alzheimer's. This person gets to say what they will and will not endure. They may not want their personality to change completely. They may not want to have to be fed. They may not want to be confined to a chair because they tend to wander around the building. I suggested a scenario where a person who has been in politics his entire life undergoes a 180-degree personality change, causing him to strip off his clothes and flirt with everyone he encounters. If this person acted happy, people would see it in a positive light. They would think he had certain wishes that he expressed when he still had the capacity to choose. Now that he no longer has the capacity to say that this is not the end of life he wanted, however, his wishes are no longer valid. That is what I am having a hard time understanding.

As long as our discussions do not focus strictly on ethics and the protection of each individual's right to choose, simply saying that we are going to hold more meetings and conduct more analyses will only prolong the debate.
We will never see the end of it in the House.
What I want is for every individual to be able to make their own decisions about how their life ends.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to this debate at length. I think my hon. colleague knows that my record stands in the House as one fighting against suicide. As I said in my speech and my comments, we are seeing a number of concerns already with the legislation as it stands. The medical community, those who have to deliver those lethal doses, those end-of-life medications, have concerns. We are asking on this side if, perhaps, this should be studied a little bit more, if we should hear from those professionals, because none of us in the House are doing that. There is nothing to prepare any of us to be able to vote on this. I do not think there has been enough study of this bill.
I think it is out of compassion that we are pushing back and fighting for those who are perhaps considering this.

Mr. Speaker, I did not have time to expand on prevention and the potential to save lives. Many of my colleagues have said that, when it comes to mental health in particular, we should start by putting all our efforts and energy into the service delivery networks. Yes, there are shortcomings.

Imagine a loved one saying that they are going through an unbearable situation and they are going to request MAID. That person is sending a cry for help in the face of suffering. I am very sensitive to the issue of suicide. It may sound crazy to say, but if the person makes that request, rather than committing an irreversible act, that is, killing themselves, they have a better chance of getting through the crisis. That person will be cared for, because they will obviously not be eligible for MAID, and they will not fall through the cracks.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague gave a great presentation on the importance of respecting the wishes of others. It should be perfectly clear that this is a choice, not an obligation. Every individual decides whether medical assistance in dying is right for them or not.

We have heard all sorts of things tonight. I would like my colleague to elaborate on what we have heard, especially the fact that MAID is still a choice and that strict guidelines are in place. It is not automatic. A person who requests MAID does not automatically get it.
I would like my colleague to tell us more about that, in light of what we have heard during this evening's debate.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to clear something up. If I am diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease, I will not directly receive MAID. If I do not want it and never will, I will never receive it. I am under no obligation. If I decide today that I want MAID, but I change my mind tomorrow, my most recent decision takes precedence. What is there to be afraid of?
Does my colleague agree that this bill could be split? We could move ahead on advance requests, and the committee could take some time to explore the mental health component a little more.

Mr. Speaker, my question is simple. We heard that there was a lack of data and that there was no basis for it. Can my colleague, a member from Quebec, give us more details about the data and the serious approach undertaken by the Select Committee on Dying with Dignity? A report was published on this issue in Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I am so proud of that. Canada should take inspiration from the approach taken by the Quebec National Assembly. If that is too complicated, Canada should either let us be or let us leave, in which case we will take care of our own affairs.

Mr. Speaker, it has been said before, and I said it in the original debate in 2016, that nothing in our lifetime prepares a member of Parliament to vote on such a consequential piece of legislation. There really is not. It truly is life or death. This legislation, as it stands today, raises serious questions about how Canada approaches medical assistance in dying, how we protect vulnerable people and what responsibilities the government has to Canadians who are suffering.

From the moment I landed as a member of Parliament, I have fought every day for those who serve our country and our community and for those who are struggling and suffering silently. For over 1,000 days, I pushed the previous government to launch a national suicide hotline, 988. I believe life is so precious that we should be doing everything to fight for every breath we have in us.

Since 2016, when I really struggled with that vote, I have contacted my pastor a number of times. It went against everything in my faith, in my fibre, everything that I had fought for in the 30 years leading up to my being elected as a member of Parliament. How could I vote with that? Since 2016, I have spoken with probably hundreds if not thousands of Canadians who had loved ones who suffered from cancer or ALS and chose MAID.

In December 2023, my mother, from whom I was estranged, was diagnosed with acute leukemia. It was going to attack her brain. It was a painful disease. She chose MAID, and she set a death date. Whatever background we had, I put it aside and sat by her bedside for probably about four months as we marched toward that death date. I was tasked with making her a mixtape, as a matter of fact, to play on that day.

Imagine my surprise and my brother's surprise, as we had mentally prepared for that day, regardless of what our background was with our mother, when we arrived to be told by the doctors that when they were preparing her, she said no. We were frustrated because we knew what was lying ahead for my mom, but that was her choice. We met with the doctors, the medical team, the MAID team, and they said they could not in good conscience administer the final dose of the medication to end her life. That is my story, so I understand where families are.

I am troubled by the number of Canadians, such as veterans, who are being offered MAID because they are struggling with PTSD or a mental illness. One in 10 Canadians knows someone who has been offered MAID. Approximately 13 Canadians die by suicide every day. Approximately 100,000 Canadians attempt suicide every year. That is 250 per day. About 20,0000 Canadians are hospitalized every year for self-harm. The MAID numbers are staggering. We are approaching 100,000 Canadians who have chosen to die by MAID. We are seeing commercials for end of life on TV and on social media.

I sat with a veteran who was offered MAID. He phoned Veterans Affairs and was offered MAID. Not once, not twice, but three times he was asked if he had considered MAID. I have sat with people who have gone to their doctor for injuries that were causing them unbelievable pain.

Our concern is with advance directives, and experts in the medical community have these same concerns. We are asking to split the bill to deal with mental illness and the advance directive separately to give us time to get this as close to right as possible, to put those further safeguards in place.

I come at this with the purest of intentions. There was a time when I was consumed with death. It was for about five years. My best friend had died by suicide, and I did not see a way forward. My childhood had been filled with dysfunction and abuse. I was struggling, and I attempted suicide numerous times. I have thought about this, and if MAID had been available at that time, I would have taken it.

Then I think about all the things I would have missed. Here I am so many years later, 38 years later, and I love life. I am so thankful I am here. I think of watching my four beautiful children grow up to be amazing adults; of my grandchildren, Ren and Meyer; and of finding the love of my life just at the end of that period of darkness.

As Conservatives, we believe that we have to do everything in our power to offer opportunities for getting better, getting the supports people need. We believe in hope. We are in a mental health crisis and an addiction crisis in this country, yet time and again we hear empty promises from the other side. Tomorrow is budget day, and I hope there will be supports in place for mental health. We now spend more money in servicing our debt than we do in health care transfers. The health care transfers that go to our provinces for mental health are pennies on the dollar. We do not view mental health in parity with physical health. If we did that, as a country, we would be healthier and happier, and we would see the numbers go further down.

This debate requires Parliament to think carefully about what kind of country we want to be. We must approach suffering people with compassion, respect and dignity, but compassion cannot simply mean offering another option at the end of someone's suffering. It must mean doing everything we reasonably can to help that person live, to provide treatment, to offer support and to ensure that they are not left alone.

On the question of MAID for mental illness, we are clear that we do not support it. I do not support it. We do not believe it should ever be permitted where mental illness is the sole underlying medical condition. Mental illness should be met with treatment, care and hope.

Canadians deserve a health care system that gives them a genuine opportunity to recover and a government that works to make care accessible. I truly understand that there are Canadians who are suffering with unbelievable illnesses for whom MAID is perhaps the right choice for them, but as parliamentarians, we must do everything in our power to make sure those safeguards are in place as we move this legislation forward.

Mr. Speaker, in a debate as sensitive as the one surrounding medical assistance in dying, I urge members to be thorough, to raise the standard of the debate and to ensure that we do not resort to oversimplifications that could hinder the public's understanding of the discussions taking place this evening.

At one point in my colleague's speech, he seemed to draw a parallel between suicide and medical assistance in dying, even though we know these are two fundamentally different things. Medical assistance in dying is an option available to people living with incurable illnesses that cause significant suffering.

There was also a point where my colleague spoke of commercial aspects related to medical assistance in dying. I must say I did not really understand that part. I believe we must be rigorous and ensure that we do not recount anecdotes or make false equivalencies that could hinder understanding of the debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to really dignify that with an answer. The member essentially said I have dumbed down this debate. I am going to keep my words parliamentary and not dignify that stupid statement with an answer.
An hon. member: Oh, oh!
I am going to deal with that. I understand what the point of order is.
That was very much on the verge of being unparliamentary. It did not imply the member was that, so it did not cross that line, but we should be trying to keep our comments above board.
Questions and comments, the hon. member for Montcalm.

Mr. Speaker, I served on the Standing Committee on Health with my colleague. I am very familiar with, and deeply appreciative of, his personal commitment and all the efforts he makes to support suicide prevention. I think it is very generous of him to share these personal stories during tonight's debate. I wanted to reassure him.

As for eligibility and MAID for mental illness, I do not know what makes him say that he would have been eligible. I do not think he would have been. The proof is that he is here and that suicidality is reversible. It is only in a situation of irreversibility that we begin to assess the issue.

Suicidality is reversible and is not inevitable. The experts' report helped establish guidelines, as did the standards of practice established by the Canadian association of providers. I urge my colleague to review these guidelines. He will see that we are not allowing people who are suicidal to access MAID.
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate our hon. colleague. I have a great deal of respect for our colleague all the way down at the far end there.

My comment is only that if this was available to those who are struggling with mental illness, again, we would have to make sure that all those safeguards were in place. I would have likely done whatever I could to access this at that time.

Mr. Speaker, I want to really thank my colleague for a profound and thoughtful speech, for sharing the story about his mother as an example of somebody who changed their mind, who thought they would want one thing and then, in a moment, wanted something else.
